====================================================================================================

Indonesia looks to mosque loudspeakers to double as earthquake warning systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:29:31 UTC
09:29:31 KST

Scientists working on an early warning system in earthquake-prone Indonesia have taken the spiritual path to designing a network of alarms that will reach even the remotest communities: they hope to use mosques to save lives.
A five-year trial is assessing whether the ubiquitous loudspeakers used to broadcast the call to prayer can double up as warning klaxons for earthquakes.
“Every community has a mosque,” says project lead Dr Inoue Hiroshi, speaking to the Guardian from Indonesia. The pilot scheme was the brainchild of the Japanese disaster scientist, who says he came up with the idea nearly two decades ago while researching deadly quakes in Sumatra, Indonesia.
Inoue, of the Disaster Prevention Research Institute at Kyoto University in Japan, is working with the Indonesian government to assess whether the country could implement an early warning system similar to Japan’s.
“I thought if Indonesia had the same service and people received the warning before the shaking came, then many people among those few hundred wouldn’t have died,” he says of a devastating 2009 quake in western Sumatra which killed at least 1,000 people.
Indonesia’s disaster agency has to grapple with huge distances and hard-to-reach territories, but it has the benefit of an already established network of regularly serviced loudspeakers, something many other countries do not.
With the largest population of Muslims worldwide, Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques, which broadcast the call to pray five times a day. The pilot scheme has already hooked up several mosques to its seismic sensor network.
For an earthquake early warning system to save lives, there are two critical factors – it needs a network of alarms, and they need to work. “The advantage of a mosque speaker is that they’re existing and well maintained,” says Inoue. “For any disaster infrastructure, maintenance is the big challenge … but the mosque speaker is maintained by the people”.
Many modern disaster preparedness strategies work using mobile phones, although those are vulnerable because earthquakes can disrupt communication infrastructure.
The country has a tsunami early warning system dating back to 2008, but the earthquake initiative could be a “breakthrough”, says Andi Eka Sakya, senior researcher at the Indonesian government-affiliated National Research and Innovation Agency and the Indonesian head of the joint research team.
While tsunamis affect coastal areas and can be predicted in minutes or even hours, earthquake waves move through the ground at incredible speeds, and Sakya says a village 50km from the epicentre could have only five to 10 seconds to respond.
“It’s still a prototype, and they don’t issue warnings to the public yet,” he says. “The ultimate goal is actually to alert the people so that they can respond as early as possible.”
The project, which runs until 2030, is also looking at installing alarm systems in school loudspeakers and using radio and television transmissions.
Indonesia and Japan both lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire and are frequently affected by earthquakes. Researchers are looking at how behaviours and survival strategies differ between Japan and Indonesia.
In Japan, official disaster guidelines focus on the widely used “drop and cover” strategy – taking immediate shelter, for example, under a table and staying indoors.
In contrast, low-rise homes in some developing countries like Indonesia are frequently built from unreinforced masonry that is highly vulnerable to collapsing, and so people have survived by escaping outside. In some cases, two-storey buildings in Indonesia have seen the first floor crushed and the second floor remain relatively intact.
“The way people react is they quickly escape out of the room,” says Inoue. “They know how to survive.”
Because standard international advice does not always suit fragile buildings, project researchers are conducting simulations and human experiments to establish guidelines grounded in science. “This is actually one of the main research topics,” says Inoue.
Other countries in the Muslim world have looked at similar systems. When the United Arab Emirates government planned to start its Barakah nuclear power plant, an official on the project said mosque loudspeakers would be part of a broader network of alarms in the event of a radiation leak.
A far more extensive mosque loudspeaker project is going on in Uzbekistan, where the Ministry of Emergency Situations announced a pilot project this year for devices to be installed in 272 mosques. The alarms would alert people to floods, mudflows, landslides and avalanches.
“The selection of mosques is not incidental,” the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), which partnered in the initiative, said in a statement. “They are traditionally perceived as authoritative social institutions with significant influence on local communities.”

Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in a province led by Imran Khan’s PTI party and suspended its government, a move a party spokesperson described as “more of a coup disguised as emergency”.
President Asif Ali Zardari declared the emergency in the north-western Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Sunday, after the federal government said authorities there had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan.
The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in the province intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan’s release.
Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters were detained before the planned march, in what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years.
Khan’s aide and PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari called the government’s move “more of a coup disguised as emergency,” adding that it risked inciting more bloodshed and instability and was intended to stop the protest.
Pakistan’s constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency, and the law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months.
Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed. The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province.
The federal government and the military accuse PTI of failing to curb militants. The party rejects the charge and says Islamabad has not provided the funding and equipment it needs.
Restrictions have been placed on the movements of Sohail Afridi, who had previously been in charge of the province, one of his close aides told Reuters.
Maulana Fazlur Rehman, leader of the JUI-F political party and engaged by the government to mediate with PTI, also condemned the move. “Imposition of emergency is an ambush on democracy,” he told a news conference in Islamabad.
In Islamabad, the government has deployed tens of thousands of security forces and lined roads with containers ready to block roads, to bar protesters from reaching parliament.
Candidates backed by Khan’s party won the most seats in the 2024 election but formed a government only in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Supporters of the 74-year-old former cricket star say the military rigged the vote against him, which the military denies.
Cases against Khan range from concerns over state gifts to instigating violence and an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one conviction have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.
President Zardari declared the emergency on the advice of the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, after a cabinet decision, the president’s office said.
Sharif told the cabinet that security forces and citizens had been under attack for two years. “We can’t just act as a silent spectator.”
Islamabad also accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who launch attacks inside Pakistan, and says PTI has sympathised with the Taliban in Kabul and its domestic affiliates. Both deny the charge.

PANAMA CITY BEACH, Florida – The big snakes had been coiled into trash cans. The male billy goats were holed up in the rabbit exhibit.
But it was the flamingos of ZooWorld in Panama City Beach, in the US state of Florida, who would ultimately become overnight celebrities after a video posted on social media during Hurricane Isaias made the rounds. It has been viewed nearly 2 million times.
The 30 flamingos, honking and frolicking, were sheltering in a bathroom, bumbling between the sink and the stalls, shedding pink feathers onto a grippy floor mat.
The crew included Mr. Sparklepants, aged 10, the largest and most dominant of the flock. Scuttle and Mango Shrimproll, both 3, who had been raised by a ZooWorld zookeeper since they were eggs, were also there.
The cramped quarters for the pink birds were necessary to protect them from ferocious winds that threatened the enclosure where they normally sleep. So the flock of flamingos was ushered into the bathroom, whose block walls served as something of a fortress.
Before Isaias made landfall on Oct 9, Kylie Appleton, the senior zookeeper, took a video, and then the team boarded up the door.
Erika Newell, the zoo’s chief operating officer, spent the night on Oct 9 in an apartment on the grounds, waking up every hour as the storm lashed the Gulf Coast to check on all the animals.
Crammed as they were, the flamingos were in the perfect spot, she said. The tight space calmed them down, much like a snug garment might calm a dog. NYTIMES

Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:14:46 UTC
09:14:46 KST

Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status
Felipe VI’s first visit to Ceuta and Melilla as king brings Spain’s territorial dispute with Morocco back into focus.
Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia are due to visit Ceuta on October 13 and Melilla the following day, in Felipe’s first visit to either city as king since he ascended the throne in 2014.
The trip comes after a major migration crisis at the Ceuta border in July and as the long-running dispute between Spain and Morocco over the two cities on the North African coast remains unresolved.
Spain considers Ceuta and Melilla part of its territory, while Morocco regards both cities and several smaller Spanish-held territories in North Africa as part of its own territory.
The city that sits on the southern side of the Strait of Gibraltar also has different names in Spanish and Arabic.
In Spain, it is Ceuta. In Arabic, it is Sabta, commonly written as Sebta in Latin script.
So why does the same city have two names? And how did a city on the North African coast come under Spanish sovereignty?
Where does the name Ceuta come from?
The name is much older than either modern Spain or Morocco.
The city was known as Sabta in Arabic. Spain’s Ministry of Culture identifies Sabta with present-day Ceuta and traces its history through successive periods of Idrisid, Umayyad, Taifa, Almoravid, Almohad and Marinid rule.
The Spanish form, Ceuta, developed from earlier forms of the name. Sabta and Ceuta are different linguistic forms of the same city.
Who controlled Ceuta before Spain?
Ceuta passed through several political and dynastic systems in the Maghreb and al-Andalus.
Under the Idrisid dynasty, the city was in the hands of the Banu Isam before being taken by the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Rahman III in 931, bringing it into the political sphere of al-Andalus.
In the 11th century, Ceuta became linked to the Taifa of Malaga. It later came under the Almoravids and Almohads. From the beginning of the 14th century, it became part of the Marinid sphere with periods when other local dynasties held power.
By the early 15th century, Ceuta was under Muslim rule.
That changed in 1415.
How did Ceuta become Portuguese?
On August 21, 1415, Portuguese forces led by King John I captured Ceuta.
The Portuguese conquest brought an end to more than seven centuries of Muslim rule in Ceuta. Ceuta’s own cultural heritage authority dates Muslim rule from 709 to the Portuguese conquest in 1415.
Ceuta remained Portuguese for more than two centuries.
Portugal and Spain were then ruled by the same monarchy from 1580 to 1640. When Portugal restored its independence in 1640, Ceuta remained under the Spanish monarchy rather than returning to Portuguese rule.
The 1668 Treaty of Lisbon, which formally recognised Portuguese independence, left Ceuta in Spanish hands.
That is how Ceuta came under Spanish sovereignty.
Why does Morocco claim Ceuta?
Morocco’s argument is rooted in the city’s history and geography.
Ceuta lies on the North African coast, surrounded by Morocco on its landward side. Morocco has claimed Ceuta and Melilla since gaining independence in 1956 and regards the two cities as occupied Moroccan territories.
Spain takes the opposite position.
Under Spanish law, Ceuta is an autonomous city. Its Statute of Autonomy describes Ceuta as an integral part of the Spanish nation and gives the city its own system of self-government.
The dispute, therefore, is not about who administers Ceuta. Spain does. It is about sovereignty.
Morocco says Ceuta should form part of Moroccan territory. Spain says its sovereignty over the city is established and Ceuta is part of Spain.
Neither side has accepted the other’s position.
Why doesn’t history settle the dispute?
Because the two sides interpret that history differently.
Morocco points to Ceuta’s long history within Muslim political systems in the Maghreb and its location on the North African coast. Spain points to centuries of Portuguese and Spanish control and to Ceuta’s present constitutional status as part of Spain.
The historical record does not provide a simple answer to a modern sovereignty dispute. The political systems that ruled Ceuta before 1415 were not nation-states with today’s borders, and the city’s current status is based on centuries of subsequent Portuguese and Spanish rule.
Morocco’s territorial claim dates from the period after independence in 1956, but Spain has continued to exercise sovereignty over Ceuta.
Why does Morocco call it Sebta?
Sebta, or Sabta, is the Arabic name for Ceuta and predates the modern sovereignty dispute.
In Morocco, Sebta is the Arabic name used for the city while Ceuta is the established Spanish form.
The choice of name can have political resonance because Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty over the city. But using Sebta is not automatically a political statement. It is also simply the Arabic name.
What about Melilla?
Melilla’s history is different from Ceuta’s.
Spanish forces took control of Melilla in 1497 when it was incorporated into the Crown of Castile.
Ceuta, by contrast, was first Portuguese before remaining under the Spanish monarchy after Portugal regained its independence.
Today, both cities are Spanish autonomous cities, and Morocco claims sovereignty over both.
Why does Ceuta still matter?
Ceuta’s importance today goes beyond its size.
Ceuta is considered part of Spain, but it is not included in the European Union customs territory. Its border with Morocco is also an external border of the Schengen area.
That has made Ceuta a focal point for migration and border policy as well as a recurring issue in relations between Madrid and Rabat.
The issue returned sharply to the headlines on July 30 when more than 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco, according to the Reuters news agency.
Now Felipe’s planned visits to Ceuta and Melilla are putting the two disputed cities back in the spotlight.

Izzi Batt-Doyle breaks Australian women's marathon record after finishing sixth in Chicago race
In short:
Adelaide runner Izzi Batt-Doyle lowered her own personal best by more than two minutes, breaking the Australian women's marathon record in Chicago.
Her time of 2:20:38 took 46 seconds off the existing record, held by Jess Stenson.
Batt-Doyle, who was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks, finished sixth in the women's race at the Chicago Marathon behind winner Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia.
Adelaide's Izzi Batt-Doyle is Australia's new marathon queen after breaking the national record with a stunning run at the year's penultimate major, the Chicago Marathon.
Batt-Doyle ran a time of 2:20:38 to take 46 seconds off the mark set by fellow South Australian Jess Stenson in Valencia in December.
It also lowered the 31-year-old's own personal best by two minutes and 21 seconds.
"I'm very, very happy. I feel a sense of relief, because it's something I really felt I could achieve and it's been on my mind the past couple of years," Batt-Doyle said.
"I'm really proud I could achieve it today and I'm so happy."
Batt-Doyle was sixth overall in the women's race, which was won by defending champion Hawi Feysa of Ethiopia in 2:13:33.
"The field here is so great, but smaller on the professional side," Batt-Doyle said.
"You don't have masses of people in groups."
Batt-Doyle was paced by her fiancé Riley Cocks.
"[We were] isolated the whole race," she said.
"The gun went off and second kilometre it was just the two of us, because we were running between groups.
"I spent most of the race trusting our plan and the pacing strategy we had hoped to run the first half in, and hope that I would feel strong in the second half."
Batt-Doyle's race was a model of control, with her splits barely moving. Every 5km block landed between 16:36 and 16:47, holding her at about 3:19 to 3:21 per kilometre from the opening kilometres to the final stretch.
She went through halfway in 1:10:29 and then ran the second half in about 1:10:09, giving her a 20-second negative split.
"We went through halfway in under the time needed to run 2:21, but I wasn't sure because I felt like I was slowing in the second half as it was warmer, and just the general fatigue of the marathon," Batt-Doyle said.
"It was quite warm and we knew going into this week that it was going to be a bit warmer than ideal marathon conditions, but we did what we could do to prepare for that.
"That's hydrating a lot beforehand, and every opportunity that there were water cups I was splashing three or four water cups to keep cool."
But Batt-Doyle didn't fade in the conditions, with her quickest 5km split of 16:36 coming between 35km and 40km. She covered the last 2.2km at about 3:14 per kilometre, when she started to sense the record was hers.
"There is a small hill about 400 to go, and then you turn into the last 150 metres, and I saw the clock and that's when I really started celebrating," she said.
"It was quite emotional. You can think you can do it and hope you can do it, and be on pace to do it, but there is so much that can happen in the last 5 kilometres, or last 1 kilometre or even the last 400 metres.
"People can cramp and have all sorts of things happen. I feel you can't really celebrate or have that sense of finish line relief until you actually get there."
Batt-Doyle said she was proud to join the list of previous Australian record-holders that included Stenson, Sinead Diver and Benita Willis.
"I think it's really validating for the hard work I've put in and it feels really special to be part of history, because there have been some fantastic runners before me, and fantastic runners to come," she said.
"I really feel honoured, that sums it up. To be in that class of athletes. I'm really proud of that."
Kenya's Amos Kipruto won the men's race in 2:01:09.

German opposition demands Trump-style diesel deal with Russia

German opposition demands Trump-style diesel deal with Russia
Two German opposition parties have called for restoring economic ties with Russia following US President Donald Trump’s example in striking a diesel deal with Moscow, challenging Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s sanctions policy as soaring fuel prices put further pressure on Europe’s largest economy.
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which together command a majority in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt’s parliament, are preparing a joint resolution demanding an end to anti-Russia sanctions and financial support for Kiev amid growing frustration over Berlin’s foreign policy and its economic consequences.
“Germany also needs a diesel deal with Russia,” Claudia Wittig, deputy leader of the BSW parliamentary group, said, according to German media.
Wittig described fuel prices at German filling stations as “a scandal,” arguing that sanctions against Moscow had “failed across the board” and were primarily hurting Germany itself. She insisted that Berlin should go further than a one-off fuel agreement and resume regular imports of Russian oil and gas to help rescue German industry.
“We need policies that think more about Köthen than Kiev,” Wittig said earlier, referring to a German town in Saxony-Anhalt. “We can no longer afford this war.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed Trump’s deal with Moscow, accusing Merz of undermining Germany’s economy with sanctions and expensive liquefied natural gas imports.
“That’s how it’s done!” she wrote on X on Saturday. “While Merz ruins Germany with sanctions and expensive LNG, Trump practices realpolitik. German interests instead of escalation!”
The initiative comes after Trump reached a surprise agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to ease a global diesel shortage. Washington subsequently suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports, allowing Moscow to release hundreds of thousands of tons of fuel onto international markets.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Vladimir Zelensky for exacerbating the global energy crisis by targeting Russian oil refineries despite Washington’s warnings. On Saturday, he suggested that Ukrainians should replace their leader, accusing Zelensky of rejecting numerous opportunities to settle the conflict.
The joint resolution is scheduled for a vote in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament in Magdeburg on October 14. AfD and BSW hold a combined majority following September’s regional elections, although the state legislature has no authority to lift federal or EU sanctions against Russia. The initiative also marks a further breach of Germany’s longstanding political “firewall” against the AfD, which mainstream parties have sought to exclude from power despite its growing electoral support.
Merz’s government flatly rejected any prospects of easing its anti-Russia stance and vowed to pursue even more sanctions against Moscow. Government spokesman Stefan Kornelius insisted on Saturday that Berlin’s support for Kiev remained “unwavering.” Meanwhile, Green Party co-leader Franziska Brantner blasted Trump’s agreement with Putin as the height of “unscrupulousness.”
The chancellor, whose popularity has sunk so low that he faces calls to resign from within his own party, has faced mounting criticism over the impact of his policies on Germany. Wagenknecht previously accused him of turning German citizens into “cash cows for Ukraine.” Moscow has likewise accused Merz of acting more like a “Ukrainian chancellor” than a German leader.

Hong Kong must ease listing rules to attract more angel funds and start-ups: HKEIA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-12
00:00:16 UTC

Hong Kong must ease listing rules to attract more angel funds and start-ups: HKEIA
Hong Kong could learn from the US market, where streamlined regulations foster a thriving ecosystem of angel funds and start-ups, an industry body says
Hong Kong would need to ease its listing rules and transaction requirements to attract more angel funds and become a hub for start-ups to go global, according to a leading industry body in the city.
The city has only around 100 active angel funds – private investment vehicles targeting very early-stage innovative enterprises. This was far fewer than Shenzhen, which had about 400 such institutions, according to Samson Tam Wai-ho, honorary chairman of the Hong Kong Electronic Industries Association (HKEIA).
Besides Shenzhen, Shanghai and the United States also had many active angel funds, helping them become start-up hubs, Tam told the South China Morning Post in an interview.
“Lack of angel funds and early-stage investors for start-ups is the weakest part of the capital market ecosystem in Hong Kong for us to attract start-up founders to come here,” Tam said.

How shadow banking feeds Myanmar while starving its military
Myanmar’s exiles and migrants rely on informal currency swaps to fund their families while starving the military regime
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
On a recent Friday night in a Bangkok dive bar, a group of young Myanmar exiles sang softly along to a mournful ballad played on an acoustic guitar.
None among the crowd had any plans to leave, either for their homeland or home for bed. They fled war, a broken economy and forced conscription into a military that seized power in the 2021 coup.
While their future in Thailand is uncertain, their ties to home are kept alive by the hard currency they send back each month to parents and siblings left behind in devastated village economies.
Aung*, a 31-year-old from the government-controlled Bago region, used to work at a state-owned bank. But since fleeing Myanmar he has relied on a shadow banking system to bypass state-sanctioned remittance channels that take a hefty cut.
That means most of the 3,000 to 5,000 baht (US$90-US$150) he sends home every month reaches his mother and sister.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Sunday sought responses of Union home secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi police commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi metro rail chief D Thara to a contempt petition for prima facie violating the court's Oct 9 order against complete shutdown of metro and train services in Delhi on Saturday to thwart CJP's protest seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. The court also said lawyers, journalists, and other professionals should not be hindered in performing their duties "in any manner whatsoever".On the ground, nearly 700 people were detained (police claimed 400), many far away from protest zones, while barricading and traffic curbs remained on the roads much like Saturday. Protesters changed strategy, staging flash protests in small numbers at short notice. Most of the action was in and around CP as small groups of protesters kept trickling in. They were detained.Around 2.30pm, All India Student Association members, including president Neha Bora, started a protest near RK Ashram Marg metro station. As detentions began, Bora and a few others broke away and ran towards CP, where they continued to protest before being detained. Around 7pm, Students Federation of India members gathered at CP to hold a women's tiranga march against alleged police excesses, especially against women protesters.
They were detained and taken away in buses. "How can they detain women at 7pm in the evening?" SFI general secretary Srijan Bhattacharya said.The widespread detentions - 7,000 estimated Saturday - figured prominently in arguments by the lawyers at SC's unusual holiday hearing on Sunday. Following the submissions, a bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said, "...we are of the opinion that the petitioners have made out a prima facie case. Accordingly, we issue notice upon the alleged contemnors". It asked them to file their responses by Oct 13.Normalise internet connectivity, ensure free movement in city: SCWe understand the gargantuan magnitude of detentions. We will have to seek a response from govt," the bench said after hearing the petitioners, who included advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, CPM MP M A Baby, RJD MP Manoj Jha and lawyer intervenors like Shadan Farasat, who was detained along with other advocates outside SC on Saturday.The bench asked for normalisation of internet connectivity and prohibition of "illegal" detentions, especially of those who gather for peaceful protest away from areas where prohibitory orders are in force. "There shall be no illegal detentions, particularly in cases of peaceful unarmed assemblage of people beyond the area where prohibitory orders under Sec 163 of BNS are in force," it said.On Oct 9, SC had restrained authorities from resorting to blanket closure of metro stations, though it said operations could be regulated depending on the situation. The order came after DMRC said 57 stations would be shut; that number was later revised to 45.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta disputed allegations of violation of the Oct 9 order and said Delhi Metro was functioning normally, though 45 out of 303 stations were closed to maintain law and order. He refuted the allegation that metro stations were closed, saying that "all metro stations are open since 10pm Saturday, trains are operating normally and internet connection has been restored".SC also issued directions to ensure free movement in the city subject to law and order situation/traffic regulations and that installing barricades shall be reviewed forthwith to ensure free movement subject to law and order and traffic requirements. "Lawyers, journalists and other professionals shall not be hindered in discharge of their professional duties in any manner whatsoever," SC said, and also directed withdrawal of prohibitory orders around SC and courts to facilitate free access to litigants and lawyers.Over 100 lawyers led by senior advocate and MP Kapil Sibal slammed the police brutalities on protesters, and accused authorities of continuing with the shutdown of metro and train services in complete disregard of the SC order and of illegal detention of protesters even in areas where the prohibitory orders were not in force.Sibal argued that internet shutdown was a blow to fundamental right to free speech and flagged detention of lawyers who participated in the protest. Senior advocate Farasat, who was detained, informed SC he was manhandled and bundled into a police vehicle. Senior advocate and TMC MP Menaka Guruswamy termed the entire episode as "undeclared emergency" worse than what Indira Gandhi had imposed (in 1975).When Sibal thanked the bench for holding court on Sunday because of the extraordinary turn of events, Justice Bagchi said, "We are always at the service of the nation." Later, Justice Bagchi said, "We know things have deeply affected you (the lawyers) and we do not want to trivialise anything."The bench issued notice to Centre and Delhi Police on a habeas corpus petition questioning detention of TMC politicians Mamata Banerjee, Derek O'Brien and Dola Sen. Solicitor general Mehta said the petition has become infructuous as the detained leaders were released last evening.
As the pro-protest petitioners backed by a team of senior advocates - K K Venugopal, N Hariharan, Shoeb Alam, Arundhati Katju, G Sankaranarayanan, Sanjay Hegde - made a concerted attempt to corner police and Centre by flagging police action, senior advocate Kirti Uppal struck a discordant note by arguing that lawyers should not be stepping into shoes of their political affiliation."I was told that a lawyer's job is inside the courts and not on the streets," he said. The pro-protester lawyers inside the courtroom shouted 'shame, shame' to silence him. The bench asked the lawyers to maintain decorum of the courtroom and maintain silence.

Pennsylvania shooter who killed eight was a grandfather, says slain child’s dad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
23:48:23 UTC
08:48:23 KST

The man who killed eight people, before turning the gun on himself, in a mass shooting in a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday was a grandfather who had not shown signs that he was capable of such violence, according to people who knew the shooter.
A man whose toddler was among those killed said on Sunday that the man never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary, the Associated Press reports.
“I think that was a front for him,” said Julius Windham during a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting. Windham’s one-year-old daughter, Amarianna; her pregnant mother; and the woman’s five-year-old son and unborn baby were among the victims.
“Him every day, him smiling and being just – you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said.
The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but the Erie police chief, Rick Lorah, said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either.
Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 pm on Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the slain woman and children and the words “Forever in my heart”.
“Words can’t even explain what I’m going through right now,” Windham said. “But I gotta be strong for my community, you know what I’m saying? My family, my daughters, my sons, everybody.”
“We don’t want that dark memory to be what defines their lives in this world,” a family friend told Cleveland 19 News. “How do you even fathom something like this? How will you go home and tell your kids: ‘Hey, your mom, your siblings, your uncles and everybody else just got murdered by your grandpa?’”
Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two “distressed” women arrived and began pounding on the door, Lorah said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.
Responding officers found the two women dead outside. After deploying a drone and robot, they went inside and found the bodies of the five-year-old boy and one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.
“Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home,” the chief said at a news conference.
“But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole,” he said.
Erie is about 120 miles (190km) north of Pittsburgh.
Lorah declined to discuss motive but suggested mental health could be a factor. He said investigators would talk to relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.
“They knew something was going on at that house,” Lorah said. “We have to figure out what that is.”
Nicole and Debra Eller, whose best friend was among the victims, told the Associated Press they have known the family for more than 30 years. Nicole Eller said the shooter “was a good guy, and then he started going downhill with everything”.
“They were a lovely family. Who would have thought this would ever happen?” Debra Eller said. “Oh my gosh, this is so upsetting. This should have never happened to her or the kids or anybody. His grandchildren, his kids, how can you do that?”
The Erie shooting was reminiscent of a 1982 massacre in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, in which a man killed 13 people, including five of his own children.
At a news conference on Saturday, Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin, addressed a portion of her remarks directly to the victims’ families.
“I am so deeply sorry,” Devlin said. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier ... Our entire community is with you, we’re grieving with you. And we are here to support you.”
“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community,” said Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, in a post on X on Saturday.

Eisenkot leads Netanyahu in Israeli PM poll as coalition falls short of majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
23:39:21 UTC
08:39:21 KST

Former Israeli army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot has overtaken Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a public opinion poll on who is best suited to lead the country, while Netanyahu's right-wing coalition remains short of the parliamentary majority needed to govern.
The poll, broadcast by Israeli public television network KAN, projected 22 seats for Eisenkot's Yashar party in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 20 seats for Netanyahu's Likud—down one seat from the previous week's survey—ahead of national elections scheduled for October 27.
In head-to-head suitability, Eisenkot secured 43 percent backing against 38 percent for Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's broader right-wing and religious bloc gained two seats to 53, leaving the incumbent prime minister eight mandates short of the 61-seat majority needed to build a viable governing coalition.
Parliamentary arithmetic
Eisenkot's opposing bloc was projected to secure 50 seats, while the remaining 17 seats were distributed among parties classified outside both political camps.
Arab factions were projected to take 13 seats collectively, eight for the Joint List and five for Mansour Abbas's United Arab List (Ra'am).
Within Netanyahu's coalition, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Jewish Power secured nine seats, United Torah Judaism eight, Shas seven, and the Religious Zionism–Zehut alliance five.
Amcha Yisrael, headed by former brigadier general Ofer Winter, cleared the electoral threshold with four seats after previously failing to do so.
The findings underline entrenched political gridlock, indicating that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition camp can form an independent government without reaching across factional divides.
The survey also revealed acute voter fluidity, with 30 percent of electors undecided and 21 percent considering boycotting the poll, whilst 54 percent supported a televised debate between the two main contenders.

Rachel deluges Southwest with rain, but battered coast catches a break
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Wide swaths of the Southwest were deluged Sunday as the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel weakened and moved inland, but coastal communities already battered by high surf emerged with less damage than some officials feared.
The National Weather Service said Sunday morning that Rachel was no longer a tropical storm. But danger remained as waves crashed into beachfront homes in Long Beach, large rocks and mud hurtled down a mountain onto a highway south of Palm Desert, and flood water submerged the parking lot of a casino on the Las Vegas Strip.
While the downgrading of Sunday’s storms brought some relief, risks continue across the California coast until Tuesday, and there is the longer-term concern of what is expected to be an active El Niño season.
The coastal flooding that damaged homes and flooded roads this week from Newport Beach to Long Beach came from a highly unusual combination of events that underscores the challenges California is facing amid predictions of a “super” El Nino winter.
“We’re not out of the woods yet,” National Weather Service meteorologist Daniel Berc said Sunday morning. Although the heaviest rain is over, according to meteorologists with the National Weather Service, people across the Southwest can expect spotty rain and high tides for the next couple of days.
On Sunday, some of the worst damage on the California coast was on the Long Beach Peninsula.
After tides swept away a portion of Long Beach’s historic wooden boardwalk Saturday, waves of saltwater rolled into a yellow two-story oceanfront house on Seaside Walk on Sunday.
The ocean completely engulfed the house’s wooden deck. A balcony had broken off and hung at a 30-degree angle toward the water. Yellow caution tape fluttered in the wind as water poured into a room strewn with wooden debris, an upturned refrigerator and a television.
A home along the Long Beach Peninsula appeared severely damaged on Sunday.
The yellow house on Seaside Walk began to collapse Sunday morning, according to two Long Beach Fire Department lifeguards. A house next door had cracks in its side, and others had wooden decks falling into or submerged in the water.
Coastal flooding is expected to remain a threat on beaches in San Diego, Orange, Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties through Tuesday, according to the National Weather Service.
Flood warnings are in effect along the L.A. County coast due to high tides driven by warm ocean water and lower atmospheric pressure with the arrival of the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, said Joe Sirard, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Oxnard. South-facing beaches, he said, were particularly vulnerable.
Early Sunday morning, as Rachel was about 255 miles north-northeast of San Diego, moving with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph, the National Hurricane Center said it was winding down its coverage and that its 8 a.m. update would be its last. But it also warned that seawater would continue to batter the Southern California coast.
 These waves, combined with an incoming long-period southerly swell, will cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.
— National Hurricane Center
“These waves, combined with an incoming long-period southerly swell, will cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the National Hurricane Center said. “Coastal flooding and erosion are expected to worsen this morning as the highest waves coincide with the high tides and water levels that are already running well above predicted levels.”
Hazardous coastal conditions could continue for the next few days, the National Hurricane Center said, and Rachel could bring a total rainfall of 1 to 3 inches, with maximum amounts in some areas of 5 inches, from Southern California into the Great Basin and the U.S. Southwest.
At a 10 a.m. briefing on Sunday morning, the National Weather Service said Las Vegas recorded 1.08 inches of rain since midnight, breaking the daily record for Oct. 11.
“And we still got 14 hours left to go,” Berc said.
Six miles south of Palm Desert in the Coachella Valley, rainfall caused flooding and a flow of rocks, mud and debris that blanketed the eastbound and westbound lanes of California 74 near Mile Marker 89, said weather service meteorologist Kyle Wheeler.
The National Weather Service in San Diego warned Sunday that elevated high tides and surf would cause coastal flooding and beach erosion through midweek, and showers and winds will linger from the coast to the mountains through Monday.
In Long Beach, with less than two hours before high tide, workers on the Peninsula raced early Sunday morning to build a sand berm stretching westward from 62nd Place.
Rachel downgraded from ‘tropical’ storm, but strong winds, rain and flooding hit Southern California
The National Weather Service says Rachel is no longer a “tropical” storm, but risks persist. Follow for live updates.
City groundskeeper Robert Quinonez, who was working with the track hoe operator, said he didn’t believe they could build the berm high enough in time to prevent water from spilling into the street like it did Saturday.
The track hoe operator repeatedly spun the machine to the west, dug into a mound of sand, spun 180 degrees and dropped the sand.
“We build as much as we can up, and just…” Quinonez said, trailing off.
Alphonso Tubbs, 56, chatted with Quinonez while looking at the work. Tubbs and his girlfriend had recently bought a condo on the street and planned to move in a week.
Tubbs said he was grateful that the condo he bought was on the side of the street where the city was building a sandbar.
“Just imagine if I was just on that side,” he said, pointing east. “They’re about to get smashed.”
Long Beach residents appeared divided on the city’s attempts to protect the oceanfront from water damage.
Long Beach resident Marianna Messina, who has lived in the community for 23 years, said the city’s work had been “excellent” as it worked to pump out water that had spilled into the street Saturday and removed a foot-thick layer of sand the water had deposited.
But another resident, Kellie Canning, complained the city had not done enough to prevent water damage. If steps aren’t taken immediately, she said, the damage would likely be far worse as winter progresses.
“Right now, you have a situation where the water is undermining the foundations of homes and streets,” she said. “I’m worried that 66th Place will rip up. Because there’s nothing to stop the water.”
Jon Cortez, 65, said he believed his house would probably be safe this season, but he expressed concern for his neighbors as the historic El Niño is expected to bring much worse in the coming weeks and months.
“With the El Niño coming, this is only the beginning, as far as I can say,” he said, watching the track hoe operator shovel sand on top of the ever-growing sand berm.
Cortez blamed the city for not taking any permanent or lasting measures to prevent the ocean from spilling into the streets, such as putting in place a concrete barrier or reinforcing the seawall.
“I think it’s going to be a mess,” he said.
In Newport Beach, there was a sigh of relief as the high tide began to recede Sunday..
Newport Beach spent the weekend working around the clock to protect homes after waves breached the city’s defenses along Balboa Peninsula.
On Friday and Saturday, super high tides caused widespread seawater flooding in the Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach, the National Weather Service said, flooding roads, closing the world-famous surf and bodyboarding spot the Wedge, and shuttering the Balboa Pier and Newport Pier.
But the streets along the Balboa Peninsula were dry Sunday. Residents walked and rode bicycles along the boardwalk as dozers and excavators moved along the beach, reinforcing the several-foot-high berms built to protect homes from the ocean waves.
Standing barefoot outside his home at 8th Street and Balboa Boulevard, holding a cup of coffee, Ross Stewart, 79, stared at the gray sky and at the berms.
“I think we’re going to be OK,” he said. “The waves haven’t breached our walls.”
Stewart, who has lived in the beach community since he was born, said the city had been working around the clock to build the massive sand berm, the biggest Stewart had seen in years.
“I’d say it’s probably 10 to 12 feet high,” he said, gazing at the wall of sand.
His neighborhood last flooded about five years ago, he said, and the city’s constant maintenance helped protect homes.
Shauna Parisi, 37, praised the city’s recovery from Friday’s flooding, noting that city crews had worked as late as 10 p.m. Saturday and as early as 6:30 a.m. Sunday to build large berms.
“I think any time there’s a little breakthrough they kind of go back over and push some more sand up,” she said. “We were worried about that today.”

US Homeland Security secretary sees no ‘risk’ from livestreamed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
23:17:05 UTC
08:17:05 KST

US Homeland Security secretary sees no ‘risk’ from livestreamed execution
The decision to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution has triggered harsh criticism and warnings that it could encourage radicalisation.
United States Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the planned livestreaming of Nidal Hasan’s execution, playing down warnings that images of his death by firing squad might be used as a propaganda tool for violent groups.
In an interview on Sunday with the CBS News show Face the Nation, Mullin framed the decision as part of President Donald Trump’s hardline approach to crime.
“I follow President Trump. He’s a commander-in chief of the country,” Mullin said, crediting the Republican leader with “restoring America values”.
Mullin also brushed aside concerns that the images of Hasan’s execution could be leveraged against the US.
“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.”
Hasan, a former US Army major, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after being convicted of shooting and killing 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The attack took place on November 5, 2009, when Hasan opened fire in a medical facility on the base where service members receive routine check-ups before deployment. The incident is considered one of the deadliest mass shootings to take place on a US military base.
Another 32 people were injured in the shooting. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down.
Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3.
But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced plans last week to livestream the upcoming execution, triggering a wave of criticism. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.
“So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution.
In a Sunday morning appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned that broadcasting Hasan’s death would “put at risk” US lives.
“Terrorist organisations will use this as a recruiting tool. It will radicalise other people, and this is not who we are,” Tillis said.
“Look, the Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life.”
Tillis, whose term as senator ends in January, also directed criticism at Hegseth for what he suggested was reckless leadership.
“It’s another example of why Pete Hegseth and all of his bravado needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader,” Tillis said.
The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure.
Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”.
She also argued that Hasan has sought public attention, something he would receive in a broadcast execution.
“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski added.
Republican Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, a former military member, issued a statement on Friday explaining that he had trained at Fort Hood a year before the attack.
He also said he opposed the public execution, despite considering Hasan “evil”.
“Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X.
“Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.”
Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
If the order against Hasan is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

The biggest concern remains airlines taking cabin bags from passengers at boarding gates to be kept in the aircraft's baggage hold.

We regret inconvenience caused to our customers due to this unforeseen situation and are making all efforts to minimise it, including offering refreshments and sharing updates. Kyiv • UNN
Russian National Guard troops are imposing a Russian military identity on schoolchildren and glorifying law enforcement officers. Teenagers are also being prepared to work for the Russian army.
In the occupied territories of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, Russian National Guard troops are holding so-called "lessons in courage" for children, where they talk about service, "patriotism," military traditions, and the glorification of Russian security forces. This is reported by the Center of National Resistance of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (CNS), UNN reports.
Details
It is noted that schoolchildren are gradually immersed in an environment where military uniforms, weapons, and service in Russian structures are presented as a natural part of life.
Through such activities, the occupation authorities are instilling in children the system of values desired by Russia — loyalty to security structures, a willingness to perceive military service as an honorable duty, and the romanticization of war. Under the guise of "patriotic education," children are in fact being forced to adopt a Russian military identity
It is pointed out that these are no longer simply isolated lessons: children are gradually being accustomed to the idea that their future should be connected with the army and Russia's security structures.
"In this way, the occupation system is attempting to shape a new generation for whom militarism will be perceived not as an exception, but as an ordinary part of life," the CNS concludes.
We remind you

Netanyahu demands probe into Israeli whistleblowers cited in award-winning Gaza film
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Sunday for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in the award-winning Gaza war documentary "NAZA".
The film is based on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers who accuse the army of killing scores of civilians in Gaza with the use of AI-powered targeting systems.
"Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this evening asked the chief of staff of the Israeli army, the head of the Shin Bet (domestic intelligence), and the state attorney to open a thorough investigation targeting the participants in the film 'NAZA' and to prosecute them," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
"NAZA" takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in airstrikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for "collateral damage".
Awarded a special jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, the film received a historic 25-minute standing ovation. The film has received praise around the world for revealing the extent of Israel's atrocities in Gaza, but has triggered a political storm in Israel.
"This film tells a false, misleading and biased story that defames the State of Israel and the army around the world," Netanyahu said, according to the statement.
He has previously declared his intention to back legislation to strip citizenship from people who "defame" soldiers.
Israel's military campaign in Gaza, determined to be a genocide by scholars and rights groups, has killed more than 74,000 people, according to the territory's health ministry.

The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.
The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for “the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village”, Bazzi said.
Displaced people
Since an agreement between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, violence in the south has lessened, but not stopped.

London Halal Forum kicks off second day with Palestinian breakfast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:06:23 UTC
05:06:23 KST

The second day of the annual London Halal Forum, bringing together entrepreneurs, investors, and industry leaders, began with a traditional Palestinian breakfast, offering an authentic experience celebrating Palestinian cuisine and heritage.
The event, being held at the Queen Elizabeth II Centre in London and organised by Halal360, is a joint initiative of the Islamic Chamber of Commerce and Development (ICCD) and the Halal Products Development Company (HPDC).
The breakfast offers traditional delicacies to participants, including hummus, zaatar, labneh, and falafel.
'Genocide continues'
Speaking at the event, Bilal Erdogan, the deputy chairman of Ibn Haldun University’s Board of Trustees, said it is meaningful to be at the forum with a group of guests who care about Palestine, who care about the conscience of humanity, "that's been tarnished tremendously throughout the last three years."
Recalling a mass pro-Palestine rally in Istanbul that was held on January 1, 2026, he said people will once again stage a demonstration next year to remember Palestine.
"We will tell the world about the genocide, and we will show solidarity with our brothers and sisters in Palestine for what they have been suffering throughout, especially in these last three years, but obviously since 1948," said Erdogan.
He underlined that an immense humanitarian situation continues in Gaza despite "the so-called ceasefire situation."
"Unfortunately, every day genocide continues. Every day, we have attacks. Every day, we have killings, not only in Gaza but also in the West Bank."
Warning that the situation in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem is "getting worse", Erdogan stressed "we have to make sure" that resources that "we can put together" are strategically managed so that "we have better outcomes".
Referring to recent sanctions by some Western countries targeting trade with illegal Israeli settlements, he noted, "That's the beginning."
"Hopefully, they will extend that to hold (whole) Israeli products at some point."
"This breakfast is sort of a complete version of what we need to do about that, really empowering the producers, empowering the investors, and empowering any startups coming from the region."
Erdogan added that it should start from the ground, from food, but it should grow into "more valued sectors", in technology, in medicine, and in other fields.
Türkiye will continue to do whatever it can, he said, adding that the issue of Palestine transcends any political lines and issues.
"Inshallah, we can get together and do these meetings in Al-Quds, all together in peace and harmony," he added.
'Israel also pursuing economic war'
Also speaking at the venue, Palestinian Ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot said the genocide is ongoing in Gaza and ethnic cleansing is ongoing in the occupied West Bank, noting "Israeli settler terrorists" attacks targeting the Palestinian olive harvest.
The ambassador said Israel is also pursuing an economic war against Palestinian people, which has continued for decades.
Türkiye's ambassador to London, Osman Koray Ertas, was also among the attendees.
A video about the Palestinian Museum, which aims to present and contribute to narratives on Palestinian history, culture, and society, was screened during the program.
Under the theme Halal Tayyib for Humanity, the forum is examining the halal economy’s expansion beyond certification and food products into investment, tourism, technology, supply chains, branding, and international trade.
The first edition of the forum was held in November 2025 at Excel London, bringing together over 1,500 participants, both in-person and virtually, highlighting London's emerging role as a key player in the growing global halal economy.

Ben Gvir left with a dilemma as Israeli parties seal election deals: How the system works
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:04:31 UTC
05:04:31 KST

Gadi Eisenkot with Yair Golan, Likud with Religious Zionism, Naftali Bennett with Avigdor Lieberman, Shas with United Torah Judaism, Ra'am with the Joint List, and perhaps Itamar Ben Gvir with Ofer Winter? Since Israel's founding, political parties have routinely signed agreements designed to maximize their electoral strength and prevent votes from going to waste in Knesset elections. 
Known as surplus-vote agreements, these arrangements allow two parties, usually ideologically aligned or belonging to the same political camp, to combine their votes for the final allocation of parliamentary seats. The goal is to ensure that votes left over after the initial count can help secure additional representation. So how does the system work, who benefits, and what could it mean for the October 27 election? Here's a guide.
Why are surplus-vote agreements necessary?
After polling stations close and all valid votes in a Knesset election are counted, seats are allocated among the parties that have passed the electoral threshold, based on the 120 seats in Israel's parliament. This begins the process of distributing Knesset seats.
The electoral threshold currently stands at 3.25% of valid votes, roughly equivalent to four Knesset seats. The number of votes needed to cross that threshold changes from one election to another, depending on turnout and the number of invalid ballots. In the previous election in 2022, a party needed at least 154,855 votes to qualify for representation.
The valid votes received by each qualifying party are then converted into a whole number of seats. The electoral quota represents the number of votes required for one Knesset seat. It is calculated by dividing the total number of valid votes cast for parties that crossed the electoral threshold by 120. In the 2022 election, the quota was 36,227 votes, meaning that approximately 36,227 votes were equivalent to one seat.
In most cases, however, parties are left with surplus votes that are insufficient to secure another full seat. These represent fractions of seats that remain unallocated after the initial distribution. This is where surplus-vote agreements come into play.
How does the system work?
Under the Bader-Ofer method, introduced in 1973, two parties that have signed a surplus-vote agreement are treated as a single list for the purpose of allocating the remaining seats. After all valid votes have been counted and the initial allocation of whole seats is completed, the remaining seats are distributed using a mathematical formula.
The calculation takes the combined number of votes received by the two parties and divides it by the number of seats they have already been allocated, plus one. For example, if two parties receive a combined 400,000 votes and are initially awarded 11 seats, their joint quotient would be 400,000 divided by 12, or approximately 33,333 votes.
That figure is then compared with the quotients calculated for all other parties or pairs of parties. The party or pair with the highest quotient receives the next available seat. The calculation is then repeated for the following seat, with the number of seats already awarded adjusted accordingly.
If a pair of parties that signed a surplus-vote agreement wins an additional seat, a separate calculation determines which of the two receives it.
That internal allocation is also carried out under the Bader-Ofer formula. In practice, the larger of the two parties often has an advantage, even if it does not have the largest number of leftover votes. However, the smaller party can also receive the additional seat, as has happened in previous elections.
The system generally favors larger parties, but a surplus-vote agreement can improve the chances of either partner securing an additional seat.
Which parties benefit from signing, and what happens to those that don't?
Surplus-vote agreements are signed between two electoral lists and may be submitted, under Israeli law, until 11 days before election day, subject to approval by the Central Elections Committee.
With the next election scheduled for October 27, just 16 days away, parties have until October 16 to decide whether to enter into such agreements. As a rule, the parties that sign these agreements are ideologically close or belong to the same political camp. Their shared objective is to maximize the number of seats their camp receives.
The electoral threshold is particularly important because a surplus-vote agreement is valid only if both parties cross it. Signing an agreement with a party that may fail to enter the Knesset therefore carries a significant risk.
If one of the two parties fails to cross the threshold, the agreement becomes ineffective, and the votes cast for the unsuccessful party are excluded from the allocation of Knesset seats.
The mechanism is not unique to Israel. Similar systems for distributing remaining parliamentary seats are used, or have been used, in other democracies. The Bader-Ofer method takes its name from former Knesset members Yohanan Bader of Gahal and Avraham Ofer of the Alignment, who initiated the legislation.
It replaced an earlier system under which the party with the largest remainder of unused votes received the next available seat, a method that tended to benefit smaller parties.
A party that does not sign a surplus-vote agreement can still compete independently for additional seats under the Bader-Ofer formula, but it cannot benefit from combining its votes with another party.
Such a decision can also expose a party to criticism from within its political camp, particularly if its refusal to cooperate is perceived as weakening the bloc's overall chances of gaining seats.
Who has signed with whom?
About a month ago, four parties opposed to another term for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced that they had signed surplus-vote agreements. The first agreement was announced by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, chairman of the Together party, and Avigdor Lieberman, chairman of Yisrael Beytenu.
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, had preferred to sign an agreement with another party in the anti-Netanyahu camp but ultimately found himself paired with Yair Golan and his Democrats party.
In a statement, Eisenkot's party took credit for organizing the opposition camp, saying he had "worked in various ways to organize the camp of change and hope as effectively as possible."
"The camp's consolidation into four parties has, fortunately, created the possibility of signing mutual, internal surplus-vote agreements, drawing lessons from previous election campaigns," the statement said.
The Joint List and Ra'am, the United Arab List, subsequently signed their own surplus-vote agreement, seeking to prevent votes from being wasted in the election. As part of the agreement, the two Arab-led lists committed to conducting a "fair and clean election campaign, without personal attacks, defamation, incitement or falsification."
They also called on activists and supporters to maintain respectful political discourse despite their disagreements.
In the previous election, three Arab lists ran separately: Ra'am, Hadash-Ta'al and Balad. None signed surplus-vote agreements with the others, and Balad ultimately failed to cross the electoral threshold.
The next agreement was between Likud and Religious Zionism. The deal between Netanyahu and Religious Zionism chairman Bezalel Smotrich left Itamar Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party with the option of signing an agreement with Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party or remaining without a partner.
That dilemma comes as Likud has intensified its campaign against Winter. The party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha also offered Winter a surplus-vote agreement, but he did not respond.
"Unfortunately, Likud refused to sign a surplus-vote agreement with us as part of an attempt to weaken our party and leave Ben Gvir outside the unity government Likud is planning with Eisenkot," Otzma Yehudit said after the Netanyahu-Smotrich agreement was announced.
The prospect of an agreement with Winter carries its own risk for Ben Gvir. If Amcha Yisrael fails to cross the electoral threshold, the agreement would have no effect.
Either way, the latest parties to sign a surplus-vote agreement were the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism.
The two parties emphasized that their agreement reflected the "continuation of cooperation between the factions, in accordance with the instructions of the leading rabbis and sages of the generation."
In a joint statement, the parties led by Aryeh Deri and Yaakov Asher said: "In the next Knesset, too, we will continue to cooperate fully on the core issues concerning the preservation of the Torah world and the status of yeshiva students."

A chemical produced by gut bacteria may accelerate Alzheimer’s disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
20:00:56 UTC
05:00:56 KST

A byproduct produced by certain gut bacteria may directly accelerate the brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated blood levels of this molecule, known as imidazole propionate, correlate with worse cognitive decline in humans and actively drive neurodegeneration in animal models. The findings were published in Nature Communications.
The human digestive tract contains trillions of bacteria that help break down food. During this process, microbes release chemical byproducts into the bloodstream. These chemicals, called metabolites, travel throughout the body and influence the function of various organs, including the brain.
Imidazole propionate is a specific metabolite generated when gut bacteria break down histidine, an amino acid found in many common foods. Previous research linked elevated levels of this molecule to metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Because metabolic problems often increase the risk of developing dementia, researchers suspected the chemical might also affect brain health.
Researchers Vaibhav Vemuganti and Jea Woo Kang from the University of Wisconsin-Madison led the investigation alongside senior authors Barbara B. Bendlin and Federico E. Rey. They aimed to test whether imidazole propionate directly influences the biological pathways involved in cognitive aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
The team began by analyzing blood samples from nearly 1,200 older adults, most of whom had no diagnosed cognitive impairment. They measured the concentration of imidazole propionate in each participant’s blood and compared those levels against the participants’ scores on standardized memory and problem-solving tests. To isolate the effects of the chemical, the researchers adjusted their calculations for age, sex, body mass index, and the APOE gene, a known genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease.
People with the highest levels of the gut metabolite performed worse on cognitive tests at the start of the study. Over years of follow-up visits, these same individuals experienced an earlier and more rapid decline in memory and executive function compared to those with lower levels. Statistical models predicted that the cognitive performance of the high-metabolite group fell below that of the low-metabolite group roughly 15 to 18 years before the participants’ average age.
To look for underlying physical changes, the researchers measured molecular markers of Alzheimer’s disease in the participants’ blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Cerebrospinal fluid is the clear liquid that surrounds and protects the brain and spinal cord. High blood levels of imidazole propionate correlated with elevated amounts of tau tangles and neurofilament light chain, a structural protein that leaks out of damaged brain cells.
The researchers then analyzed the genetic material of gut bacteria from fecal samples provided by 294 participants. They specifically searched for a bacterial gene called urdA, which provides the biological instructions for making the enzyme that produces imidazole propionate. They identified this gene in several bacterial families, including certain strains of Streptococcus.
A higher abundance of bacteria carrying this gene was linked to lower cognitive scores and elevated Alzheimer’s biomarkers in the human participants. To investigate if this relationship is a direct cause and effect in humans, the team turned to large genetic databases. They used a statistical method that treats genetic inheritance like a randomized trial to evaluate whether naturally occurring biological traits lead to specific diseases.
The analysis revealed a specific genetic variant on chromosome 12 that causes some people to naturally accumulate higher levels of imidazole propionate in their blood. Carrying this genetic variant was associated with an increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, suggesting the metabolite actively promotes the condition rather than acting as a harmless bystander.
The researchers then conducted small studies using two different mouse models genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s-like brain changes. One model mimics the buildup of amyloid plaques, while the other mimics the accumulation of tau tangles. The researchers added imidazole propionate to the animals’ drinking water for several months.
In mice predisposed to accumulating amyloid plaques, a sticky protein fragment associated with Alzheimer’s, the treated animals developed more plaques in their brains than mice drinking regular water. In a second group of mice predisposed to tau tangles, the treatment caused severe inflammation and triggered the hyperactivity of star-shaped support cells called astrocytes. By analyzing the entire spectrum of proteins in the mouse brains, the researchers also detected elevated levels of proteins linked to structural breakdown in the nerve fibers.
Because the metabolite originates in the gut, it must travel through the blood to reach the brain. The researchers tested how the chemical affects the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed layer of cells that lines brain blood vessels and protects neural tissue from circulating toxins.
They exposed human brain blood vessel cells to the metabolite in a laboratory setting. The molecule reduced the electrical resistance of the cell layer, indicating a breakdown in barrier integrity. In a separate test, the researchers injected a blue dye into the bloodstream of treated mice. The dye leaked extensively into the brain tissue, showing that the chemical damages blood vessels and allows substances to abnormally enter the brain.
In a final set of experiments, the team applied the metabolite directly to isolated mouse neurons grown in culture. They also added a chemical inhibitor that blocks an enzyme called GSK3-beta. This enzyme is known to abnormally attach phosphate molecules to tau proteins, causing them to tangle and destroy brain cells.
Exposure to the gut metabolite caused the cultured neurons to rapidly accumulate damaged tau proteins. Blocking the GSK3-beta enzyme completely reversed this effect, outlining the specific molecular pathway the gut chemical uses to damage brain cells.
While the human observational data points to a strong relationship, it cannot definitively prove that lowering imidazole propionate will prevent dementia. The animal experiments relied entirely on male mice given the chemical in their drinking water, which may not perfectly replicate how the metabolite is naturally produced and absorbed in the human digestive system.
Future studies will need to test female animals to determine if the biological effects differ by sex. Researchers will also need to explore whether specific dietary changes or targeted medications can safely reduce the production of this metabolite in the human gut.
The study, “Gut bacterial metabolite imidazole propionate potentiates Alzheimer’s disease pathology,” was authored by Vaibhav Vemuganti, Jea Woo Kang, Qijun Zhang, Eric R. McGregor, James R. Hilser, Ruben Aquino-Martinez, Sandra Harding, Joseph Lawrence Harpt, Katharina R. Beck, Hailey Bussan, Jessamine F. Kuehn, Yuetiva Deming, Rachel Studer, Sterling C. Johnson, Sanjay Asthana, Henrik Zetterberg, Kaj Blennow, Corinne D. Engelman, Hooman Allayee, Rozalyn M. Anderson, Tyler K. Ulland, Fredrik Bäckhed, Barbara B. Bendlin, and Federico E. Rey.

Benzene spike near Haifa refineries closes two schools; residents urged to limit outdoor exposure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The Health Ministry ordered two schools near the Bazan oil refinery complex in Kiryat Ata to suspend classes at their regular campuses for the next 24 hours following unusually high benzene concentrations detected in the area, officials announced Sunday night.
The directive, issued in consultation with the Environmental Protection Ministry and in coordination with the Kiryat Ata Municipality, applies to the Social High School and Arazim School, both located near the refinery complex. Classes are to be transferred to alternative locations during the temporary closure.
The ministries also issued precautionary guidance for residents living or staying within one kilometer of the refinery complex, recommending that they avoid unnecessary time outdoors.
The recommendation applies to the general population, with particular emphasis on children and pregnant women.
Workers in the nearby industrial zone were advised to keep windows closed and operate air conditioning systems.
The emergency measures follow the detection of unusually high benzene concentrations near the Bazan refinery complex. The announcement did not specify the measured concentrations or indicate how long the elevated readings had persisted.
