Two killed near Israeli-occupied zone in south Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
19:57:08 UTC
04:57:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Two killed near Israeli-occupied zone in south Lebanon
Two men were killed in south Lebanon on Sunday, one by Israeli fire and the other by an explosive remnant of war, as they took part in the annual olive harvest, according to state media and local officials.
South Lebanon has been the scene of two wars since 2023 between Israel and Hezbollah, and Israeli troops still occupy a band of territory 10 kilometres (six miles) wide running along the border.
The official National News Agency (NNA) said one of the men was killed in Yater, in Bint Jbeil district, when Israeli "shelling targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest".
The Lebanese army blamed Israeli tank fire and called the ongoing attacks "a flagrant breach of existing agreements".
Afterwards, the Yater municipality urged residents "to avoid the outskirts of the town and refrain from crossing the earthen barrier separating some unsafe neighborhoods" for fear of Israeli attacks.
In the village of Froun, in the same district, the NNA reported that "a foreign object" left over from previous Israeli operations exploded and killed an engineer as he and others tended their trees.
The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.
The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for "the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village", Bazzi said.
Since a framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, the violence in the south has diminished but not stopped.
Israel continues to carry out sporadic strikes and demolitions in and around the territory it occupies, while Hezbollah refuses to submit to government plans to disarm it.
About eight kilometres (five miles) away, in Jibshit, volunteers from the north came to help locals with the harvest in a show of solidarity.
"From north to south, one people and one land," said organiser Ahmad Chahhal.
As workers swatted at branches to make the olives fall, an AFP photographer saw drones and heard fighter jets overhead, and explosions could be heard in the distance.
Israel has ramped up its bombardment of Lebanon since March, with intense strikes and a ground invasion.
The framework deal between Israel and Lebanon involves Hezbollah's disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region.

Israel election poll: Eisenkot bloc continues slump as Netanyahu's coalition gains ground

A new Israeli election poll published by public broadcaster Kan Sunday shows former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc shrinking by two seats, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc rises two seats, bolstered in part by far-right Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael crossing the electoral threshold,
Eisenkot's bloc stands at 50 Knesset seats, down from 52 last week, while the governing coalition rose from 51 to 53. 61 members are necessary for a majority in the Knesset. The Arab parties, meanwhile, hold steady at 13 seats.
Eisenkot's Yashar party loses one seat compared with last week but remains the largest party, with 22 seats. Likud also loses one seat, falling to 20. Bennett's Together holds steady at 12 seats. Yisrael Beiteinu drops one seat to eight, while Otzma Yehudit gains one to reach nine.
The Democrats, the Joint List and United Torah Judaism remain unchanged at eight seats each. Shas loses one seat, falling to seven, while Mansour Abbas' United Arab List holds steady at five. Religious Zionism also stands at five, down one seat from last week. The Reservists, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, remains at four seats.
Winter's Amcha Yisrael crosses the threshold, after failing to do so in Kan's previous poll, standing on four seats.
Blue and White remains below the electoral threshold, with just 0.9 percent of the vote, as does the Haredi Public party, also at 0.9 percent.
In a question about suitability for prime minister, Eisenkot leads Netanyahu by 43 percent to 38 percent. The poll also found that 30 percent of respondents have yet to decide whom they will vote for.
The poll was conducted by Kantar, headed by Dudu Hasid, among 552 respondents. The margin of error is 4.2 percentage points.

Mexican president urges residents to shelter as Hurricane Simon approaches

Mexican president urges residents to shelter as Hurricane Simon approaches
The Mexican community of Cabo Corrientes faces the risk of a direct hit as the Category 4 storm churns off Jalisco.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has urged residents along the Pacific Ocean to stay indoors as Hurricane Simon’s powerful winds and heavy rains pound coastal communities.
As of Sunday, the hurricane’s eye was moving offshore of Mexico’s Jalisco state, with winds of at least 240km/h (150mph).
Torrential rain has already battered residents living between the Sierra Madre mountain range and the ocean. Communities in hilly and mountainous areas have been warned to brace for mudslides.
Simon reached Category 4 strength, on a scale of five, on Saturday, as part of an unusually active Pacific hurricane season.
“With the approaching impact of Category 4 Hurricane Simon, we urge residents of coastal municipalities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain sheltered until authorities officially declare that the danger has passed,” Sheinbaum wrote in a post on the social media platform X on Sunday.
In a midday advisory, the United States’ National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned that Simon could produce “additional rainfall totals of 8 to 16 inches (20 to 41 cm) over portions of southwestern Mexico”.
Precipitation totals as high as 76 cm (30 inches) were possible in areas of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco until Monday.
It’s not clear whether the storm will make landfall. But the greatest risk of a direct hit lies at the moment with Cabo Corrientes, a town that sits on a cape in Jalisco, jutting into the Pacific Ocean.
Mexico’s National Civil Protection Coordination (CNPC) placed 28 municipalities in Jalisco and Colima under its highest cyclone alert level, while another 93 municipalities were under a high alert level, according to civil protection bulletins.
Classes were suspended in the affected areas, and efforts to evacuate residents were under way.
Businesses in popular tourist destinations like Puerto Vallarta boarded up windows and placed sandbags at entrances as the storm approached.
Jalisco’s Governor Pablo Navarro warned that the high-powered hurricane was creating “high-risk marine conditions” along the coast of his state, with waves reaching as high as eight metres (26 feet).
On Sunday, he also shared video on social media of the storm surge crashing onto sidewalks and flooding waterways.
“Here is the current state of Jalisco’s beaches this morning — from Barra de Navidad to Puerto Vallarta — as Hurricane Simon passes through,” he wrote in the video’s caption.
“I ask everyone to heed official instructions, take precautions and avoid putting themselves at risk. The safety of Jalisco’s families is the top priority.”

Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, to which the US later replied via Qatari intermediaries.

US-Israel relationship may be irreparably damaged, former Biden official warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
19:22:07 UTC
04:22:07 KST

Phil Gordon, who served in the Biden administration as then-vice president Kamala Harris's national security advisor, issued a stark warning in an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that Israeli-US ties have been severely damaged.
"It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that," Gordon told the Post.
Gordon believes the damage inflicted on relations between Israel and the United States in recent years may be far more enduring than many Israelis realize, potentially extending well beyond the political careers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump.
"I have rarely seen a turnaround in attitudes on an issue as rapid and comprehensive," Gordon said, referring to the dramatic decline in American support for Israel over the past year.
"You have a whole generation of Americans," he continued. "Look at the numbers on sympathy for Israelis versus Palestinians or favorable to Israel. It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that."
Gordon does not rule out the possibility that the deterioration could prove permanent.
Asked why he recently described the damage to the relationship as "perhaps irreparably," he explained that his choice of words was deliberate.
"I write perhaps because I think it's still an open question, but I also don't rule it out," he said. "The more important word is irreparably because it's honestly possible."
Why Gordon is speaking out now
Gordon's interview comes a day after he publicly challenged efforts by Netanyahu supporters to portray a new book and interviews by Brett McGurk, a senior Biden administration official closely involved in negotiations over the Gaza war and the Israeli hostages, as vindication of the prime minister's wartime decisions.
In a post on X, Gordon argued that McGurk's account, while valuable, should not be treated as the definitive version of what happened behind the scenes.
"While Brett's front-row account is valuable, that doesn't mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared, including among former members of the Biden administration," Gordon wrote.
"I would say most of my former colleagues think that President Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner," he added.
Gordon also wrote that few former administration officials believed Biden's biggest mistake had been publicly distancing himself from Israel, what he described as showing "daylight" between Washington and Jerusalem.
Speaking to the Post, Gordon explained why he decided to enter the debate over one of the most contentious periods in recent Israeli-American relations.
"Everything's charged and this is sensitive and important, which is why I thought it was important for me to weigh in with my perspective," he said.
His account focuses particularly on the efforts to secure a hostage agreement during the summer of 2024, including a crucial phone conversation between Biden and Netanyahu that, Gordon says, revealed just how difficult reaching a deal would become.
The July 4 call: 'We were not hearing a yes… but something closer to no'
On July 4, 2024, president Joe Biden called Netanyahu at what American officials believed could be a significant turning point in the negotiations to release Israeli hostages held in Gaza.
According to Gordon, Hamas had just indicated it was willing to abandon one of its central demands, creating what Washington saw as a genuine opportunity for progress.
To understand the significance of that moment, Gordon traced the negotiations back to the spring of 2024.
For months, Hamas had insisted that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released. Israel refused to make such a commitment.
That dispute remained the main obstacle throughout May.
But toward the end of that month, Gordon said Israel signaled it could accept a phased ceasefire arrangement in which a permanent ceasefire would remain the ultimate objective without requiring an immediate Israeli commitment.
"With clever drafting, we were able to put together the proposal that President Biden rolled out publicly on May 31," Gordon said.
Under that framework, Israel would not have to commit to a permanent ceasefire during the first phase, but good-faith negotiations over the final arrangements would allow for what Gordon described as "sustainable calm."
The proposal represented a breakthrough because it created a possible path toward a permanent ceasefire without requiring Israel to accept Hamas's original condition upfront.
For weeks, however, Hamas did not respond.
Then, around July 2, Gordon said Hamas finally agreed in principle to the framework.
"Hamas finally came around and sort of agreed, in principle, with the framework, including dropping its demand that a permanent ceasefire be agreed up front," he recalled.
"That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult."
With that development, Biden called Netanyahu on July 4 to urge him to move ahead.
"The plan was to really urge him to take the deal," Gordon said.
"This has gone on far too long. The hostages had suffered far too long. There was far too much catastrophic damage, Palestinian lives lost. Humanitarian conditions were horrific."
But Gordon said Netanyahu's response quickly dampened American expectations.
"I think we, the American side, were pretty deflated to hear Netanyahu say, 'Okay, you know, I hear you, Joe, but here are all the things that will have to happen for this to work,'" Gordon recalled.
Netanyahu then began listing those requirements during the call.
"I could tell in that moment that we were not hearing a yes or even a yes, I can work with this, but something closer to no."
According to Gordon, Netanyahu subsequently began what he described as "clarifying" Israel's position, clarifications that Washington regarded as effectively introducing additional conditions into the negotiations.
Philadelphi Corridor, Gallant, and the political question
One of the most consequential Israeli demands involved retaining military forces along the entire Philadelphi Corridor, the narrow strip of territory separating Gaza from Egypt.
Gordon emphasized that Israel had not even fully controlled the corridor when the original proposals were developed.
"In that sense, it really was a new condition," he said.
Netanyahu continued insisting on that position throughout the fall of 2024, despite objections from senior Israeli officials.
Gordon specifically cited then-defense minister Yoav Gallant, who, he said, considered continued control of the entire corridor militarily unnecessary and an obstacle to reaching a deal.
Another disputed condition involved an Israeli screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza, which would have required Israeli forces to remain in central Gaza.
In his earlier X post, Gordon argued that these conditions made an agreement impossible for another six months.
During that period, he wrote, nearly 9,000 additional Palestinians were killed, while more Israeli hostages died, including the six hostages executed by Hamas in August 2024.
He noted that both Israeli conditions were ultimately dropped from the agreement reached in January 2025.
Asked directly whether Netanyahu deliberately delayed the agreement to preserve his governing coalition, Gordon declined to judge the prime minister's motivations.
"I can't speak to or speculate about his motives," he said.
"I know there was a lot of talk that he feared that he would lose his coalition if he compromised on certain issues."
Gordon acknowledged that Netanyahu might genuinely have believed that continued Israeli control of the Philadelphi Corridor was militarily necessary.
"He certainly articulated over and over again that total victory was the only option," Gordon said.
But he added that the political implications were difficult to ignore.
"It also seemed to be the case that keeping his coalition together depended on rejecting that proposal, so yeah, you can draw your own conclusions."
Gordon stressed that no one could know with certainty whether greater flexibility by Netanyahu would have produced an agreement during the summer of 2024.
Nevertheless, he argued that Netanyahu's insistence on those conditions had a clear consequence.
"We do know that by digging in and taking the positions that he did, which seemed to align with his political interests, and certainly aligned with his emphasis on the need for total victory, that made any deal at that time impossible," he said.
A warning for Israel: Arms conditionality is now mainstream among Democrats
For Gordon, one of the most significant consequences of the Israel-Hamas War in the Gaza Strip is not merely the deterioration in relations between Netanyahu and the Biden administration, but a broader transformation in American political attitudes toward Israel.
Positions once considered marginal in debates over US military assistance have increasingly moved into the Democratic mainstream.
"Arms conditionality has now gone from a kind of fringe view to a mainstream Democratic position," Gordon said.
He pointed to the growing number of Democratic senators supporting measures that would condition American assistance to Israel, including legislation concerning Israel's planned development in the E1 area east of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
Gordon cited a Senate proposal he said virtually all Democrats supported and that would withhold assistance over E1.
Although the shift has been particularly pronounced among Democrats, Gordon emphasized that declining support for Israel is not confined to one political party.
"I know people are mostly focused on Democrats, and it's true there's sharper criticism of Israel among Democrats, but it exists in both parties," he said.
A future Israeli government adopting different policies could begin rebuilding the relationship, Gordon argued, but reversing the damage would require a sustained effort.
"I think with a new Israeli government and different policies, the relationship could improve, he said.
"With work on both sides, maybe it can be repaired, but I don't think anybody should underestimate the challenge."
Should Biden have withheld more weapons from Israel?
While sharply critical of Netanyahu, Gordon does not absolve the administration in which he served of responsibility.
Asked what concrete pressure Biden should have applied, he rejected the idea that Washington faced only two options: continuing military assistance without conditions or imposing a comprehensive arms embargo.
"We had great respect for Israel's need to defend itself against Hezbollah, against Iran," Gordon said.
He noted that the threat of Iranian military action was particularly real during that period, including the ballistic missile and drone attack Iran launched against Israel in April 2024.
He explained that this security threat was a major reason the Biden administration did not support broadly withholding weapons.
But Gordon argued that Washington had many other available tools.
"There's an awful lot between doing nothing and withholding all weapons," he said.
"It starts with diplomatic pressure. It starts with calling out Israel and pushing it to accept these agreements. You can take diplomatic measures at the United Nations and elsewhere, and then yes, you can also start conditioning weapons."
He cited the administration's decision to withhold certain 2,000-pound bombs as an example of using military assistance to signal serious disagreement with Israel's conduct of the war and its handling of the humanitarian crisis.
One episode particularly demonstrated the potential effectiveness of American pressure, Gordon argued: Biden's response to the Israeli strike that killed aid workers from World Central Kitchen.
According to Gordon, Biden called Netanyahu and delivered a direct warning.
"You will do these things on the humanitarian front, and I need to see them immediately, or US policy is going to change," Gordon recalled Biden telling Netanyahu.
"Israel did, and opened up further crossings, and that was an example of how US pressure could work."
Gordon also pointed to the pressure McGurk and Steve Witkoff applied during negotiations over the January 2025 agreement, during the presidential transition following Trump's election victory.
"When Brett McGurk and Steve Witkoff were pressing the Israelis to accept the final deal in January, and Trump behind the scenes, I think that kind of pressure also worked," he said.
Iran before the elections: 'A volatile and dangerous stalemate'
Gordon also addressed another question now dominating discussions in Jerusalem and Washington: Could Israel or the United States resume major military operations against Iran before Israel's elections and the US midterms?
He refused to offer a definitive prediction, warning instead that the current confrontation was unusually volatile.
"We've learned over the last two years and beyond not to exclude anything," Gordon said.
"The situation is extremely volatile."
One of his central concerns is that both Washington and Tehran believe time is working in their favor.
"I'm afraid that both the United States and Iran feel that time is on their side," he said.
"The United States thinks that the blockade is working or squeezing Iran or the economy, but Iran feels like midterms looming and pressure on the US economy means it can resist and last longer."
That competing assessment, Gordon argued, explains the current diplomatic and military impasse.
"That's what explains this current stalemate. But it's a volatile and dangerous stalemate."
Gordon fears that the pressure campaign may produce further escalation before Tehran agrees to American demands.
"One is that before Iran collapses, which is sort of the goal, either capitulates or collapses, which is the goal of maximum pressure, it will lash out," he said.
He cited recent Houthi attacks against Riyadh and the earlier attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as examples of how regional escalation can spiral, while noting that the Houthis, rather than Iran directly, were responsible for those attacks.
Gordon also offered a notable assessment of Trump's military decision-making in recent months.
"I would say that over the past couple of months, every time Trump has threatened it and considered it, he's backed off because he has realized that the consequences could be devastating," he said.
"I don't know if that will hold, but I do think it's worth keeping in mind."
Gordon argued that the war has already demonstrated the danger of unintended consequences.
"I think this war, after six months now, has proven to be catastrophic, with all sorts of unintended consequences," he said.
"If Israel or the United States did decide to resume a major escalation, for reasons of Israel's election or our elections, I fear that we would just see even more unintended consequences of the tragic sort that we've been seeing for the past six months."
Gordon's criticism of Trump: A year of missed opportunities in Gaza
Toward the end of the interview, Gordon turned his criticism toward Trump's handling of Gaza during the first year of his administration.
The January 2025 hostage and ceasefire agreement, Gordon argued, had created an opportunity to put Gaza on a different trajectory: bring home the remaining hostages, preserve the ceasefire, establish a new governing arrangement, and begin reconstruction for Palestinians.
Instead, he said, that opportunity was squandered.
"Once we finally got the deal in January 2025, that was an opportunity to at least start putting it on the right path, get all the hostages out, have a ceasefire, a different government in Gaza, and rebuild for Palestinians," Gordon said.
"But instead, Israel broke the ceasefire in March. Trump did nothing about that," he argued.
According to Gordon, a complete blockade on food, water, and medicine followed for two months, dramatically worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
He contended that Trump did not begin applying serious pressure for a renewed ceasefire until after Israel struck Doha later that year.
"Trump sometimes gets credit for getting the ceasefire and the 20-point plan in place, and give him credit for that, fine," Gordon said.
"I think it's obviously a good thing that the ceasefire was achieved, and there's a path forward in Gaza."
But he argued that the administration's earlier inaction should not be forgotten.
"People shouldn't forget that it took a year, including turning a blind eye to a complete blockade of Gaza that severely deteriorated the humanitarian situation, and then the entire summer before he got motivated," Gordon said.
"And that was again only after Israel struck in Doha."
For Gordon, the criticism of Netanyahu, Biden and Trump is part of the same broader argument: The Gaza war presented extraordinarily difficult choices, but he believes opportunities to end the fighting and secure the release of hostages were repeatedly missed.
Now, he warns, Israel faces another formidable challenge: Rebuilding the trust and standing it has lost among the American public.
"With work on both sides, maybe it can be repaired," Gordon said.
"But I don't think anybody should underestimate the challenge."

A planned non-Zionist Jewish school in Boston hopes to ride the momentum of the left
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
19:22:05 UTC
04:22:05 KST

In the middle of a conversation about her future children, it dawned on Leah Robbins that the school she imagined for them did not exist.
Robbins envisioned a Jewish school where children studied Jewish texts, history, and observance, as she did at the school run out of her Conservative synagogue in northern Florida. But having long ago rejected the allegiance to Israel that was entwined with her education, she could not fathom sending her children to a school that promoted Zionism, which ruled out all the Jewish day schools she knew.
“I was just overwhelmed with a sense of grief that my kids could be less Jewishly educated than I was,” Robbins, who has lived in Boston for 10 years, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “I would never ever consider sending my kids to any of the local day schools because of total values misalignment.”
Plans to open non-Zionist school
Four years after that conversation, Robbins is building her own institution for the children she hopes to have. She plans to open Achvat Olam, a “diasporist” day school whose name translates to “global solidarity” in Hebrew, in the Boston area in fall 2029. The school aims to launch with eight to 10 families, starting with a kindergarten and adding grade levels until ultimately becoming a K-8 school.
Achvat Olam is fiscally sponsored by Beloved Builders, a Massachusetts-based nonprofit that supports progressive Jewish projects. Robbins, who has a background in fundraising for Jewish nonprofits, hopes to raise $625,000 for the launch. She said she has met about 20 local families who expressed interest and will start formal recruitment efforts, including focus groups and open houses, next year.
Achvat Olam will teach about Jewish history, cultures, and languages outside of Israel, while engaging with Hebrew and Israel’s history from a non-Zionist perspective. The school’s website includes a page on “Israel/Palestine,” saying its community will share a belief that “the pursuit of justice, dignity, and thriving for all people is a Jewish moral imperative.”
“This includes an age-appropriate, honest confrontation with Zionism and the ongoing Nakba against the Palestinian people,” the website says, using the Arabic word for the displacement of over 700,000 Palestinians at the time of the State of Israel’s founding. The school also says that students will consider “the complicity and support of the US government and Diaspora Jews.”
Micah-Shalom Kesselman is the parent of a 4-year-old in Medford, Massachusetts, and participates in local left-wing Jewish groups such as the Boston Workers Circle. He’s disappointed that his son Oren will age out of Achvat Olam by the time it is scheduled to open as a kindergarten. “I would super want Oren to attend something like what Achvat Olam is shaping up to be,” he said.
Kesselman, who studies Yiddish with his son, explained that he would like Oren to be steeped in Jewish traditions and culture. But as a parent who is “not a supporter of Zionism,” he said he has found few Jewish educational opportunities that match his beliefs.
Jewish day schools have historically encompassed a range of orientations toward Israel, according to Jonathan Krasner, a historian of American Jewish education at Brandeis University.
The modern day school movement was born in the 1920s and initially dominated by orthodox schools, some of which did not emphasize Zionism.
In the 1950s, secular Yiddishist schools taught varied attitudes toward Israel. Some yeshivas in the orthodox Haredi movement still today oppose Zionism on religious grounds, believing that Jewish sovereignty should only be established through the coming of the Messiah.
But Krasner could not name another day school that has Achvat Olam’s goal: education for Jewish families who disavow the current-day political realities of Israel and Zionism. In the aftermath of the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, many day schools went the opposite direction, adding curricula to strengthen solidarity between Diaspora Jews and Israel.
“The initial response of the organized Jewish community was, understandably, to circle the wagons and to reinforce their connections to Israel and to the Israeli people,” Krasner said.
Jack Wertheimer, a professor of American Jewish history at the Conservative movement’s Jewish Theological Seminary, isn’t convinced that Achvat Olam will change that trend. He said he was “highly skeptical” that Robbins could attract enough families to sustain a school. According to historical data, he said, Jews who lean more politically left tend to be less engaged in Jewish life.
“From what I know, the overwhelming majority of parents who are interested in sending their children to Jewish day schools are pro-Israel,” said Wertheimer.
Surveys have seen drop in Americans’ support for Israel
Nonetheless, Robbins believes that the market for her school is growing. Survey after survey has captured a drop in Americans’ support for Israel since the Gaza war, and Jews are not an exception to the trend.
After decades of being treated as fringe in many of their communities, left-wing Jews who are anti-Zionist, or simply do not see Israel as part of their identity, say that instead of adapting to their congregations and Jewish schools, the institutions should adapt to them.
There are signs that this group makes up a substantial portion of Jews in the United States.
About 30% of Jewish adults believe that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, according to a June poll of 1,022 Jews from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, which had a 5% error margin. Less than 40% said that “supporting Israel” was crucial to their Jewish identity.
At the same time, among adults who identified as religiously Jewish, younger people said they emphasized Jewish traditions more than their older counterparts. Younger Jews were more likely than older ones to say that “celebrating Jewish holidays” and “celebrating or marking Shabbat” were important to them, while Jews over 45 placed more emphasis on “remembering the Holocaust” and “supporting Israel” than younger ones.
This finding could reflect the growing share of younger Jews who are Orthodox. It also comes amid a boom in Jewish leftist organizations that explicitly ground their activism in religious tradition.
IfNotNow, an anti-occupation group that has grown from 1,000 dues-paying members in 2023 to 7,000 this year, says it is “growing a community rooted in Jewish values and ritual.”
The anti-Zionist Jewish Voice for Peace, which has amassed 32,000 dues-paying members, often frames its protests through Jewish holidays, texts and prayer.
Robbins is betting that a significant pool of younger Jews, many of them now parents to young children, are seeking avenues to both protect their Jewish traditions and reset their community’s relationship with Israel for the next generation.
Instead of supporting Israel, Achvat Olam says that its students will learn a curriculum of “collective liberation at home, globally, and in Israel/Palestine.”
“This is a very experimental moment in Jewish history. The Jewish left is growing by leaps and bounds,” said Robbins, referencing estimates of dozens of anti-Zionist congregations and prayer groups sprouting across the country. “There is hunger for this.”
Boston is a hub for such new organizations. Since 2024, the city has hosted the Conference on the Jewish Left at Boston University, a gathering of left-wing Jewish scholars, students, activists and faith leaders.
The first annual meeting drew 300 people, the second 700, and the third in February saw more than 900 participants. A poll of Greater Boston by Combined Jewish Philanthropies, the central fundraising arm of Boston’s Jewish community, found earlier this year that 38% of Jews aged 18 to 29 identified as “anti-Zionist,” and another 30% said they were “uncommitted” to Zionism or anti-Zionism.
Rabbi Greg Hersh left his congregation at Temple Emmanuel in Wakefield, north of Boston, in 2024. He said he became increasingly alienated from his congregants after Oct. 7. Hersh felt that the congregation, focused on supporting Israel and fighting antisemitism locally, did not share his anguish about the deaths of Palestinians.
Last year, Hersh founded V’ahavtah, a mostly Cambridge-based congregation devoted to “practicing Judaism beyond Zionism.” V’ahavtah joined Jews, like him, who felt uncomfortable with the norm of Israeli flags flying inside synagogues.
Their Shabbat services regularly draw 30 to 40 people, numbers he said he never saw in Wakefield. He believes that is proof of growing demand for non-Zionist Jewish institutions.
“You take Israel out of the equation and the Jews will show up, and that’s what happened with V’ahavtah,” said Hersh. “My expectation is Achvat Olam is going to be very well poised to fill that void.”
Challenges in funding the school
On the ground, Robbins faces formidable obstacles to funding Achvat Olam. Jewish day schools struggle across the country to attract enrollment in the face of tuition that many families can’t afford, along with budgets strained by economic uncertainty and heightened spending to ward off security threats.
Earlier this year, MetroWest Jewish Day School in Framingham, a suburb of Boston, shuttered and said that its “model of highly individualized Jewish day school education is no longer sustainable.”
Heavy investments from local philanthropies have helped day schools offset high costs. Prizmah, a national network of 305 day schools, recently reported that it saw enrollment rise across denominations for the first time last year, thanks in large part to philanthropy.
But many groups that fund Jewish education hold values that are antithetical to Robbins, including CJP, which calls itself a “pro-Israel, Zionist organization.” Prizmah and CJP declined requests for comment from JTA.
The individual donors who fund Jewish schools also tend to be older, more conservative than Robbins and more motivated by support for Israel, according to Krasner.
“The people who are most likely to be in a financial position to support day schools with generous philanthropic gifts are demographically very different from the population that Leah is trying to attract,” he said.
Robbins admitted that funding challenges meant the success of Achvat Olam was not “any sort of inevitability.” But she believes there is inevitability to the political momentum that could drive families toward such a school. “Something I want to convey to people is that the train has already left the station,” she said. “There is no stemming the tide of the growth of the Jewish left.”
Robbins has turned to funding from left-wing organizations, which already siphon much of their resources to grassroots activism, legal defense and awareness campaigns.
“It can be hard to get in the face of people to make the case for something that requires long-game thinking,” she said. “I’m trying to make the case, when the last fire has been put out, what’s going to be left if we’re not building it right now?”

UK PM Burnham says Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote

04:22:02 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit vote, as he warned voters in France and Germany about Moscow-backed efforts to influence their politics.
Burnham, who took over as Britain's leader in July and said last month that Britain could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, is the first British prime minister to say openly there was evidence of Russian interference in the referendum a decade ago.
"I asked the question coming to Downing Street, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I've had the clear answer that yes, there was," Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday.
Burnham did not spell out how he believed that Russia interfered in the referendum and gave no details on what evidence this statement was based.
The Russian embassy in London did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia has previously denied meddling in the Brexit vote, casting Britain as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.
Burnham's Russian interference claims contrast with Boris Johnson's position
Burnham's comments mark a departure from those of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU, and said in 2020 there was no evidence of Russian interference in the referendum.
Britons voted 52%-48% to leave the EU in 2016, plunging the country into its biggest political crisis since World War Two.
Burnham said voters in European democracies needed to be better informed about efforts to disrupt their politics.
"I mean, these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said.
2020 UK intelligence report failed to establish Russian interference in Brexit vote
Britain's government failed to establish whether Russia meddled in the 2016 referendum on membership of the EU, according to a report by parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee in 2020.
The report also found that Russia had sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, in which voters rejected independence.
Burnham last month said he could campaign to take Britain back into the EU at the next general election, reopening the country’s divisive debate on its relationship with the continent.

Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

04:19:50 KST

Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
US President Trump’s bid to bring down diesel prices by easing sanctions on Russia has prompted rare Republican criticism.
United States Senator Thom Tillis has questioned the legality of President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily relax sanctions on Russian diesel, in an effort to bring down record-high fuel prices caused by the US-Israel war against Iran.
During a Sunday interview on the NBC News television show Meet the Press, Tillis argued that the sanctions relief could violate congressional law.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” said Tillis.
Trump’s decision has unsettled some Republican lawmakers who continue to support Ukraine in its war with Russia, which began in February 2022, after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of the eastern European country.
Tillis warned that his vote in support of Trump’s legislative priorities would be contingent on the White House reversing course.
“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” Tillis said.
Tillis has become a critical voice within the Republican Party, denouncing what he sees as overreach from the Trump administration.
But his time as a senator is nearly at a close. In June 2025, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in the November 3 midterm elections, after Trump threatened him with a primary challenge in his home state of North Carolina. His term ends in January.
Separately on Sunday, Tillis joined a bipartisan group of senators in issuing a letter to denounce the sanctions relief for Russia.
The group included Republicans like Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Curtis of Utah, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal.
“The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” the senators wrote.
Another retiring Republican lawmaker, Representative Don Bacon, also said on Friday that “propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities”.
The pushback points to schisms within the Republican Party over Russia’s invasion.
Figures from the party’s establishment wing have generally pressed for robust support for Kyiv, while other party members have been sceptical of continued US support for Ukraine.
Trump himself has been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusing the government in Kyiv of impeding a US-negotiated ceasefire.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does,” Trump said on Saturday. “That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
A day earlier, Trump had announced that a call with Putin had concluded with an agreement to provide 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the global marketplace, with a further 500,000 tonnes to be delivered in November.
In an interview with Fox and Friends on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the administration’s decision to ease some sanctions on Moscow was necessary to obtain relief from surging diesel prices.
“We’re going to do it with all the legal authorities we have,” Bessent said.
Analysts have said that the decision is unlikely to bring prices down in the long term. Critics like Tillis have also pointed to previous law barring the importation of Russian fuel, including a 2022 executive order.
A law signed last month — named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — also prohibits US investment in the Russian energy sector.
This year’s rise in global fuel prices has largely been attributed to the US-Israel war against Iran, which began in February. As a result of that war, Iran has limited commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the fuel trade.
Tillis pointed to those circumstances in his remarks to Meet the Press.
“ If President Trump wants to end the strain on energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran, and number two, recognise that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war,” Tillis said.
“It’s Vladimir Putin who owns the responsibility for energy prices to the extent that they come from that part of the world.”
Trump’s decision also garnered international criticism, with the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issuing a statement in support of Ukraine.
“This agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” Carney’s office said in a read-out of a call on Sunday with Zelenskyy. “It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine.”

Two Indian sailors missing after vessel attacked off Oman

Bennett says Netanyahu could serve as minister in his cabinet, drawing fury from opposition leaders

04:00:07 KST

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett triggered a public clash within the camp seeking to replace Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday after saying he would have no objection to the incumbent prime minister serving as a minister in a future Bennett-led government, provided he accepted a series of fundamental reforms. Within hours, three other opposition leaders rejected the prospect, insisting Netanyahu should have no place in the next cabinet.
Speaking at an election conference organized by the Hador newspaper, Bennett, chairman of the Beyachad party, said: "As long as we get our fundamental principles, I have no problem with Netanyahu serving as a minister in our government." The statement came just over two weeks before Israel's October 27 election, with the makeup of a possible alternative coalition a central point of contention.
"In 2003, Netanyahu, and I say this to his credit, was one of the best finance ministers Israel has had," he said. "I don't know whether a man approaching 80 still has the energy for that, but if he accepts all our central principles, including an immediate state commission of inquiry, conscription for everyone and a constitution for Israel, he should pick up the phone."
Bennett gave no indication of contacts with Netanyahu or any offer of a portfolio. He made the possibility conditional on reforms that are central to the election campaign, particularly accountability for the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack and military conscription. But the suggestion alone brought a swift backlash from opposition leaders.
Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan reject idea
Former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, responded at the same conference. "I don't accept that," he said. "Anyone who was in office on October 7 is not fit to hold positions of command and leadership, including as finance minister." His response rejected the idea that Netanyahu's economic record justified a return to government.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Lieberman demanded that Bennett withdraw his statement. "I call on my colleagues in the Zionist bloc to make it absolutely clear: Even if the world turns upside down, we will not sit with Netanyahu," he said. "In the next government, Netanyahu will not be able to serve even as regional cooperation minister."
Yair Golan, a retired major general and chairman of The Democrats, issued an equally categorical rejection. "Netanyahu will not sit in any government as long as it depends on The Democrats. Not as finance minister, not as water minister and not as a minister without portfolio," he said.
"The man responsible for the October 7 failure, who led a government that promoted mass draft evasion during wartime and the judicial overhaul, will not receive from us any approval to return to power," Golan said. "We will not sit with Netanyahu and his partners. Period."
Draft policy sharpens divide
Earlier Sunday, Bennett had taken a far more confrontational tone toward Netanyahu while unveiling what he calls a "service revolution," a program intended to channel public money toward soldiers and reservists and away from Israelis who avoid military service. Bennett pledged to redirect 30 billion shekels from what he described as subsidies for draft dodgers to those who serve.
His proposal includes free daycare for reservists, 50% discounts on certain payments and a housing subsidy of 1 million shekels for eligible service members. He accused Netanyahu of funding draft evasion for political survival and warned that the IDF faces a shortage of 20,000 soldiers.
"A vote for Netanyahu and Deri, who promise another four years of state-funded draft evasion, is a vote that guarantees the next disaster," Bennett said, referring to Netanyahu and Shas leader Aryeh Deri. "For 17 years, Netanyahu has funded draft evasion in exchange for staying in power. Netanyahu is dismantling the IDF, and he knows it."
The contrast between that earlier attack and the later suggestion of a possible ministerial role for Netanyahu sharpened the dispute. The same issue Bennett made central to his campaign, military service for all, was one of the conditions he said Netanyahu would have to accept to join his government.
A fractured election landscape
Military service has also become a dividing line among smaller parties. Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party unveiled a proposal Sunday to increase pay for soldiers and double the salaries of combat troops toward the end of mandatory service, while allowing up to 25% of each Haredi draft-age cohort to be recognized as full-time Torah scholars, exempting them from army service.
Winter has repeatedly said he would recommend only Netanyahu to lead the next government. Yet Likud has launched a paid social media effort against Winter's party, seeking to keep it below the electoral threshold. That campaign has prominently targeted Winter's No. 2 candidate, Arab Israeli activist Yoseph Haddad, who, according to the earlier report, rejected efforts by Netanyahu's aides to recruit him onto Likud's Knesset list.
Taken together, the disputes leave the parties contesting the October 27 election arguing not only over the draft, accountability and political reform, but also over the composition of any government formed afterward. Bennett has now laid out conditions under which he would be willing to serve alongside Netanyahu; Eisenkot, Lieberman and Golan have made clear that, for them, a Netanyahu-free cabinet is itself a condition.

War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:47:57 UTC
03:47:57 KST

War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
The US-Israel war on Iran and its inflationary impact will dominate the agenda.
Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
The US-Israel war on Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact are slated to dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, held outside Washington for the first time in three years.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters News Agency that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023.
Notably absent will be United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some “domestic engagements”, a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16.
Several other finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said.
Bessent’s decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine’s battle against Russia’s invasion, and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
Fossil energy reserve release
The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who is keen to see lower petrol prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
More than one billion barrels of oil have been released, mainly from onshore commercial inventories, since the start of the war on February 28. But industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fuelling pressure on prices.
The IMF has signalled little change in its forecast for three percent global growth in 2026, and may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia’s invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.
One headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War II and will exceed 100 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) before 2030.
Advanced economies, led by the US, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, weather extremes triggered by the El Nino climate phenomenon, and a lack of investment in artificial intelligence (AI), which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.
Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400bn in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10 percent of revenue on average.
Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programmes that call for fewer but deeper reforms as a condition for approving lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.

The president who can’t say his name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:45:36 UTC
03:45:36 KST

Three weeks before Michigan decides whether to send the first Muslim senator to Washington, the president still cannot or will not say the man’s name.
“Mike Rogers, the great American Patriot and Republican Candidate for the U.S. Senate from Michigan, completely obliterated Mohammed El-Sayed in the big debate tonight,” Trump wrote on Truth Social after Thursday’s debate.
Rogers had skipped it.
“Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the U.S. fail.”
The candidate’s name is Abdul El-Sayed. Mohamed is his middle name, inherited from his Egyptian immigrant father. He rarely uses it. Yet the president repeats it so relentlessly that it reads less like a mistake than a strategy distilled into a single word.
El-Sayed has stopped pretending to be surprised.
“He knows my name is Abdul,” he said. “He says it every day.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the attacks “bigoted bulls—,” adding that El-Sayed “is on the road to being the next Senator from Michigan no matter how much bigoted bulls— a weak and desperate Donald Trump throws at him.”
Dawud Walid, of the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, recognized the tactic for what it was.
“He is intentionally saying his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, to say, ‘Look, this guy is outside what we would consider to be a normative America.’ It’s a political tactic, and we’ve seen it before.
READ: American Senate candidate accuses Netanyahu of pushing US into Iran war
The cruelty is not what is remarkable here. The timing is.
A sitting president does not usually spend the final weeks of a campaign fixated on a single state’s Senate race unless he believes something larger rides on it.
Something does.
Michigan’s open Senate seat, vacated by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, sits inside a chamber Republicans currently control 53 to 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats on Nov. 3 to take it back, and Michigan would not count among those gains. It is a seat they already hold, and one of the two Democratic-held seats Republicans most want to flip.
A Rogers victory would enlarge the Republican majority and make an already narrow Democratic path elsewhere even tighter. An El-Sayed victory would leave the arithmetic exactly where it stands.
The real stakes, then, are not whether Michigan can flip the Senate in a single stroke. The question is whether Republicans can afford to miss even one opportunity to widen their majority, particularly in a state the president carried twice.
The polling suggests they may not be able to.
El-Sayed led by just over three points in the RealClearPolitics average through Oct. 6, 48.1 to 44.9. Marist put him up seven points in late September. So did Suffolk. Even Fox News, hardly a sympathetic outlet, found him ahead by one point among likely voters in its most recent poll. That marked a reversal from August, when Rogers led by four.
Bettors on Polymarket now give El-Sayed a 69 percent chance of winning.
Money has followed the nerves.
Through Oct. 10, Republican-aligned spending in the race had reached $78 million, compared with $63 million from Democrats. Nearly all of it has been funneled into advertisements branding El-Sayed, a Rhodes Scholar and physician, as “dangerously radical” and “too extreme.”
The ads tie him to Hasan Piker, a streamer who once said America “deserved 9/11,” in the hope that the association will stick where attacks on his policies have not.
Trump himself has yet to set foot in Michigan to campaign for Rogers. El-Sayed has turned the president’s absence into a taunt of his own.
Standing before a crowd in Port Huron this month, dressed in a black V-neck shirt and gripping a handheld microphone, he issued a challenge.
“Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man.”
He has called Rogers a coward. He has called the president afraid.
The nerves extend far beyond Michigan.
READ: Former military secretary accuses Netanyahu’s office of falsifying Oct. 7 records
Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by roughly nine points in Nate Silver’s running average, their widest margin of the cycle. For the first time, they have broken 50 percent support. Trump’s approval rating sits in the high 30s across most tracking polls.
Forecasters now give Democrats an 82 percent chance of retaking the House and better-than-even odds of capturing the Senate.
Should both chambers fall, the final two years of this presidency would unfold before a Congress armed with subpoena power and with nothing left to trade.
That is the arithmetic from which a lame duck is made. It is why one Senate race in one Midwestern state has drawn the kind of presidential attention usually reserved for an election with Trump’s own name on the ballot.
El-Sayed is not without self-inflicted wounds.
Leaked audio captured him declining to take a clear position on the death of Iran’s former supreme leader, out of deference to grieving constituents in Dearborn. The recording gave Republicans an opening they have refused to relinquish.
Some Michigan Democrats, including strategist Adrian Hemond, have worried aloud that El-Sayed’s reluctance to court skeptical factions within his own party could cost Democrats a seat they should hold comfortably.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who remained neutral during the primary, has since worked to unify the party behind him. The alternative, she warned, is a senator “beholden to President Trump.”
Even El-Sayed’s allies acknowledge that his candidacy is built on remaking the electorate, not courting its center.
None of this guarantees him a seat in the Senate.
Three weeks is a long time. Leads within a poll’s margin of error can vanish overnight. Michigan Republicans have not won a Senate race since 1994, for reasons that reach far beyond any single candidate.
Rogers knows that history better than most. He lost to Slotkin by less than a point in 2024—close enough to keep him running, but not close enough to make Republicans comfortable about running him again.
Yet a president reduced to repeatedly misnaming his opponent on a platform built for far graver pronouncements is offering an answer of his own.
Strength does not usually sound like that.
Fear sometimes does.

====================================================================================================

Saudi Arabia needs allies against the Houthis, but will it turn to Israel? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:30:52 UTC
03:30:52 KST

US President Donald Trump lives in a transactional foreign policy universe. You give, you get. You don’t give, don’t expect much.
Israel has given a lot and, in return, gotten a lot. It has fought wing to wing with the US in Iran, provided valuable intelligence and demonstrated the military capabilities Washington wants to see in an ally.
In April, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, “To our Israeli allies, thanks for being a brave, capable and willing ally on this battlefield. The rest of the world and the rest of our so-called allies saw what real capabilities look like. They should take some notes.”
America’s “legacy” allies – from NATO countries to South Korea – have not stepped up to anywhere near the same degree. They have consequently been on the receiving end of more than just harsh words.
Trump ordered joint military exercises with South Korea scaled back, citing Seoul’s refusal to help with the Iran campaign, and threatened to cut off trade with Spain after Madrid denied Washington the use of its bases for strikes on Iran.
And then there is Saudi Arabia.
Many have been puzzled by Washington’s reluctance to intervene directly in the Saudis’ battle with the Houthis. This battle took a particularly deadly turn on Saturday when the King Khalid Airport in Riyadh was struck by a missile, killing 12 people and injuring more than 300, the most serious attack in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
This came as tensions between the Saudis and the Houthis steadily escalated – Saturday’s attack was the third such attack in a week, since the Saudis launched a counter-offensive against the Houthis to push them back from the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Despite all that, Trump has wavered. Washington has provided intelligence and targeting assistance, but the president has so far stopped short of direct military intervention. On Saturday, he said he was considering joining the Saudi strikes.
Why the hesitation?
The explanations offered range from reluctance to become engaged in another major military campaign less than a month before the midterm elections to concern about weapons stocks depleted by the war in Iran.
Saudi Arabia's refusal to join the Abraham Accords
Another possible explanation is Trump’s frustration with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s steadfast refusal to join the Abraham Accords. Saudi normalization with Israel would have given Trump an important diplomatic prize before the elections.
If this is indeed the case, then it fits into a pattern. In July, the US and Saudi Arabia signed a nuclear cooperation agreement, opening the door to a major commercial role for American companies. Trump then said he would not proceed unless the Saudis joined the Abraham Accords.
You give, you get.
Saudi normalization with Israel has long been the Middle East’s diplomatic holy grail.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, said in a long, revealing interview with Israel Hayom on Thursday that the desire to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords helped explain Israel’s restraint toward Hamas and Hezbollah in the run-up to October 7.
Israel wanted to avoid an escalation that could derail the normalization process. He said the two countries were “closer than people realize” to a deal.
But Israeli action didn’t scuttle the process. Hamas did that all on its own.
Since then, the Saudis have made clear – even as the Iranian threat loomed larger and normalization with Israel made good strategic sense in trying to create a new security architecture for the region – that without a pathway to a Palestinian state, they were not going to normalize.
That leaves a familiar gap between strategic logic and political feasibility, since – with October 7 so fresh and raw – it is highly unlikely that any Israeli government in the foreseeable future would agree to a Palestinian state.
Israel and Saudi Arabia face threats from Iran and its allies. Both have an interest in preventing the Houthis from threatening shipping, airports, and regional stability. Those shared interests provide a strong argument for cooperation. They have not, however, proven enough to overcome the political obstacles to establishing an open relationship.
Further evidence of where Riyadh was looking for its regional security architecture came in August, when it signed a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. Rather than bringing its relationship with Israel into the open, Saudi Arabia was strengthening an alternative framework with two Muslim powers.
The pact’s promise was sweeping: an attack on one would be considered an attack on all. So far, the response to the Houthi campaign has not matched that rhetoric. Turkey has reportedly begun providing defensive and technical assistance, but that is a long way from joining Saudi Arabia in striking the enemy attacking it.
Signing this pact showed that Saudi Arabia – while interested in maintaining intelligence cooperation with Israel and keeping it discreet – was seeking far-reaching security arrangements elsewhere.
Then an Omani pilot planned to crash a flydubai plane full of Israeli passengers into Ben-Gurion Airport, only to be thwarted by some brave and resourceful passengers and crew members, and Jerusalem got an unvarnished view of where it stands with the Saudis.
Yes, the Saudis allowed a distressed plane full of Israeli passengers to land at a civilian-military airfield in Tabuk. And, yes, Saudi medical personnel cared for Israeli passengers. Both were consequential acts of assistance in a moment of acute danger.
But Riyadh adamantly refused Israel’s request to send its own aircraft to collect the passengers. A replacement flydubai plane brought them home.
Cooperation, but to a point
This exposed the boundary between practical cooperation and public acceptance. Allowing an Israeli plane to pick up the passengers would be one gesture too far on the road to normalization: one which would have been staunchly opposed by much of the Saudi public and undoubtedly weaponized against the Saudis by the Iranians.
Whatever the precise calculations behind that refusal, the political message was clear: cooperation could proceed, but only so far.
Ten days later, Saudi Arabia’s own airport was targeted, and all of a sudden it is looking for allies in its fight with the Houthis.
That attack inevitably led to speculation that this might bring Israeli-Saudi security cooperation into the open and lead to closer ties to combat a common threat. Weakening the Houthis, after all, would serve Israeli interests as well as Saudi ones. The group’s hostility toward Israel is not exactly a secret.
But shared enemies don’t necessarily lead to joint military operations. Public Israeli involvement could carry political costs for Riyadh and provide ammunition for those seeking to portray the Saudi campaign as serving Israel.
The Saudi leadership would have to weigh those costs against the benefits of the assistance. Israel, in turn, would have to decide what risks it should take on the Saudis’ behalf and what it could expect in return.
While the airport attack does not guarantee a breakthrough between Israel and Saudi Arabia, it does force Riyadh to face this question: does it make sense to keep one of its potentially strongest regional partners at arm’s length?
And for Israel, the question is a variation on Trump’s transactional theme: How much should it give when the Saudis are still unwilling to publicly be seen taking?

Nude Trump sculpture sparks political controversy at European Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
18:26:08 UTC
03:26:08 KST

Nude Trump sculpture sparks political controversy at European Parliament
TEHRAN- A gold-covered sculpture depicting US President Donald Trump naked and sitting on the back of a frail man has sparked a political controversy at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, drawing criticism from several European lawmakers and a call by Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico for its removal, while others have defended the artwork as a form of political satire and freedom of expression.
Created by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, the 2.6-meter sculpture, titled “The Orange Plague” and also known as “The King of Injustice,” was unveiled on October 7 as part of a three-day exhibition hosted by Danish Member of the European Parliament Per Clausen. The installation was removed on October 8, according to Italian broadcaster Sky TG24, which reported that the exhibition had been scheduled to run for three days.
The work portrays Trump as a naked, overweight figure covered in 23-karat gold leaf, holding a golf club in one hand and scales of justice in the other. He sits on the shoulders of a smaller, frail man, whose posture suggests that he is struggling under the weight, while a globe resembling a golf ball lies near the man's feet.
An inscription at the base of the sculpture offers a pointed commentary on the relationship between power and responsibility.
“I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back,” the inscription reads.
The text presents an ironic image of a powerful figure who claims to help those beneath him while refusing to abandon the position that causes their suffering.
According to Euronews and The Art Newspaper, Galschiøt conceived the work as a protest against Trump's climate and foreign policies, which he believes undermine international cooperation and efforts to address the climate crisis.
Slovak prime minister calls for removal
The exhibition drew criticism from Robert Fico, who called on European Parliament President Roberta Metsola to have the sculpture removed.
According to Slovakia's news agency TASR, Fico objected to the installation despite acknowledging his disagreements with some of Trump's policies. He argued that political differences should not justify what he regarded as an insult to a partner country on the premises of a European institution.
Fico also questioned whether those supporting the display would accept similar depictions of French President Emmanuel Macron or German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. His remarks brought diplomatic sensitivities into a debate over the limits of political satire.
Other lawmakers also criticized the artwork. Belgian MEP Barbara Bonte described the installation as a disgrace, while Hungarian lawmaker Ernő Schaller-Baross questioned what he considered a double standard in the treatment of political leaders. Irish MEP Barry Cowen also called the sculpture “silly and objectionable” and said he had written to the parliament to express his opposition.
The objections highlighted divisions within the European Parliament over whether the sculpture represented legitimate political expression or an inappropriate use of the institution's premises.
Danish lawmaker defends the display
The sculpture was brought to Strasbourg at the invitation of Danish MEP Per Clausen, who defended the decision to exhibit it.
Clausen, who invited Galschiøt to exhibit the sculpture, dismissed concerns about a possible negative reaction from Trump.
“If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage,” Clausen said, according to Euronews.
The exhibition was approved by the European Parliament's quaestors, a cross-party group responsible for certain administrative matters. The approval allowed the work to be shown in designated exhibition space but did not make it an official artwork commissioned or endorsed by the institution.
Galschiøt has described the sculpture as a personal attack on Trump, an approach he said differed from his usual focus on political systems.
“Normally I attack systems, but in this case, I will attack Trump personally,” the artist told The Art Newspaper.
 
Galschiøt said the work was intended to draw attention to the reluctance of governments and organizations to challenge the US president openly because of potential economic and political consequences.
“Nations as well as NGOs are afraid to openly raise the subject [of] how to deal with Trump and his policies, fearing tariffs, fund-cuts, deportations or the like,” the artist wrote on his website, in a statement quoted by The Art Newspaper.
The sculpture's gold finish also carries a satirical message. Galschiøt told the publication that Trump's extensive use of gold in his properties, including the Oval Office, inspired the decision to cover the figure in the precious metal.
The artist also drew inspiration from Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale “The Emperor's New Clothes”, in which a vain ruler parades naked while those around him pretend that he is wearing magnificent garments. The story's central theme — the reluctance to challenge authority even when its failings are obvious — reinforces the sculpture's political message.
Miniature replicas extend the protest
The Strasbourg exhibition was accompanied by an effort to circulate the artwork beyond the parliament building. Galschiøt produced approximately 20,000 miniature, 3D-printed versions of the sculpture, distributing them to visitors and parliament staff. He also made the digital design files freely available online for people wishing to print their own copies.
The idea was inspired by Hong Kong's democracy movement, whose supporters produced miniature reproductions of Galschiøt's "Pillar of Shame". The original sculpture, created in 1997 to commemorate human rights violations including the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, was dismantled in Hong Kong in 2021.
“The Orange Plague” had previously appeared at demonstrations in Copenhagen opposing US pressure over Greenland and at the COP30 United Nations climate conference in Belém, Brazil, in 2025.
Following its Strasbourg appearance, Galschiøt planned to display the sculpture again at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, in November 2026.
In a report published on October 9, Euronews also placed the installation within a broader tradition of satirical art targeting Trump, noting how artists have used exaggerated and often gilded depictions of the president to challenge his public image and political influence.
The controversy surrounding the sculpture illustrates how political art can become a point of contention over freedom of expression, diplomatic sensitivities and the role of public institutions.

Tehran hosts art exhibition, live painting workshop on True Promise
TEHRAN- The second edition of the painting exhibition and live art workshop “True Promise in the Mirror of Art” is currently underway at Palestine Square in Tehran, with artists and members of the public taking part in the event.
The program runs daily from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. and will continue until October 16, Mehr reported.
The event is part of the visual arts section of the second international “True Promise in the Mirror of Art” program. It is hosted by the Greater Tehran Basij of Artists, in cooperation with the Basij unit of the National Iranian Oil Products Distribution Company and the artistic affairs department of the Foundation of Martyrs and Veterans Affairs’ cultural and educational deputy, the report added.

The second international “True Promise in the Mirror of Art” event is organized by the Basij Organization of Artists, with Mohammad Najjari serving as its secretary.
The “True Promise” operations are a series of Iranian military actions launched in response to Israeli attacks. The first operation, in April 2024, involved missile and drone strikes against Israel following an Israeli attack on Iran’s diplomatic compound in Damascus on April 1. A second operation took place in October 2024, after the killing of senior figures in Iran and allied groups. In June 2025, Iran launched Operation True Promise III in retaliation for Israeli strikes on Iranian territory, during the 12-day conflict. The operations have become a prominent theme in Iran’s official discourse on national defense and are also reflected in cultural and artistic events.
