US Lt-Gen Salene critiques Netanyahu, Israeli government for stalling Trump's Gaza plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:43:40 UTC
23:43:40 KST

US Security Coordinator Lt.-Gen. Sean M. Salene has made a speech in which he, as softly as possible yet firmly, went after the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for stalling aspects of the Trump administration that strengthen the Palestinian Authority in Gaza, especially regarding training a new Palestinian police force.
Speaking recently at the Reichman University Institute for counterterrorism (ICT), Salene did not name Netanyahu, but said that counterterrorism is a much broader campaign than just using military force.
He stated that counterterrorism, in his view, meant that "you cannot address it only through the military lane. Addressing counterterrorism also has to address the ideology, has to address the education, and has to address the societal conditions which support the evolution of a terrorist organization."
"While some of these would be outside the authorities and the arena that I have, I will also share with you that there are very few serving officers in the United States military who focus on the West Bank problem set, 16 to be exact," he continued.
In contrast to Salene's argument, which is definitely supported by many counterterror academics and also some in the Israeli defense establishment, Netanyahu has focused almost entirely on using military force to defeat Hamas.
US officials accuse Netanyahu of delaying postwar Gaza security, governance plans
Netanyahu has publicly opposed making plans for any "Day After" in Gaza for three years. Regarding even the October 2025 Trump ceasefire plan he signed on to, top US officials have accused him of delaying those aspects designed to replace Hamas with new Palestinian political and security mechanisms in Gaza.
Salene also framed Israeli society as having jumped toward a new state of hyper risk-aversion when facing terrorism and other security dilemmas, "Because in your society and where we are right now, with the open fronts and the open question of Iran, I know that the risk tolerance here is very low, perhaps non-existent. The risk tolerance is low and non-existent."
"I would also share with you a reflection: the way that it appears to me that the IDF and other security professionals view threat. Normally, our doctrine tells us we view threat…as capability plus intent. What I have noticed now is that they reflect threat as capability. That many IDF security professionals view capability as equal in a threat, I think they're reflecting some of the policy guidance they receive and some of the societal pressures that they feel. But in this regard, it's helping to understand this environment," he noted.
In other words, Salene, while sympathetic to Israeli trauma after October 7, was telling his Israeli audience that going to the extreme of always focusing on the worst-case scenario of what enemy capabilities are is counterproductive and problematic.
While he wanted to support Israeli military officials in some respects, he challenged them to consider whether politicized policy guidance and social pressures, rather than expert judgment, are shaping their professional assessments.
Salene warns Hamas threat extends far beyond Gaza, West Bank
Next, he warned that the threat of Hamas itself is also much broader than its immediate forces on the ground confronting Israel.
"Hamas is then not confined just to one place. It's not confined to just Gaza. It's not confined to Judea and Samaria. It exists in Jordan and in Syria, and in Lebanon, and we have financiers in Florida, and in Europe. So this understanding is priority number one for counterterrorism: a broader view of Hamas as an ecosystem," stated the US general.
Here, Salene encouraged Israeli political and defense officials to look beyond the obvious physical battle space before them to think of Hamas as a movement, idea, and series of relationships which extend across the globe, and cannot be shut down by more force in Gaza and the West Bank alone.
In addition, Salene specifically complimented IDF Central Commander Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, saying, "You have an incredibly principled leader. An incredibly principled leader in IDF Central Command. Very difficult environment inside of your society. I'm speaking as a military officer to see another military officer attempting to enact his policy with the instruments he had, which now touches your political level."
With these remarks, Salene laid bare problems which Bluth and the Shin Bet have highlighted in terms of a lack of support from the political echelon and from the police in cracking down sufficiently against Jewish extremist violence and terror in the West Bank, even as all Israeli forces have worked well together to keep the larger Palestinian terror problem down.
Discussing security coordination with the PA, he said, "Security coordination. What is it then the United States can do to support the security coordination? There are two parts. The first part, respect and understand what exists and not get in the way."
"The second part is when that begins to break down and becomes very difficult. Where is it the United States can step in in order to assist if it gets difficult, there's tragedies this summer you can tell," he added.
Moreover, Salene said, "Tragedy. How is it that it didn't spiral? I will just share with you. There was effective security coordination. There was communication. There was an effort to de-escalate and contain the crisis so it did not spread. Why? If I zoomed out for a moment and said that if the crisis has spread and destabilized, would the destabilization only be confined to Judea and Samaria?"
Continuing, he asserted, "A destabilization is likely to affect the stability of Jordan. As a US Central Command officer, the stability of Jordan matters. It's important to you. It's important to us. It's important to the bigger picture, to the wider strategic question, which remains open."
Salene highlights role of Israeli-Palestinian security coordination in preventing escalation
Here, Salene was arguing that when Israeli and Palestinian security officials work well together, his office can just stay out of the way, but when they are not, he has stepped in at crucial moments to calm tense situations which could have blown up into much larger unnecessary conflicts.
Salene also reminded everyone that a destabilized West Bank can have concrete national security implications with Jordan, which has been an invaluable ally in counterintelligence against Palestinian terror.
Trying to convince some of the skeptical Israelis listening that US and Israeli security coordination with the PA pays off, he said, "21 years ago, we received funding from my government to provide police forces non-lethal training…we're not paying for an army. We don't support an army. We support police forces, and I offered that there were questions about what it is for the IDF and the security services."
He said that his office helps "enable the training, in accordance with international standards, human rights, and the rule of law, of a security partner to counter Hamas and terrorist threats. This is a particularly difficult conversation today. It's a particularly difficult conversation to have in this environment, but it is a necessary one."
He then asked rhetorically: "Because what is the alternative? What is the alternative? Is the alternative that the security forces in Judea and Samaria are not on the field? Would the gap remain open, or would it be filled? And if it be filled by a terrorist organization, or it be another command upon the IDF."
Realizing how hard it might be to convince some Israelis of the necessity of a US coordinator is necessary to help train PA forces, he volunteered that skeptics exist in the US as well, noting, "There are folks in my own government who say, 'Why should we spend another dollar? Over here in the Palestinian Authority, that's a corrupt institution. Yes, there is corruption. This is the instrument that we have. I am not a politician.
This is a political discussion, and it will quickly get to the political. I will speak to the practical and the technical."
Continuing, he stated, "In a practical and technical institutional capability in accounting, I will share with you that there are people on the other side who work on de-radicalization, who push on education, who know that their structure is wrong."
These comments hit Netanyahu at his most sensitive point. Of all of the aspects of the October 2025 ceasefire which Netanyahu did not like, but signed on to get the Israeli hostages back, allowing PA police into Gaza, trained by the US, Egypt, and Jordan, was the provision he opposed most vehemently.
Yet, where Netanyahu viewed creating a new Gaza police force associated with Fatah as strengthening PA military power which could confront Israel in the Strip, Salene said that any other alternative will lead to Hamas or Palestinian power brokers who disregard human rights and any vision of a stable future for Gazans.
Next, he revealed strengths and weaknesses of the process of the US and other countries coordinating with the PA.
He said that these allies are "a coalition of nations who also support the security of Israel, even when the political place gets very difficult at the technical place, at the military place to maintain this military architecture together for the day when the political winds have shifted, but the architecture remains for the support for defense of Israel."
"Now, the coalition that we lead has nine other nations inside this coalition. The United States coordinates inside this coalition to ensure it is not too far left, not too far right, down the middle to align these efforts. Other actors are on the stage who are not in our coalition. I want to argue there are other actors that have a relationship with the Palestinian authorities that's not in our interest. Russia and China would come to mind," he cautioned.
Salene urges negotiations, de-escalation to counter Hamas recruitment
Waxing philosophical, Salene then asked some additional rhetorical questions about some of the x-factors which go to the heart of the counterterrorism mission, "Back to the fundamental question: Which way is the terrorist ideology the people who are being marketed to being recruited, which way are they going to go? I would argue it is in our interest for those people to stay with the negotiation track, de-escalation, coordination to support a future negotiation, not to succumb to Hamas and the call to jihad."
Next, he stated, "So in this case, the provision of basic social services…undermines the Hamas' argument, which then helps us in the wider picture in a struggle with the movement, which extends far beyond this country."
"These are the ways that we do at the security system to disrupt, coordinate capability, legitimacy, and order, to get to a more durable stability, to one day open the stage for a larger conversation," he added.
Here, Salene tried to convince Israelis that providing a better life to Gazans is in Israel's interest since more stability will bring less conflict.
While a hard sell to Israelis after October 7, Salene argued there is still no real alternative.
CENTCOM and Lt.-Gen. Salene's office declined to comment regarding the article.

Where are the pilots who saved us? Flydubai survivor questions crew’s role in attack - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:43:35 UTC
23:43:35 KST

Eleven days after helping to overpower the co-pilot accused of trying to crash a flydubai flight bound for Israel, passenger Asaf Rajuan wants two flight attendants who were on board to be investigated. He has also called for the two additional pilots who were traveling and who landed the aircraft in Saudi Arabia to be questioned.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post on Sunday, Rajuan said he suspected the attendants had assisted the attacker. He described confrontations with passengers, objections to filming and exchanges between the two men that left him afraid the danger had continued after the co-pilot was restrained.
The September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the co-pilot attacked the captain with an aircraft emergency axe.
His allegations remain unsubstantiated. The UAE’s account on Friday credited a flight attendant with helping subdue the attacker. It said the co-pilot had confessed to acting alone, while making clear that investigators were still checking for accomplices and other connections.
Rajuan wants Israel involved in establishing what happened. In our conversation, he kept returning to the crew’s behavior and the difficulty of knowing whom to trust while the aircraft was still airborne.
He had been returning from Phuket, Thailand, with his wife and their two daughters, approaching 12 and 14. He was seated in 7D when a woman ran down the aisle shouting that someone had a knife. He looked toward his family and saw them thrown into the air.
He thought he was watching his daughters die.
He ran toward the front. The captain’s resistance had already weakened the attacker, Rajuan said, making it easier for passengers to overpower him. He suffered a small head wound and emerged covered in blood, much of which, he said, was not his own.
The suspicions about the attendants
Rajuan made his most specific accusation in an interview with N12’s Ulpan Shishi, broadcast Friday. He alleged that one attendant began loosening the attacker’s restraints after passengers had subdued him. Several passengers noticed and challenged the man, he said.
He also described an attendant approaching the wounded captain with a tablet while the captain was receiving medical treatment. Rajuan said passengers intervened because they could not understand why someone would try to give him a pill in that condition.
“I have no proof,” he said when asked whether the attendants had cooperated with the attacker.
In the interview with the Post, Rajuan described grabbing, pulling at clothing, and repeated confrontations with the attendants. One asked whether he was a police officer. He remembered their physical strength and their determination to stop passengers filming. He feared someone would produce another weapon.
There was uncertainty even about where the aircraft was heading. Passengers checked GPS locations and offered competing answers: Iraq, Jordan, Saudi Arabia. Rajuan wondered whether they were still being hijacked.
“I became paranoid,” he said.
He acknowledged that he had begun suspecting everyone. Yet he wanted investigators to examine the specific encounters he and other passengers remembered, including the attendants’ interactions with those guarding the attacker. He described an atmosphere of mutual fear and pressure that persisted after the immediate struggle had ended.
The pilots who took over
Rajuan also wanted to know what had become of the two additional pilots. He said he had looked for their public accounts and had not found them. On N12, he recalled last seeing the pilot who saved the aircraft as he disembarked.
Their presence aboard Flight FZ1073 has an explanation we reported on September 30.
There were four pilots: the captain who was attacked, his co-pilot, and a second flydubai cockpit crew traveling in the passenger cabin. The additional captain and co-pilot were available to operate the return flight from Israel.
A person familiar with the arrangement told the Post that possible regional diversions could add hours to the flight and leave the operating crew beyond its permitted working hours. The additional pilots had been assigned as a staffing precaution, without advance warning of an attack.
When I interviewed Tal, an Israeli businessman aboard the flight, at Tel Aviv’s Carlton hotel on October 1, he described having to get those men forward while other passengers fought the attacker.
“I had to shake them to get them to move to the front and take control of the plane,” he said.
Tal recalled an interval when the cockpit was empty. One pilot eventually took control; the other, he said, took longer to recover from the shock. We have not independently established the duration of that interval or the precise sequence inside the cockpit.
The UAE’s account described the relief captain noticing unusual movements of the cockpit door, entering with an access code and helping passengers and a flight attendant overpower the attacker. He and his co-pilot then restored control and landed in Tabuk.
It did not address Tal’s account of their initial hesitation or the empty cockpit.
The relief pilots have spoken to investigators: prosecutors said they had taken statements from both men. The statement did not name them.
Our interviews have reconstructed the emergency from the passenger cabin: people fighting at the front, an injured captain being treated, two other pilots being urged toward the controls. Rajuan wants the men who eventually flew the aircraft to give their own account, including what they saw of the attendants’ conduct.
“I hope that Israel will investigate it as it should be,” he said. “Because it’s something that needs answers.”

FEDA urges UN and European Parliament to take urgent action to protect hunger-striking detainees in Egyptian prisons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:42:56 UTC
23:42:56 KST

The Families of Egyptian Detainees Association (FEDA) has called on the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) to take urgent action following reports of hunger strikes and collective protests among detainees in several Egyptian prisons, particularly during 7th–9th October. The association warned of potential risks to detainees’ lives and health amid reported restrictions on fundamental rights and concerns over access to medical care.
In an urgent appeal dated 10th October 2026, FEDA urged the UN Working Group to seek clarification from the Egyptian authorities regarding the reported hunger strikes and the grievances behind them, and to take appropriate steps within its mandate to protect detainees from death, serious injury, ill-treatment, and reprisals for participating in peaceful protests.
As part of its international advocacy efforts concerning the situation of detainees in Egypt, FEDA has also sent similar letters to the European Parliament, urging urgent attention to detainees’ conditions, action to protect hunger strikers, and efforts to end reported violations in Egyptian prisons. The association called for respect for detainees’ fundamental rights, particularly the rights to life, healthcare, family visits, and a fair trial.
According to information received by FEDA, which the association says it is continuing to verify, the protests have been linked to deteriorating detention conditions, repeated alleged violations of detainees’ basic rights, and the absence of effective remedies for their complaints. Reports have referred to protests in several places of detention, including Minya, Abu Zaabal, Badr, the Tenth of Ramadan, and New Valley prisons. FEDA stressed that the level of available information and documentation varies between facilities.
Restrictions on family visits, exercise, and medical care
FEDA identified the main grievances reported by detainees and their families as the denial or severe restriction of family visits, deprivation of outdoor exercise and sunlight, obstruction or delay of necessary medical treatment, and prolonged pretrial detention in cases reportedly extending beyond applicable legal limits.
The association also expressed concern that despair arising from years of detention and repeated legal proceedings without a final resolution has led some detainees to resort to hunger strikes as a means of protesting their conditions and demanding that their grievances be addressed.
READ: Detainees to begin hunger strike in Egypt prisons
FEDA warned that hunger strikes can cause serious health complications, particularly for detainees with chronic illnesses or those denied adequate medical monitoring. It also called for scrutiny of reports of security interventions, detainee transfers, communication restrictions, and confiscation of personal belongings, stressing that such measures must not be used to punish individuals for peaceful protest.
Postponement of the new Criminal Procedure Code adds to detainees’ concerns
FEDA linked the growing frustration among detainees to prolonged pretrial detention and the postponement of Egypt’s new Criminal Procedure Code, Law No. 174 of 2025. The Code had been scheduled to enter into force on 1 October 2026, but its implementation was postponed for one year, until October 2027, according to the information cited in the appeal.
The association said that some detainees had hoped the new Code’s provisions concerning pretrial detention would lead to a review of their legal status or their release. The postponement, it argued, has deepened frustration among those who have already spent extended periods in custody.
FEDA stressed that postponement of the new Code should not justify detention beyond the limits established by the legislation currently in force. It called for the review of cases in which detainees may have exceeded applicable legal limits and for scrutiny of any use of successive cases or repeated proceedings to circumvent those limits and prolong detention.
FEDA concluded its appeal by urging urgent action to prevent further harm and address concerns regarding arbitrary and prolonged detention in Egypt. It also called on international and human rights institutions to monitor the situation of hunger strikers and work to ensure the protection of their fundamental rights.

Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
Trump has long criticised US military support for Ukraine and has lambasted Zelenskyy since his first term.
United States President Donald Trump has called for the removal of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after blaming the Ukrainian leader for rising diesel prices, which have put pressure on the Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections.
The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have increased after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Saturday, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump added.
Zelenskyy on Sunday pushed back, vowing to continue striking Russian oil refineries. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
This is not the first time Trump has lambasted Zelenskyy. Their tense relationship goes back to Trump’s first term as president, when he pressured Zelenskyy to investigate his rival, Joe Biden, and his son, Hunter Biden.
Here’s a timeline of some of the occasions when Trump has been critical of Zelenskyy:
October 2026: In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.
Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.
The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries.
Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished, he added.
April 2025: On April 15 , Trump criticised Zelenskyy and implied Kyiv had started the war against Russia, saying the Ukrainian leader was “always looking to purchase” US missiles. “You don’t start a war against someone 20 times your size and hope people give you some missiles,” Trump said.
Then on April 23 , he criticised Zelenskyy for making “very harmful” statements after the Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea of ceding occupied Crimea to Russia in a potential peace deal.
Zelenskyy had ruled out ceding any territory, declaring, “There is nothing to talk about – it is our land, the land of the Ukrainian people”.
In a post on his social media platform, Trump accused Zelenskyy of stoking tension by “boasting” that Kyiv would not legally recognise ceding Crimea to Russia.
“This statement is very harmful to the Peace Negotiations with Russia,” Trump said, adding that Russia invaded the Crimean Peninsula and annexed it back in 2014 “without a shot being fired”.
“It’s inflammatory statements like Zelenskyy’s that makes it so difficult to settle this War,” Trump said. “He can have Peace or, he can fight for another three years before losing the whole Country.”
Despite the tension, the two leaders held a private meeting at the Vatican on April 26, 2025, during Pope Francis’s funeral.
Feb 28, 2025: During their fiery Oval Office meeting, Trump and Vice President JD Vance clashed with Zelenskyy over rare earth mineral agreements, security assurances and peace negotiations with Russia.
Trump warned Zelenskyy, “You’re either going to make a deal [on ending the war with Russia] or we’re out,” and accused the Ukrainian leader of having “disrespected” the United States and “overplayed his hand”.
The US president and Vance also berated Zelenskyy for lacking gratitude and refusing to compromise to end the war, with Trump arguing that Zelenskyy was unready for peace.
The meeting devolved into a shouting match and Zelenskyy departed the White House abruptly.
February 19, 2025: A month after returning to power for a second term, Trump called the Ukrainian president a “dictator without elections” and accused him of wanting to keep the “gravy train” of US military support going while Washington tries to end the war with Russia.
In a lengthy and scathing post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump accused Zelenskyy of taking US money and embroiling the country in an endless conflict.
He later doubled down on those comments, telling an audience at an investment summit in Miami that Zelenskyy had “done a terrible job, his country is shattered, and millions and millions of people have unnecessarily died”.
“A dictator without elections. Zelenskyy better move fast or he’s not going to have a country left. Gotta move. Gotta move fast cause that war’s going in the wrong direction,” Trump said on stage at the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute summit.
“In the meantime, we’re successfully negotiating an end to the war with Russia. Something I’ll admit that only Trump is going to be able to do and the Trump administration – we’re going to be able to do it. I think Putin even admitted that,” he said.
“Biden never tried. Europe has failed to bring peace and Zelenskyy probably wants to, maybe he wants to keep the gravy train going. I don’t know what’s the problem, but he has been able. He’s very upset,” he added.
Trump had been critical of Biden’s financial and military support to Ukraine during the war. He had vowed to end the war within 24 hours of his taking office, but later said he was being “sarcastic”.
2024 Campaign trail: On the 2024 US presidential election campaign trail, Trump repeatedly criticised Zelenskyy for not trying hard enough to end Russia’s war on Ukraine. In September, at an election rally speech in North Carolina, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy for refusing to negotiate, stating that even the “worst deal” or giving up a small amount of territory would be better than ongoing death and destruction.
July 2019: During his first term, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to work with Rudy Giuliani and the US attorney general to investigate Democratic political rival Joe Biden. That is according to a five-page memo summarising the July 25 call.
At the time of the call, the Trump administration was also withholding from Ukraine nearly $400m in congressionally approved security assistance, prompting speculation the US president was using the money as leverage to get his desired investigations.
Zelenskyy expressed willingness to look into new cases and cooperate with US investigations, though he and Ukrainian officials later maintained they did not feel directly threatened or pressured during the conversation itself.

Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:25:03 UTC
23:25:03 KST

Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Airport reveal the limitations of even the most high-tech air defences.
Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), are hitting deep inside Saudi Arabia with waves of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times by the Houthis since their new military campaign against the kingdom began in September.
An attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded 309, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority was forced to suspend operations and diverted all flights, while the United States and United Kingdom issued new travel warnings for citizens.
The Houthis claimed two other attacks on the air hub earlier this week and on Sunday warned people to avoid Saudi airports.
Houthi weaponry
Saudi Arabia possesses one of the best-equipped militaries in the world, boasting advanced, multilayered air defence systems.
Saudi warplanes have pummelled Houthi positions across Yemen in the past week, seeking to roll back the Iran-backed group’s recent advances against the Yemeni government army, which Riyadh supports.
The Houthis’ own arsenal has come a long way since the group seized control of Sanaa from the government in September 2014.
Their drones and missiles have reached as far as Israel and, as their accuracy has shown, can hit particular targets such as Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Here’s what we know about the Houthis’ weaponry, how their tactics have changed and why Saudi air defences are struggling to keep pace.
How advanced is the Houthi arsenal?
The exact type of weapon used to attack Riyadh airport is unknown, but the Houthis have fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the 2015 intervention. The Iran-backed group has also targeted Israel and allegedly Israeli-linked vessels since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
The group has used its weapons in concert, mixing drones and missiles of varying speeds to confound air defences. The same mix has shaped Yemen’s ground war, with the Houthis pounding government positions for weeks before seizing the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month.
Among the group’s most advanced options are medium-range ballistic missiles such as the Palestine-2, a two-stage solid fuel missile believed to have a range of 2,000km with hypersonic capabilities. Another is the Toufan, which appears to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr missile, thought to have a range of between 1,350km and 1,950km.
The reach of those missiles – some carrying cluster warheads – has allowed the Houthis to breach Israel’s air defence network, some 2,000 km from Yemen.
The Houthis also maintain a number of short-range missiles, such as their Burkan and Badr series. They are also believed to be of Iranian origin and have been used in cross-border strikes into Saudi Arabia.
According to Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at Kings College War Studies Department, the Houthis’ missile arsenal is essentially derived from Iranian weaponry, with some Chinese technological influences.
“The Houthis have demonstrated little evidence of significant indigenous technological innovation,” he said. “Their domestic capabilities are largely confined to producing certain lower-end missiles and drones.”
Last month, Yemen’s government forces alleged that the Houthis have been receiving help from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to develop a new capability – loitering cruise missiles.
Why are Saudi defences struggling to keep up?
Saudi authorities say their forces shot down a number of projectiles over the past week, including a pair of ballistic missiles aimed at the capital on Thursday. But they failed to intercept the projectile that hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.
Nawaf Obaid told Al Jazeera that occasional penetration of Saudi air defences is to be expected, given the size of the kingdom and its border with Yemen.
“As much as you can have a multi-layered air defence system, one will always come through,” he said, pointing out that dozens of Houthi attempts are thwarted for each successful attack.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the main focus of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defence system was countering threats from Iran.
However, as the attacks from the Houthis increase, he views it as likely that the Saudis are re-orienting some of these defences towards Yemen.
There is also the issue of interceptor stocks. Saudi Arabia – along with many of the United States’ regional and global allies – has struggled with limited stockpiles of Patriot and THAAD munitions. These were rapidly expended by the US and its allies during the early months of the war with Iran.
Last month, Riyadh had reportedly reached out to a number of friendly countries to deploy air defence or other support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis.
Limitations
However, the Houthis are also fighting under serious constraints. The group is under a UN-mandated arms embargo, a years-long Saudi blockade, as well as fighting on several fronts across Yemen.
“Militarily, the Saudi-led coalition has the upper hand, but the Houthis can still dominate the headlines with occasional strikes against Saudi Arabia,” Obaid said.
“As the world’s largest crude oil exporter and a G20 economy, Saudi Arabia carries global responsibilities that make such attacks disproportionately visible.”
The exact size of the Houthis’ missile arsenal is unknown, calling into question the group’s ability to sustain attacks on Saudi Arabia, while simultaneously fighting a fierce ground war where missiles and drones have been used by the Iran-backed group.
Obaid said that Saudi Arabia’s air campaign in Yemen has focused heavily on targeting the group’s missile depots, underground installations and drone production facilities. The group is “inflicting enormous damage” on the Houthis’ military capabilities, he added.
Pusztai told Al Jazeera that the Houthis likely have just a limited number of short-range ballistic missiles left.
This would mean they would be incapable of launching saturation attacks, where multiple missiles and drones are fired at targets, such as in Saudi Arabia.
Instead, they could focus on aiming single missiles at less-defended civilian targets “to maximise the strategic impact of these attacks, in this case to disrupt civilian air traffic”.

Victor Mair and Benjamin Franklin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:21:01 UTC
23:21:01 KST

Victor Mair and Benjamin Franklin
« previous post | next post »
Wikipedia’s article on Benjamin Franklin starts this way:
Benjamin Franklin was an American polymath active as a physicist, philosopher, statesman and inventor.
The article goes on to list (some of) his other achievements, including his role as a writer, and as the founder of institutions such as the American Philosophical Society and what became the University of Pennsylvania. It omits many other things, including his contributions as an orthoepist and phonetician.
Franklin did none of this because he was trained to do it or hired to do it, but because he was curious about the world around him, and followed up in unexpected and consequential ways on chance encounters both common and rare.
Victor Mair was also active throughout his life in many different intellectual and cultural and physical areas. For regular readers of this blog, I don’t need to make a list — but I learned several new things about his history at yesterday's memorial service.
And Victor’s diverse activities were Franklin-esque. Like Franklin, he was involved in the world around him; curious about both ordinary and unique aspects of his experiences; and able to turn that curiosity into insights, discoveries, communications, and organizational support.
This pattern is less common among today’s academics than perhaps it should be, but Victor’s example shows us what’s possible.

Palestinian election delay fuels anger over political legitimacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:17:30 UTC
23:17:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Abbas' Palestinian election delay fuels anger over political legitimacy
The postponement of Palestinian elections until September 2027 has reignited questions over political legitimacy, accountability and the willingness of Palestinian factions to relinquish power, with citizens in Gaza questioning who benefits from another year without a vote.
The decision came after the Central Elections Commission announced it had completed its technical and administrative preparations to receive applications for candidacy for legislative elections scheduled for November 28, 2026.
On Saturday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas subsequently issued a decree cancelling the previous arrangements and setting 11 September 2027 as the date for simultaneous presidential and legislative elections.
According to the Palestinian news agency WAFA, the decision followed consultations with political factions and a recommendation from the Executive Committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO).
The presidency cited Israeli restrictions on movement, the inability of election officials and observers to access Gaza and East Jerusalem, and the failure to complete arrangements for an international stabilisation force, deploy Palestinian police in Gaza, and begin reconstruction following Israel's withdrawal.
The PLO Executive Committee reaffirmed its commitment to elections, arguing that the new date would help ensure the participation of Palestinians across Jerusalem, the occupied West Bank, and Gaza.
However, the announcement has revived concerns about a political division that has persisted for nearly two decades, particularly after the 2021 legislative elections were also postponed.
For many Palestinians, the question is whether another year will create the conditions for meaningful democratic participation or simply extend the tenure of an entrenched political leadership.
Palestinians question who benefits
Tayseer Abu Shahla, a resident of Jabalia in northern Gaza, doubts elections alone could bring meaningful change amid the current political fragmentation but argues that postponement offers no solution either.
"Fragmentation, division and the absence of a genuine vision for citizens' futures could produce representatives driven by self-interest rather than a common national project," he told The New Arab.
Abu Shahla said Israeli restrictions and military checkpoints across the occupied territories would already have complicated participation, but stressed that these obstacles did not justify indefinitely delaying Palestinians' right to choose their representatives.
In Gaza City, Salah Abu Warda believes those most likely to benefit are political factions and officials concerned about losing their positions or facing a fresh test of public support.
He argued that the delay gives incumbent leaders more time to consolidate their influence, avoid internal competition and pursue political arrangements without direct electoral accountability.
Young candidates and electoral lists are also affected, he added, while Palestinian institutions face a deepening legitimacy crisis.
Riyad Issa, a resident of Al-Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza, offered a more blunt assessment.
"Those who fear the people's voice benefit from postponing elections, while the people themselves pay the price," he told TNA, arguing that Palestinians had been deprived of their right to choose and hold their leaders accountable.
"We are tired of slogans, speeches and promises. We want to know who governs us and who makes decisions on our behalf without consulting us. The homeland is not anyone's private estate, and our votes do not belong to factions or parties," he added.
Hamas calls for dialogue as divisions persist
Hamas welcomed the postponement as a "step in the right direction", arguing that the necessary conditions for free and fair elections across the Palestinian territories, including Jerusalem, were absent.
The movement called for a comprehensive national dialogue to agree on a political strategy and to reform Palestinian institutions, including the Palestinian National Council and the Legislative Council.
It also expressed readiness to participate in talks producing binding outcomes.
However, previous reconciliation efforts have failed to overcome political divisions, raising questions about whether renewed dialogue will yield concrete results.
The Democratic Reform Current within Fatah, led by Mohammed Dahlan, also remains part of the wider debate over the Palestinian political system and the future of the Palestinian Authority, amid continuing disputes over leadership and representation.
For Gaza-based political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim, the postponement effectively gives the Palestinian leadership another year without renewing its popular mandate.
Despite their disagreements, factions often converge when political processes threaten their positions and interests, Ibrahim argued, leaving citizens waiting while leaders remain absorbed in internal power struggles.
He said the crisis extends beyond factional disputes to the question of who has the right to represent Palestinians without a renewed electoral mandate or meaningful accountability.
Postponement, he added, would prolong rather than resolve the legitimacy crisis.
Gaza's needs must come first
Political researcher Tayseer Abdullah, also from Gaza, told TNA that the cancellation of the previous electoral arrangements should not become a pretext for denying Palestinians their constitutional and legal right to vote.
Although initially hesitant about holding elections while Gaza was enduring such devastation, he ultimately supported the process as a right delayed for 16 years.
Abdullah argued that the additional year should be used to prioritise urgent humanitarian needs rather than allow factions to consolidate their internal positions or escape electoral pressure.
He called for addressing the plight of displaced families living in tents, providing medical care for the wounded and people with disabilities, repairing schools and hospitals, restoring essential infrastructure, and ensuring access to clean water and electricity.
He also urged the opening of crossings to facilitate travel and the entry of essential goods and equipment, alongside social protection for Palestinians struggling with poverty and destitution.
In the coming period, he said, it should demonstrate whether political factions are prepared to place citizens' interests above their own.
For Palestinians facing the consequences of war, displacement and political paralysis, the central question remains whether September 2027 will bring a genuine opportunity for democratic renewal or another missed chance to reclaim their political voice.

Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:09:12 UTC
23:09:12 KST

Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on.
Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.
However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
What did Eritrea and Ethiopia say at the UN?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.
In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.
Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.
He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.
“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.
Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts.
“Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said.
“The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.”
What is the latest fighting about, and how is Eritrea allegedly involved?
Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city.
In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims.
The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified.
The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.
That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.
The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated.
Has Ethiopia sent troops north towards Eritrea?
Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday.
Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city.
Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops.
Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat.
Are Ethiopia and Eritrea inching towards war?
Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation.
BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.”
He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”.
Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours.
Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera.
“The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted.
“It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.”
Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.
“The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control.
“A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.

Grace Wu's tribute to Victor Mair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:06:54 UTC
23:06:54 KST

Grace Wu's tribute to Victor Mair
« previous post | next post »
I spent yesterday afternoon at the Memorial Service for Victor Mair, where many of his relatives, friends, students, and colleagues told stories about Victor and his influence on their lives.
Because Grace Wu was not able to attend, she sent me a tribute to read on her behalf, which I've reprinted below.
I have always been deeply grateful to Professor Mair and to his extraordinary contributions to Taiwanese language education. In fact, Penn’s Taiwanese language program, which began in 1993, would not have existed without his advocacy. More than 30 years ago, at a time when there were not yet any Taiwanese language courses being offered even in Taiwan, he had the vision to establish Taiwanese at Penn. I often think about what a remarkable idea and commitment that was.
Over the years, Professor Mair also wrote extensively about Taiwanese in Language Log. For example, on 6/16/2018, in a post with the title “Mother tongue is like mother’s milk”, he mentions the Taiwanese dictionary that my father helped compile.
And on 10/16/2009, in “National Language vs. Mother Tongue”, he led with a photo that I sent him, and discussed the campaign to replace topolects with Putonghua.
But the essay I love most is “How to Forget Your Mother Tongue and Remember Your National Language”.
There is one passage that has always been especially meaningful to me:
“The simplest way to make speakers of a language feel that their tongue is inadequate is to stigmatize it as sù 俗 (‘vulgar’), lǐyǔ 俚語 (‘slang’), tǔhuà 土話 (‘earthy speech’), and so on. Once such evaluations are accepted by the speakers of a given language themselves, the psychological impact is tremendous. Subjected to such indoctrination, they lose confidence in their mother tongue and may become acutely embarrassed when outsiders hear them speaking it.”
This idea was a real revelation to me. Having grown up under a Mandarin-centered language system, I had never fully understood how deeply the stigmatization of Taiwanese during the martial-law era had affected our attitudes toward our own language.
Professor Mair helped me understand this history and, more importantly, helped me feel proud of my own language. His work also taught me to be more respectful of my students’ accents and to approach dialects and language varieties with greater openness, empathy, and understanding.
I will always be grateful for Professor Mair’s lifelong dedication to East Asian scholarship and Taiwanese language education, and for the profound humanistic spirit with which he approached language, culture, and the people who speak them. His intellectual work touched many lives, including mine, and his influence will continue through generations of students and teachers.
Above is Grace Wu's tribute to Victor Mair, composed for his 10/10/2026 Memorial Service.

Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:04:32 UTC
23:04:32 KST

Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
IRGC warns against ignoring the ‘security and rules’ of the strategic waterway as US CENTCOM says it disabled vessel trying to run naval blockade.
US bombs cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman 'trying to run Iran blockade'
Tehran, Iran – Strikes around the strategic Strait of Hormuz have picked up again as mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Saturday night that an unnamed crude oil supertanker hit a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route in the waterway with navigation systems turned off. In a statement, it warned of a similar fate for any oil tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
On Sunday, a senior Iranian army official told state television that the country’s forces remain prepared for both defensive and offensive operations, more than seven months since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran on February 28.
“We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” said Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint coordinator of the army.
His comments came after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several incidents of military action or warnings against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman over the past day. It said ship masters in the vicinity of Ras al-Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), had been directed via radio broadcast overnight to move from their anchorages. And on Sunday afternoon, UKMTO reported an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker heading outbound through the Strait of Hormuz.
Separately, the UAE said its coastguard had rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out at an unnamed tanker close to its shores, although it did not identify the cause of the blaze.
Early on Sunday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) released footage of a fighter jet bombing the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and disabling its propulsion to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports.
Since the US reimposed the blockade in mid-July, CENTCOM says its forces have disabled four commercial vessels, turned around 135 ships and destroyed 10 tankers linked with Iran. Washington says Tehran has exported no oil through the blockade line.
This comes as at least a dozen ships were attacked over the week ending on October 5, the highest number since the war began. At least one was hit off the north coast of Qatar, signalling that the danger extends beyond the immediate Hormuz passage as Iran and the US vie for control.
The ship attacks appear to have decreased energy flows that had surpassed pre-war levels at the start of the month. Kpler data cited by CNBC on Friday showed that average crude passing through the strait for the week ended October 7 was 8.5 million barrels per day, roughly 40 percent below the normal level.
To reopen the strait and reach a resolution to the war, Iran has demanded a return to a now-collapsed memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June, as well as Washington’s backing of an already finalised Iran-Oman deal that designates temporary coordinated entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the strait.
Messages continue to be exchanged between the two sides through mediators, although no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks leading to the US midterm vote, set to take place on November 3, and Israel’s election, due on October 27.
US Vice President JD Vance said last week that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the war, signalling a potential easing of the oft-repeated US demand that zero enrichment must take place on Iranian soil.
Tehran has said a nuclear agreement potentially involving diluting its high-enriched uranium can be part of the later stages of talks, but has emphasised it will not abandon enrichment altogether.
“The achievements of our indigenous nuclear industry cannot be stopped,” Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said during a speech on Sunday, pointing to electricity generation as a main use case.
He also renewed criticism against the International Atomic Energy Agency for not condemning repeated US threats to again bomb Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, told reporters on Sunday that authorities plan on using military and diplomatic avenues to get what they want.
“The Islamic Republic will decisively pursue the country’s interests,” he said. “If those interests can be secured through diplomacy, that is much better, but if not, we will secure them in the field of battle”.

“The state project faces the test, and the security of the Lebanese is in great danger,” he warned.
Earlier this month, the Lebanese military also thwarted an attempt from Syria to bring in 245kg of TNT, four IEDs, detonators and other explosives. This smuggling attempt has not been publicly attributed to Hezbollah.

Antidepressants in pregnancy not tied to extra autism or ADHD risk beyond maternal depression, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
14:00:29 UTC
23:00:29 KST

Children whose mothers had a recorded depression diagnosis around the time of pregnancy were slightly more likely to need special educational support in school, and those whose mothers were also prescribed antidepressants had a small additional increase in risk. However, the researchers could not rule out that this extra risk reflects more severe depression rather than the medication itself. The research was published in PLOS Medicine.
Expectant mothers often face difficult decisions regarding mental health treatment, especially given concerns about how medications might affect fetal brain development. Fears about potential side effects lead some pregnant women to stop taking prescribed antidepressants, which can leave both mother and child vulnerable to the harms of untreated depression. In an educational setting, a special educational need refers to situations where a child requires additional support at school to help with learning, communication, physical, or behavioral challenges compared to their peers.
Early observational studies fueled worries about medication safety during pregnancy. A 2016 study reported that taking antidepressants during pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of autism spectrum disorder in children. Follow-up research, however, suggested that the mother’s underlying depression and shared family traits might actually explain the connection.
Studies that accounted for those factors often saw the link fade. For instance, a 2018 systematic review found that apparent risks of autism and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder largely shrank or disappeared when researchers properly accounted for the mother’s mental health history. Similarly, a 2017 study using sibling comparisons showed that links to neurodevelopmental conditions, which affect how the brain develops, such as autism and ADHD, largely disappeared when comparing exposed children to their unexposed siblings, pointing to shared family factors rather than the drugs themselves.
Recent research covered by PsyPost in 2025 also found that children exposed to antidepressants in the womb showed no increased risk of anxiety or depression once maternal depression was factored in, while another study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that population-level risks are largely driven by shared genetic and family factors.
To help address this ongoing debate, Saraid McIlvride and her colleagues at the University of Glasgow evaluated both depression and antidepressant use side by side in a large population. The authors sought to separate the potential side effects of the medications from the developmental effects of the illness itself.
“Women want to have confidence in their decision to take medication during pregnancy and know that long-term studies investigating potential effects have been carried out,” study lead author Saraid McIlvride, a Daphne Jackson Research Fellow at the University of Glasgow, told PsyPost. “Many studies have focused on pregnancy and neonatal outcomes, but fewer studies have looked at longer-term outcomes, particularly for newer or less common antidepressants, and there have been conflicting results.”
“This dataset, which linked child education and health records with their mother’s health records across the whole of Wales, allowed us to follow children up during primary school and gave a large enough sample size to look at some individual antidepressants and other educational outcomes beyond ASD and ADHD.”
Because this was observational research, the scientists analyzed existing health and education databases rather than assigning treatments to participants. The dataset linked primary care, maternity, and school records for 167,447 children born in Wales between 2009 and 2016. By tracking the children through 2022, when they were just under 6 years old on average, the team could identify any special educational needs recorded by schools.
Children were grouped by two separate measures: whether their mother had received at least one antidepressant prescription during pregnancy or in the month before conception, and whether she had a depression diagnosis recorded by her family doctor in the two years before giving birth. Overall, 7.6 percent of the children were born to mothers who had a recorded depression diagnosis but received no antidepressant prescriptions. Another 4.2 percent were exposed to both a maternal depression diagnosis and antidepressant prescriptions, while 3.6 percent were born to mothers prescribed antidepressants without a recorded depression diagnosis. The remaining children, who formed the comparison group, had neither exposure recorded.
The researchers adjusted their models for factors such as child sex, age, ethnicity, maternal age, smoking habits, and the level of deprivation in the family’s neighborhood. The analysis indicated that both untreated maternal depression and antidepressant prescriptions were associated with higher odds of a child developing a special educational need. Among children with neither exposure, the baseline rate of requiring special educational support was 20 cases per 100 children. For children whose mothers had untreated depression, this rate rose to 23.6 cases per 100 children.
Children whose mothers had both a depression diagnosis and antidepressant prescriptions had a predicted rate of 26.5 cases of special educational need per 100 children, while those whose mothers were prescribed antidepressants without a depression diagnosis had a rate of 26.3 per 100. When examining the additional risk linked to medication, the gap depended on whether the mother had a depression diagnosis. Prescriptions were associated with an extra 6.3 cases per 100 children among mothers without a recorded depression diagnosis, but only 2.9 additional cases per 100 children among mothers who had a recorded diagnosis.
The authors note that the smaller gap reflects the already elevated rate among children whose mothers had untreated depression, meaning the higher risk linked to maternal depression cannot be attributed solely to medication. Compared with unexposed children, both maternal depression and antidepressant exposure were associated with higher odds of autism, ADHD, learning difficulties, and behavioral, emotional, and social difficulties.
But when children of mothers with treated depression were compared with children of mothers with untreated depression, the differences for autism and ADHD were not statistically significant; only learning difficulties and behavioral, emotional, and social difficulties showed small differences, of about one additional case per 100 children each.
The researchers also looked at different types of antidepressants. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the standard first-line antidepressants, which include drugs such as sertraline and fluoxetine, made up about 83 percent of prescriptions and followed the same general pattern as the overall results.
Two less common classes, tricyclic antidepressants, an older type of medication, and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, showed a larger gap between treated and untreated depression, with about 8.8 extra cases of special educational need per 100 children for each. Because relatively few children were exposed to these drugs, the estimates were imprecise, ranging from roughly 3 to 15 extra cases per 100.
The tricyclic result is consistent with a 2026 meta-analysis, which found that tricyclic antidepressants were the only class where links to neurodevelopmental conditions persisted after accounting for maternal mental health, though that study also could not rule out underlying illness severity.
“Maternal depression during pregnancy was associated with an increased chance of children having special educational needs,” McIlvride said. “Taking antidepressants during pregnancy was linked to a small increase in this risk, compared to untreated depression, but we weren’t able to show if this increase is due to these women having more severe depression or an effect of the medication. Untreated depression can have a serious impact on the well-being of both mother and baby so it is vital to keep taking antidepressants if they are needed.”
Independent specialists reviewing the research for the Science Media Centre emphasized that the modest differences in risk should be interpreted with caution. Asma Khalil, a professor of obstetrics and maternal-fetal medicine at City St George’s, University of London, who was not involved in the study, said in her comments that the work provides helpful context but cannot determine causation.
Khalil pointed to the gap of roughly three cases per 100 children between mothers with treated and untreated depression. “That difference is worth studying, but it does not show that antidepressants caused it,” Khalil said. “The researchers could not measure how severe the mothers’ depression was, and women prescribed medication may have differed in important ways from those who were not. A prescription also does not establish that a medicine was taken throughout pregnancy.”
“The main outcome was a broad measure of special educational needs, which is not the same as a clinical diagnosis,” Khalil added. “This study adds valuable evidence about the needs of children and families, but it cannot tell an individual woman whether taking or stopping an antidepressant would change her child’s developmental risk.”
McIlvride similarly emphasized that population-level statistics do not translate directly into an individual pregnancy’s personal outcome.
“This study has estimated an association at a population level and so can’t tell an individual about their personal risk,” McIlvride noted. “It gives women and their families information which could potentially benefit their child’s development by identifying a need for support earlier. This study also shows that antidepressant use during pregnancy is increasingly common – around 1 in 12 women were taking antidepressants in our study, and we can expect this figure to be even higher today – therefore this is an area which deserves more research.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The biggest limitation is that the researchers had no data on how severe each mother’s depression was. Because doctors typically prescribe medications like tricyclic antidepressants for more severe or treatment-resistant depression, the higher risks seen with these specific drugs might simply reflect the fact that the mothers prescribed them were experiencing a more intense form of the illness.
“This study does not show that depression or antidepressant use during pregnancy causes autism or ADHD in children – it shows an association, which could be due to many different reasons,” McIlvride emphasized. “The increased risk associated with antidepressants we observed in our study could be due to more severe disease, as it is likely that women who are taking antidepressants will have more severe depression.”
Angelica Ronald, a professor of psychology and genetics at the University of Surrey who was not involved in the study, said in comments to the Science Media Centre that shared genetic influences could account for part of the link, while describing the large sample size and linked records as notable strengths of the study.
“There is evidence from a range of sources that depression and neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism and ADHD share some genetic influences,” Ronald said. “This means we expect autism, ADHD and depression to run in the same families to some degree. This new study does not account for the fact that autism, ADHD and depression share some inherited (genetic) influences. Shared genetic influences might explain some of the associations found here between maternal depression in pregnancy and maternal use of antidepressants in pregnancy and offspring special educational needs.”
David Curtis, an honorary professor at the UCL Genetics Institute at University College London who was not involved in the research, questioned in his comments to the Science Media Centre whether the depression link reflects any harm in the womb at all.
“Although this study shows that children of mothers who suffered depression or took antidepressants have increased rates of special educational needs, we cannot assume that this represents a causal relationship,” Curtis said. “In fact, for me it seems somewhat implausible that a mother being depressed in the two years before birth would somehow cause the child to be at subsequently increased risk of having learning difficulties. Typically, a depressive illness per se does not produce profound physiological changes such as might be expected to substantially disrupt fetal development. Alternative explanations seem more likely.”
“A mother depressed in the years before delivery would be more likely to have subsequent episodes of depression and these subsequent episodes might impact a child’s psychosocial development,” he explained. “A mother with a previous diagnosis of depression might have more contact with support services which could result in a higher probability of problems with the child being detected.”
The researchers also lacked some data. The group of women prescribed antidepressants without a recorded depression diagnosis likely included many with unrecorded depression or anxiety, as well as some treated for other conditions, such as migraine and chronic pain, for which tricyclic antidepressants and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are also prescribed. The researchers did not have data on maternal alcohol or illicit drug use, nor could they account for the mental health of fathers or the potential influence of breastfeeding.
McIlvride pointed to several next steps for expanding on this line of inquiry. “The average age of children in our study was just under 6 years old, so it would be of interest to follow the children up for a longer period,” she said. “Further research is needed to answer questions around the dose of medications or how taking medication while breastfeeding could affect children’s development.”
Future studies that include detailed measures of depression severity, environmental factors, and longer follow-up windows could help better explain the relationship between maternal mental health care and long-term child development.
The study, “Prenatal exposure to maternal depression and antidepressants and neurodevelopmental outcomes: A population cohort study,” was authored by Saraid McIlvride, Neha Rao, Sarjit Singh, Scott M. Nelson, Jill P. Pell, and Michael Fleming.

Archaeologists unearth medieval convent’s heating system during renovations in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
13:43:36 UTC
22:43:36 KST

A well-preserved medieval stone-chamber heating system was found during renovations of a property in Basel, Switzerland, the Canton of Basel-Stadt announced in late September.
The system had once belonged to the now-excavated Gnadental convent for women, established in around 1231 outside of Basel’s city walls, and was found beneath what had once served as the dining hall in the east wing of the convent.
It is almost completely preserved, and is one of the most significantly known examples of heating systems of its type in both Switzerland and Europe at large.
Based on the sites’s architectural history, archaeologists have estimated that the heating system was built between the 13th and 14th centuries.
The underground chamber where the heating system was found contained fieldstones which served to store heat, typical of stone-chamber heating systems. After removing the stones, archaeologists were able to study the firing channel beneath.
Made up of ashlar blocks, the channel also revealed two pointed arches standing in their original position.
Additionally, eight closable openings were still carefully preserved. Warm air would exit through these openings, rising from the heating chamber into the dining hall once the smoke from lighting the fire had cleared.
After uncovering the chamber, the Archaeological Soil Research Basel-Stadt created a 3D model of the find for additional documentation in research. The find will be added to the Petersgraben 52 renovation project and be subject to further study down the line.
What is the Gnadental convent?
Gnadental convent was built outside the city wall for Franciscans around 1231, later becoming a temporary home for several orders while their own convents were built inside the city or before they left.
Some 20 years after construction, the Franciscans moved from Gnadental convent to the newer Barfüsser Monastery, founded in what is now Barfüsserplatz. From then on, the older convent buildings housed several women's orders, including the Cistercian nuns and the Order of Poor Clares.
In 1279, lay sisters from Gnadenthal near Niederwil (AG) moved in, after whom the convent received its name. They were incorporated into the Poor Clares and lived there until the Reformation and the dissolution of the convent.
After the convent was abandoned, the buildings continued to be partially used. In 1573, building materials were taken from the convent to be reused into a granary.
Watercolor paintings done by Johann Jakob Schneider from the 19th century still depict the older convent buildings. However, towards the end of the 19th century, the granary was demolished to make way for a vocational school at the site.
