At least 139 dead, 84 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti
Search and rescue operations conducted after vessel carrying more than 300 people capsizes near Guhere.
At least 139 people, including 15 children, have died and 84 are missing after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti, according to the United Nations migration agency.
In a statement on Sunday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) quoted survivors as saying that the incident happened near Guhere off Djibouti’s eastern coast in the Gulf of Aden near the Bab al-Mandeb strait from Thursday night to before dawn on Friday.
The boat was heading from Djibouti to Yemen with more than 300 people on board. More than 80 people – all Ethiopians – survived the shipwreck while Djiboutian search and rescue operations continued.
“Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance,” IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac said, lamenting the “devastating loss of life”.
That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won’t be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the Associated Press.
“This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities,” Coissac added.
Undeterred by instability
Crossing Bab al-Mandeb, a waterway that measures just 20km (12.4 miles) at its narrowest points between Djibouti and Yemen, is a popular but dangerous route for thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa.
Many embark on this journey in search of employment and safety in Gulf countries, undeterred by the rising instability in the region due to the US-Israel war on Iran and the resumption of fighting in Yemen between government forces and Houthi fighters last month.
The IOM said it had recorded “more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia” since September 10. Last year, more than half a million people tried to move along this route into Yemen, and at least 900 people died or are missing, according to the agency.
Djibouti is not only a place where migrants depart from, but several thousand people are also fleeing to the country from Yemen due to the renewed conflict.

Iran’s Medical Council urges global health bodies to act over US sanctions
TEHRAN – The Iranian Medical Council has called on the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and the World Medical Association (WMA) to take immediate action against the use of patients’ lives as a tool of political and military pressure.

Mohammad Raiszadeh, head of the Iranian Medical Council, urged the leaders of international health organizations to respond promptly and responsibly to what he described as inhumane acts and the weaponization of medical resources in armed conflicts.
He cited previous reports of direct attacks on healthcare facilities, medical infrastructure, and pharmaceutical facilities, adding that the US attack on the Touska, a vessel carrying medicines and, in particular, vital supplies for dialysis patients, was another clear example of directly endangering patients’ health and lives.

DOE advances conservation efforts for reptile and amphibian species
Unknown

DOE advances conservation efforts for reptile and amphibian species
TEHRAN – The Department of Environment (DOE) is developing national conservation programs for priority reptile and amphibian species, with a focus on deploying modern monitoring technologies, strengthening local community engagement, and providing ongoing training for experts.
The plan primarily targets salamanders, marsh crocodiles, spider-tailed horned vipers, and Talysh toads through new methods of monitoring, census, and conservation measures, IRNA quoted Peyman Ashouri, an official with the DOE, as saying.
Razi University in Kermanshah province has already estimated the population of the yellow-spotted salamander using artificial intelligence (AI), and a census of the marsh crocodile is planned to be conducted from February 20 to May 21, he added.
The official elaborated on adopted measures to address human-wildlife conflicts, stating that a project is currently underway to mitigate threats, reduce conflicts, and restore the habitats of the Lorestan newt and Talysh toad; the initiatives include installing signage, producing wildlife awareness posters and brochures, organizing educational programs for tourists and local communities, and removing waste from the habitats.
Referring to spider-tailed horned vipers, Ashouri said the DOE is drafting a conservation plan for the protection of the species, which will be implemented soon.
Data-driven strategies to strengthen biodiversity conservation efforts
The DOE is implementing a comprehensive range of conservation, scientific, legal, and operational initiatives to strengthen the protection of wildlife species and habitats across the country based on a targeted and strategic approach, with priorities guided by data and scientific research.
According to Peyman Valizadeh, an official with the DOE, the DOE focuses on a more scientific approach to develop and implement conservation efforts tailored to the specific needs of each species and habitat, IRNA reported.
It has so far prepared plans for the preservation of 25 endangered species, with thirteen more plans being developed. The plans provide a clear framework for species conservation by delineating the species’ status, major threats, conservation priorities, necessary actions, and assessment indicators, he noted.
However, the DOE faces some challenges in implementing these measures at national and provincial levels. One of the biggest challenges is securing funding to implement the plans. Developing specialized capacity to preserve species is the other problem. Lack of trained, specialized forces has made it difficult to implement the conservation action plans effectively. Therefore, training specialized personnel, developing experts’ capacities in provinces, and strengthening scientific and technical capabilities of the headquarters are put on the agenda, the official highlighted.
Referring to adopted measures to combat wildlife trafficking, Valizadeh said to foster greater coordination among the responsible agencies, the DOE has established a national committee on combating wildlife trafficking; the committee has held three expert meetings so far. Furthermore, the drafting of a comprehensive plan to combat and prevent wildlife trafficking is nearing completion. Furthermore, a comprehensive program to combat and prevent wildlife trafficking is being drafted.
To manage human-wildlife conflicts, efforts have been made to shift the approach from a reactive posture to the identification of critical hotspots, understanding the drivers of conflict, and implementing preventive measures. The DOE has identified some conflict hotspots for species like leopards, black bears, and herbivores; collecting data on black bears in Hormozgan and Kerman provinces is underway.
Moreover, the DOE has signed an agreement with the National Environment Fund and the Agricultural Products Insurance Fund to support local communities and compensate their losses, Valizadeh further noted.
Accurate information on species distribution, habitats, movement paths, and ecological corridors makes conservation efforts more effective, he added.
In this regard, the DOE, in cooperation with Shiraz University, has carried out research to prepare comprehensive distribution maps to identify migration and movement corridors for herbivores and carnivores.
The maps will serve as a management tool for habitat conservation, prevention and management of human-wildlife conflicts, development of conservation priorities, and proper use of smart monitoring and conservation programs, thereby providing a more accurate basis for conservation decision-making, Valizadeh said.
The official went on to say that the DOE will secure funds, train skilled human forces, and foster intersectoral cooperation to establish an integrated system that benefits from scientific information, field data, capacities of local communities, and the capabilities of executive agencies to develop and implement conservation plans for each species and habitat.

“Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:28:27 UTC
20:28:27 KST

“Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”
TEHRAN – World Migratory Bird Day serves as an opportunity to highlight the vital role these birds play in maintaining ecosystem balance and the need to protect their habitats. These tireless travelers cover thousands of kilometers each year to survive, yet face mounting threats, including drying wetlands, habitat destruction, illegal hunting, and climate change.
World Migratory Bird Day is a global observance aimed at raising awareness of the importance of conserving migratory birds and their habitats. It was first established in 2006 through an initiative by the Secretariat of the Agreement on the Conservation of African-Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds (AEWA) and the Secretariat of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), with support from the United Nations.
The observance seeks to draw public attention to threats such as habitat destruction, environmental pollution, illegal hunting and climate change, while underscoring the need for international cooperation to protect migratory birds.
World Migratory Bird Day is observed annually on the second Saturday of May and the second Saturday of October, coinciding with the main bird migration seasons in the Northern Hemisphere. In 2026, the observance falls on May 9 and October 10.
This year’s theme, “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!”, highlights the role of citizen science and public participation in migratory bird conservation. The initiative emphasizes the value of field observations recorded by birdwatchers, researchers, local communities and nature enthusiasts in understanding migration patterns, monitoring population trends and identifying threats affecting different species.
Iran plays a particularly important role in migratory bird conservation due to its geographical position in West Asia and its location along the seasonal migration routes of numerous species. The country’s wetlands, lakes, coastlines and other natural habitats serve as stopover, feeding and resting sites, as well as wintering grounds, for large numbers of waterbirds and shorebirds throughout the year.
Anzali Wetland, Miankaleh, Gori Gol and Shadegan wetlands, along with aquatic habitats in the Lake Urmia basin, are among the areas where continuous monitoring can provide valuable information on species occurrence, relative abundance, arrival and departure dates, and seasonal population changes.
Recording observation dates, bird numbers, geographic locations, habitat conditions and evidence of threats can help improve ecological assessments, particularly when data are collected using standardized methods over extended periods. Such records make it easier to compare findings over time and identify ecological changes. In this context, public participation in documenting bird sightings can complement professional bird census and monitoring programs nationwide.
On World Migratory Bird Day, the theme “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter!” serves as a reminder that effective conservation requires not only expertise and planning but also informed public participation and the transformation of individual observations into reliable, usable data.
Every accurate observation can help reveal a larger picture of the status of migratory birds and the vital routes they depend on — a picture that is essential to protecting this shared natural heritage.

Three Years After October 7, This former Israeli Soldier Still Wakes Up at 6:29 A.M. every Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:26:20 UTC
20:26:20 KST

Shalev Ben Simon wakes up every morning at the same time. He opens his eyes, looks at his mobile phone and sees – 6:29 A.M. "It doesn't matter what time I go to sleep. Even if I fall asleep at six, after half an hour I wake up and can't go back to sleep. It's this urge, I feel haunted."
Three years have passed since that hour was seared into the collective memory of Israelis. But unlike most other Israelis, Ben Simon was actually there, at 6:29 A.M., in uniform, not far from the border fence near Gaza. "I was actually trying to get out of Shabbat duty that weekend," he admits. "I told all sorts of stories hoping they'd let me go home, but my request wasn't approved. The truth is I wanted to go to Nova," he says, referring to the music festival near Kibbutz Re'im, where hundreds of Israelis were murdered on October 7. "So I would have been screwed either way."
He returned alive after that Saturday, but it is hard to say he returned to life. "I see blood on my hands, hear gunshots, feel my heart pounding. It doesn't go away, I can't shake the sights."
Ben Simon, who is 22, enlisted in Battalion 51 of the Golani Brigade in March 2022. He was trained for combat, served in Hebron in the West Bank, completed a squad commanders course and then returned to his company. Two weeks before October 7, he was promoted to sergeant first class, with his company responsible for the Kissufim sector in southern Israel.
Ben Simon and his comrades were sent to a small outpost, made up of a combined combat team in a wooded area, near the Gaza border. Eight infantry soldiers in an armored personnel carrier and four armored soldiers in a tank – this was the force manning the border outpost that weekend.
"On Friday evening, we all made Kiddush together," he says, referring the recital of the blessing over the wine on the eve of Shabbat. "We stayed up until 2 A.M., it was the time of our lives." At 5:30 A.M., Ben Simon woke his soldiers for a routine round at sunrise. "Five of us entered the armored personnel carrier, sat and talked a bit, and then I decided to nap and asked one of the soldiers to listen to the radio."
The 6:29 Wake-up
At 6:29 A.M., he woke up. "My soldier tells me there's 'purple rain' [code for rocket and missile fire]. I didn't understand what was happening, I asked if they said the word 'chicken' [code for drill] on the radio." The soldier replied in the negative.
"I immediately yelled at the rest of the soldiers to get into the armored personnel carrier," Ben Simon says. Five minutes later, a mortar shell landed near them, creating a crater in the ground. After a few more seconds, another mortar shell hit, this time striking the APC itself. "Everything shook," he recounts. "I immediately called my officer to try and understand what was happening. He told me: 'It looks like there's going to be a hell of a war now. Get the guys ready, follow me.'"
Until then, they had never moved the APC from its spot. "Not even in drills," he says. This was the first of many times that day that Ben Simon was to perform actions he had never practiced. But in real time, there was no time to think about it. They had to act, and fast.
A few minutes after they started driving, Ben Simon opened one of the APC's hatches – and a drone appeared above it. "It was huge, enormous. It cast a shadow over the entire APC. I told the soldiers: 'Listen, I don't know why we got into this, but everyone has to be alert and focused. Load your weapons, and shut up.'"
A few more minutes passed until they reached the breached border fence. "We saw a huge number of motorcyclists just streaming in endlessly," Ben Simon recalls. "Bullets hit the APC again and again, there was also RPG [rocket-propelled grenade] fire. The tank with us went up to a position (a high earthen rampart), and we secured it and started taking down militants with the 'lethal weapon' [a firearm mounted on military vehicles]." At one point, Ben Simon noticed the tank's engine cover was on fire. Get ready to dismount, he told his soldiers. But just before they exited into the chaos, he saw the tank move backward, and he stopped them from exiting.
"Follow me," the armored officer in the tank ordered him. The destination was a path dense with vegetation, which the army anticipated would be used by militants to infiltrate in case of an attack. However, even the most extreme scenario they had trained for did not prepare the small force for what happened next. "We trained for an infiltration of six militants, maybe 10. Not hundreds," he explains. On their way, they joined up with another small force from the battalion, and were immediately ambushed. Bullets were fired from all directions, one hitting the abdomen of a soldier. Ben Simon took out the stretcher and placed the wounded soldier inside the APC. Then they got a new order: "Drive to the kibbutz."
When they reached the entrance gate of Kibbutz Kissufim, located a mere 1.5 kilometers (less than a mile) from the Gaza border, Ben Simon was stunned. Militants on motorcycles moved in one after another. One of them aimed an RPG at the APC and fired. Ben Simon ordered his driver to run him over. As they continued into the kibbutz, the chaos only intensified.
"The APC was just taking insane amounts of fire, I felt it was a miracle it kept moving," Ben Simon recalls. "We drove around the kibbutz and tried to understand what was happening, but it was impossible — there was fire from all directions. I didn't understand where to dismount, where I could drop off the wounded. Even distinguishing between our forces and the enemy was difficult. Some of them were in uniform." Only their Kalashnikov assault rifles gave away their identity, he says.
Ambushed again and again
Then, for the first time that morning, they exited the APC, near the kibbutz dining hall. At that very moment, another force dismounted near them – and one of its soldiers immediately took a bullet to the neck. "The medic came and stopped the bleeding with his finger, and I put him in the APC." Afterward, they began to move through the kibbutz on foot. There was one incident after another. Again and again they were ambushed, again and again they returned fire. "They pushed us to the limit, we had no grenades, and ammunition was running out. I replenished magazines from [the ammunition of] the wounded," he says.
Near the kibbutz kindergarten, there was a particularly fierce battle. At the height of the commotion, a sergeant first class from another platoon in the battalion stood next to him. "Suddenly I hear on his radio that one of the soldiers is wounded and needs to be extracted. I look and don't understand where he is, and then I suddenly identify him about a hundred meters from me. Insane fire was directed there," he recounts, "I thought they were doing it because they wanted to kidnap him, so I ran to him. I felt the bullets whistling past me, flying over me. One of them hit the sole of my shoe, but didn't penetrate."
When he reached the wounded soldier, Ben Simon called his name, but there was no response. "I pulled him along with another soldier to a nearby fortified shelter. I removed the front part of his vest and checked his pulse. I felt something faint. I started to massage him, and after 10 minutes I understood that was it, he was no longer with us. His hands grew cold, his eyes closed.
"I removed the back part of his vest and saw an exit wound from a bullet and large amounts of blood. I covered his face, took his personal belongings from him and apologized. Afterward, I carried him about 250 meters, to the evacuation point." His vest did not have a protective ceramic plate, Ben Simon learned later on. "He took a bullet straight to the heart, he didn't have much of a chance." Sgt. Guy Bazak was only 19. Four days later, he was buried in the military section at the Kochav Yair cemetery. "Every time I drive to the center of the country I visit him."
"It was a battle of few against many," the military investigation into the Kissufim battle concluded many months later. "The chances of the soldiers of Battalion 51 and the [kibbutz] security squad members stopping the enemy's attack were very low."
According to the investigation, the first reinforcement force, from Battalion 450 of the non-commissioned officers school, arrived there only at 1:06 P.M. Ben Simon encountered them about an hour and a half later, around the time he met Sa'ar Margolis, who had been the kibbutz's security coordinator for 11 years. About a year before the massacre, he left the position but remained a member of the security squad.
"I need a force," Margolis told him. Ben Simon did not hesitate, even though he didn't have much to offer. Two of his soldiers suffered combat shock, and another soldier evacuated them. The force under his command remained meager, and joined the force from Battalion 450 commanded by Staff Sgt. Adam Agmon. At 2:52 P.M., they departed.
"We advanced through the kibbutz and saw several bodies of militants, and then the body of an Israeli civilian," Ben Simon says. They continued to move and noticed a house consumed by fire. The military investigation revealed that it was the home of Ivan Illarramendi-Caesar and Dafna Garcovich. The fire left them no chance, and their remains were identified only about a month later.
The force continued on its way, trying to save whoever could still be saved. Next to the burned house stood the home of Kissufim's current security coordinator. "Margolis told me, 'I'll go in from here, and you from the other entrance.' Then he changed his mind: 'No, actually, the other way around.'" Ben Simon complied, and Margolis and Agmon advanced toward the stairs. "I hear the door opening, and then a burst of gunfire." Both were killed on the spot.
"I signaled to everyone to fall back because the guys from [Battalion] 450 were in shock, they still didn't understand what they had gotten into," Ben Simon says. "I started shooting at the house. I was terrified," he admits. "One of the militants came out of the house and fired bursts at me. After I was discharged, I went back there and saw the bullet impacts; to this day, I don't believe I survived it."
Non-stop shooting
The shooting did not stop, and Ben Simon realized he had to change his approach. He decided to outflank the militants through the burned house, together with one of his soldiers. "I started firing in their direction. I knelt, and then I hear the sound of something rolling, and I spot a grenade. I immediately retreated."
Ben Simon returned to the kibbutz entrance and sought reinforcements to extract the bodies. A force from the Dekel Battalion of Bahad 1 [officers training school] joined the mission. They moved to the house, killed the militants inside and carried out the bodies of Margolis and Agmon on stretchers.
Ben Simon continued to encounter militants right up until the evening. He went from one encounter to the next without stopping. Only when the sun began to set did he return to his APC and meet his soldiers. "They made several rounds of evacuating the wounded and dead; everything was full of blood." Afterward, they worked together to clear the nearby Kissufim outpost of militants.
In the days following October 7, they stayed in one of the kibbutz houses near the border. They ambushed militants who were still in the area. On October 12, the last militant was killed, and the kibbutz was cleared. The investigation revealed that about 150 militants from the Gaza Strip had infiltrated the kibbutz and outpost area. The army killed about 105 of them. The kibbutz became a memorial to the battle. "I looked around and felt my mind was messed up. The destruction remained, bodies everywhere, ash and dust."
Not the same person
In mid-October, Ben Simon and his comrades were transferred to a training base, and from there to a school in the town of Ofakim. There, for the first time, members of his family were given the opportunity to visit him. "I didn't exactly process the situation, I had responsibility for my soldiers and was required to maintain composure. I didn't express emotions, but inside I was broken."
At the end of October, when the IDF ground maneuver began, Ben Simon entered the Gaza Strip. His platoon was positioned as the spearhead force of Division 36. They operated mainly in the Rimal neighborhood in western Gaza City. "We had encounters near the sea; it felt as if the militants were emerging from the water — it was surreal." Afterward, they moved to the Zeitoun neighborhood, then to Shujaiyeh, and then to the Bureij and Maghazi refugee camps. Only at the end of December did Ben Simon go home, for the first time since October 1.
In those days, when he briefly returned to reality, he realized he was no longer the same person. The breaking point came in the evening, at nightfall. "I went for a drive with a friend in my parents' car," he recounts. "Suddenly I see a large van speeding toward me, trying to cut me off from the left. It honked at me, and everything came rushing back." Ben Simon stopped and got out of the vehicle. In his hand, he held a crowbar he had brought with him from the Gaza Strip. He approached the driver and cursed him. "I almost broke his window." A girl sat next to the driver and burst into tears. Ben Simon's friend brought him back to the car, to the passenger seat.
"After a few minutes, I asked him, 'Why are you driving?' and he looked at me with a stunned expression. 'Don't you remember what happened? Are you crazy? Do you know what you just did?' he asked, and I replied, 'Not really.'"
Afterward, his friend recounted what had happened. "I didn't believe it, at first I didn't remember anything. It was as if a demon had entered me, I wasn't myself." His friend suggested he seek psychological treatment. He initially refused, but at some point, he relented. "The therapist told me: 'You're not in a good state, you must ask to see a mental health officer.'"
Meanwhile, Ben Simon returned to the army. His brigade, Golani, left Gaza and was transferred to the northern border. "I asked to see a mental health officer, but they strung me along. My condition worsened, I had violent outbursts, I was full of rage." After his company commander refused to allow him to go for treatment, Ben Simon took his things and left, and has not returned since. "I was a deserter for a month, they called and threatened me with arrest."
Eventually, with a bit of help from officers with connections, Ben Simon met with the division's female mental health officer. "I told her everything I had been through, and she just started to cry. At the end of the meeting, she said I had PTSD." She sent him to another mental health officer, who referred him to the Taatzumot center, which provides intensive treatment for combat soldiers dealing with PTSD symptoms. "I was there for four months, and they diagnosed me with severe PTSD. My condition didn't improve, and they decided to discharge me from the army."
Ben Simon is not the only one in his platoon to be discharged early due to his mental state. "Four of us, from the team that was in the APC that morning, were discharged. That's fifty percent."
In the days following his discharge, all the traumas began to surface. "I started to isolate myself, to cut myself off from friends. I suffered from violent outbursts, from dissociative episodes. My parents couldn't provide me with a solution, but I understand them. It's hard to see your child falling apart." Ben Simon tried a wide range of treatments, but didn't stick with most of them. "I hopped back and forth between psychiatrists and psychologists, but I felt judged. I couldn't open up. The only treatment I have managed to stick with is Chinese acupuncture, it helps me."
'Feel betrayed'
At the same time he began seeking recognition for his condition with the Defense Ministry's Rehabilitation Department. About four months ago, he appeared before the medical committee. "I told them everything, but I didn't try to exaggerate," he says. A week and a half later, he was informed that he would be recognized with a 40 percent disability for 10 years. The Rehabilitation Department's new policy, revealed in Haaretz, is to minimize the granting of permanent disability status for PTSD sufferers as much as possible. Especially now.
"I felt betrayed," he says, "I didn't understand how it could be that after everything I went through, this is what they give me." Since then, he says, his symptoms have only worsened. Flashbacks return and surge, and anger swells. "I am ashamed of my country, I feel like they spat in my face. Do you really think that after everything I went through, my mental disability will disappear? I can barely leave the house, certainly not work. I'm not asking for pity, just a safety net, and some peace of mind. That's all. After everything I've given, don't I deserve that?"

New high-speed rail line connects Tekirdağ and Edirne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:17:33 UTC
20:17:33 KST

AA Photo
Service on a new high-speed rail line running from Tekirdağ’s Çerkezköy district to the Kapıkule border crossing with Bulgaria officially began on Oct. 9, Transportation and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu has announced.
With President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in attendance for its opening, the new Çerkezköy-Kapıkule high-speed rail line is part of the Istanbul Halkalı-Kapıkule High-Speed Train Project. The line reduces travel time to 54 minutes, according to the minister’s written statement.
The high-speed service operates three round-trips. Trains heading from Çerkezköy to Edirne depart at 10:45 a.m., 3 p.m. and 7:30 p.m., while the trains in the opposite direction depart at 9 a.m., 1 p.m. and 5:45 p.m.
“Our trains serve our citizens with a total seating capacity of 411, including two seats reserved for wheelchair users,” the minister stated.
Uraloğlu noted that regional train schedules have been updated to accommodate the new line, with two daily round-trip trains now running between Istanbul’s Halkalı station and Edirne’s Uzunköprü district along the same rail corridor.
Uraloğlu noted that these regional trains depart from Istanbul’s Halkalı station to Uzunköprü at 8:25 a.m. and return from Uzunköprü to Halkalı at 3:40 p.m. Passengers traveling between Istanbul and Edirne can now easily complete their journey by transferring between the regional and high-speed trains at Çerkezköy station.

Man hurls rocks at cars from bridge over major Tel Aviv highway, then flees | Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:17:02 UTC
20:17:02 KST

An unidentified man threw rocks from an overpass onto vehicles traveling north on Tel Aviv's Ayalon Highway on Sunday morning, damaging several cars near the Halakha Interchange. Footage captured by one of the vehicles reportedly shows the suspect dumping rocks onto the roadway before fleeing toward Ramat Gan. Police have opened an investigation.
Edward Rees, whose Tesla was struck during the incident, described the frightening moments in an interview with ynet. "I was driving north in the left lane, minding my own business. As I approached the bridge, I suddenly saw stones flying, actual rocks, toward my lane and the lane next to me. We were traveling at 80 to 90 km/h, and I didn't have time to react. I heard the rocks hitting my car. Luckily, I got off lightly."
According to Rees, a taxi traveling alongside him appeared to have taken the brunt of the rocks. "My car suffered some paint damage and a few marks on the windshield, but it didn't break. The taxi next to me probably took most of the rocks."
Rees said he initially did not realize the incident was deliberate and assumed the stones might have come from construction work nearby. Because there was nowhere to pull over safely, he continued driving and decided to examine the footage from his vehicle's cameras once he reached his destination.
"At first, I thought maybe there was construction work going on. There was nowhere for me to stop, so I told myself that since I have a Tesla with cameras, I'd check afterward to see exactly what had happened," he recalled.
"A few minutes later, when I parked, I looked at the footage and saw someone simply standing on the bridge, emptying a bag or bucket of rocks onto the traffic. As soon as he finished, you could see him start running toward Ramat Gan."
Only after reviewing the recording did Rees fully appreciate how dangerous the incident had been. "From the noise, I was certain the rocks had hit my windshield. When you see that many rocks, you think they could actually penetrate the car. Apparently, I was lucky in terms of my position and timing."
Rees filed a police complaint and plans to retrieve higher-resolution recordings from his vehicle's cameras, hoping they might reveal details that could help identify the taxi involved.
Police from the Lev Tel Aviv precinct have launched an investigation into the incident. The identity of the suspect and his motive remain unknown.
Rees expressed concern that the person responsible might attempt something similar again, potentially with fatal consequences.
"My fear is that this might have been a nationalist-motivated incident, or simply someone who could come back and do it again. Next time, it could kill someone," he said. "At 90 km/h, if your windshield suddenly shatters or a rock hits someone in the head, it could end in disaster."
He added that the experience had shaken his sense of security while driving on one of Israel's busiest highways.
"It's frightening. I'm a little afraid to drive on Ayalon now. I stressed to the police investigator who took my statement just how serious this is. Someone stood on a bridge and threw rocks at moving cars. This time, we were lucky, but next time it could end very differently."

Psychologists map the emotional borders between social anxiety and narcissism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
11:00:20 UTC
20:00:20 KST

Social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism share deep roots in feelings of inadequacy, yet they relate to different dimensions of human shame. A study of 400 adults revealed that social anxiety is uniquely tied to internal feelings of defectiveness, while vulnerable narcissism involves a wider array of emotional vulnerabilities, including a fear of outside judgment and a heightened expectation of rejection. The research was published in Personality and Individual Differences.
Social anxiety involves distress in situations that carry a potential for public scrutiny and negative evaluation. Some psychologists view this anxiety as an evolutionary mechanism designed to keep people affiliated with a group. By heightening a person’s sensitivity to status loss, social anxiety prompts self-protective behaviors in threatening interpersonal situations. When these feelings become severe, they can manifest as an impairing clinical disorder, but social anxiety also exists on a spectrum of everyday interpersonal concerns.
Elevated social anxiety often overlaps with certain personality traits, particularly those related to narcissistic vulnerability. Narcissism is generally understood as existing on a continuum, ranging from normal self-regard to pathological configurations. Psychologists divide clinical narcissism into two broad expressions: grandiosity and vulnerability. Grandiose narcissism features overt entitlement and arrogance, whereas vulnerable narcissism involves hypersensitivity to evaluation, fragile self-worth, and defensive behaviors designed to protect the ego.
Both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism feature a heightened sensitivity to interpersonal threats. One primary mechanism connecting these traits is rejection sensitivity. This concept describes a disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive, and intensely react to social rejection. This sensitivity is thought to develop from early experiences of criticism or exclusion, which bias individuals to interpret ambiguous social cues as signs of impending rejection.
This pattern aligns with a psychological framework known as the Interpersonal Acceptance-Rejection Theory. The theory posits that perceived acceptance or rejection in close relationships, particularly early in life, is linked to later psychological adjustment. Rejection experiences involving caregivers or peers have been linked to a greater tendency to perceive rejection and heightened anxiety in response to potential rejection. When this rejection-related distress is directed inward, it can trigger intense feelings of shame.
Shame acts as a powerful social emotion tied to feelings of inferiority. Psychologists categorize shame into two distinct types: internal and external. Internal shame involves viewing oneself as fundamentally flawed or inadequate, leading to harsh self-criticism. External shame centers on the perception that other people view one negatively, which often prompts defensive strategies like avoiding social contact or constantly trying to repair one’s public image.
Psychologist Giulia Rosa Policardo at eCampus University in Novedrate, Italy, alongside colleagues from Sapienza University of Rome and the Institute of Behavioural and Cognitive Psychology and Psychotherapy, designed a study to map these overlapping traits. Previous research had documented associations between rejection sensitivity, shame, and these two psychological profiles. It remained unknown how internal and external shame might differ in their unique associations with social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism when evaluated together.
To investigate these emotional profiles, the research team recruited 400 adult volunteers from the general population. The participants were predominantly Italian women, with an average age of 33 years. Because the researchers conceptualized both social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism as traits that vary across the general public, they opted to study a community sample rather than a specific clinical population.
The participants completed a series of online questionnaires designed to measure their psychological traits. To assess vulnerable narcissism, respondents rated their agreement with statements about feeling poorly about themselves when ignored by others. To measure social anxiety, participants rated their fear and avoidance of various social situations, such as making a phone call in public.
The researchers also assessed interpersonal rejection sensitivity by asking participants to imagine hypothetical scenarios, such as asking a family member for a financial loan. Respondents then rated their anxiety regarding the outcome and the likelihood of being rejected. Finally, the survey measured internal shame by asking respondents how often they felt something was fundamentally wrong with them, while external shame was measured by asking how frequently participants believed other people despised them.
In their initial analysis, the researchers looked at simple correlations between all the variables. They observed that interpersonal rejection sensitivity, internal shame, and external shame were all positively associated with both social anxiety symptoms and vulnerable narcissistic traits. At a surface level, individuals who scored high in either psychological profile tended to experience a broad range of shame and a persistent fear of rejection.
The researchers then ran multiple regression models, a statistical technique that isolates the unique contribution of each variable while holding the others constant. In the model predicting vulnerable narcissistic traits, they accounted for the participants’ age, sex, rejection sensitivity, and both types of shame. They found that vulnerable narcissism was associated with being younger, expecting more rejection, and experiencing high levels of both internal and external shame.
A distinctly different pattern emerged in the regression model predicting social anxiety symptoms. When all the variables were analyzed simultaneously, internal shame emerged as the sole independent predictor of social anxiety. Age, sex, interpersonal rejection sensitivity, and external shame were not statistically significant in this model.
These results suggest that while social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism share overlapping features, their emotional cores differ. Social anxiety appears specifically tied to an internalized view of the self as inadequate or defective. Even though socially anxious individuals fear public scrutiny, their distress is most strongly anchored to their own self-directed criticism rather than just the belief that others are judging them.
In contrast, vulnerable narcissism involves a much wider interpersonal and affective profile. The persistence of rejection sensitivity and both forms of shame in the model suggests that vulnerable narcissism involves a broad pattern of interpersonal vulnerability, which may be expressed through defensive strategies that protect a fragile self-image. People with these traits struggle with fragile self-worth internally, but they also remain highly preoccupied with how they are perceived externally and are constantly on guard for potential rejection.
The study relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the data was collected at a single point in time. Because of this, the results establish associations but cannot confirm a sequence of events. It remains unknown whether heightened shame and rejection sensitivity cause the development of social anxiety and vulnerable narcissism over time, or if the relationship works in reverse.
The composition of the sample also limits how broadly the results can be applied. Women made up more than 80 percent of the participants in this particular cohort. The observed emotional patterns might be particularly characteristic of female respondents, and caution is required when extending these findings to men or populations with a different gender balance.
The researchers exclusively used self-report measures, which can sometimes inflate associations between variables. Participants might lack insight into their own psychological traits or misrepresent their feelings due to a desire to appear socially acceptable. This type of bias is particularly common when assessing narcissistic traits, as individuals may hesitate to admit feelings of entitlement or hostility.
The survey did not collect information regarding participants’ psychiatric history or previous psychological trauma. Shame and self-conscious emotions have been linked to trauma-related symptoms and broader psychological vulnerability. Some of the observed associations might reflect unmeasured trauma or previous mental health difficulties within the sample.
Future studies could benefit from longitudinal and experience-sampling designs that track how these processes unfold over time. Recruiting more gender-balanced samples and directly examining potential sex and gender differences would help clarify these psychological profiles. Additionally, accounting for participants’ trauma histories, psychiatric history, and previous psychological treatment could provide a more complete picture of how interpersonal vulnerabilities develop.
The study, “Internal and external shame and rejection sensitivity as correlates of vulnerable narcissism and social anxiety,” was authored by Giulia Rosa Policardo, Cristian Di Gesto, Nicola Marsigli, Francesco Lauretta, Duccio Baroni, and Gioele Salvatori.

Here is what you need to know:
What happened at Riyadh airport?

The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack on Sunday.

“Take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions,” military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X.

Al Jazeera was not able to independently verify the competing claims.

While the internationally recognised government’s forces said they had retaken Mocha and the Dhubab district near the strait, the Houthis have disputed the claims.

Will the US join Saudi strikes against Yemen’s Houthis?

Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack

Fear and uncertainty for civilians as Yemen’s capital comes under attack
Sanaa has come under intense bombing since the Yemeni government announced a campaign to take the capital from the Houthis.
Sanaa, Yemen – At midnight on Tuesday, air strikes rattled the Yemeni capital Sanaa, a city that has been mostly spared bombing since a truce was announced between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis in 2023.
The head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, Rashid al-Alimi, had recently announced a new military offensive was being launched, named Operation Dawn of Yemen, to take Sanaa from the Houthis, who have held the city since September 2014.
Government ground forces remain hundreds of miles away from the capital and embroiled in fighting with the Houthis on Yemen’s west coast and around Taiz.
This means attacks on Houthi positions in Sanaa must come from the air, but the air campaign has caused civilian casualties.
An air strike on Monday hit a location in the Sa’wan area of Sanaa governorate, killing a child and wounding seven other civilians.
The Yemeni government has pledged to continue its attacks until it achieves its objectives, notably the recapture of Sanaa. Regardless of the political opinions of Yemenis in the capital, most fear their city, far from the front lines, will become a war zone once again.
Decisive Storm
Strong memories remain of the Saudi-led coalition’s Operation Decisive Storm, launched against the Houthis in March 2015, which saw hundreds of civilians in Sanaa killed in air strikes.
Since the start of the new Yemeni government offensive, dozens of strikes have hit the capital, including an attack on Sanaa’s international airport, which killed two workers. Both operations were aimed at Houthi sites.
Ghamadan Abood, a 30-year-old courier and Sanaa resident, said the new wave of attacks on the city has heightened fear among residents.
“When I learned about the new operation on Sunday, my feeling of security shrank,” he told Al Jazeera. “At any time and anywhere, air strikes may hit, and civilians could become the next casualties.”
On Monday, Abood was travelling on his bike when air strikes hit Sa’wan, just two kilometres from where he was. With Houthi military facilities believed to be positioned in the city, and the government sometimes hitting residential areas, the bombing highlights the vulnerability of civilians in Sanaa.
“The strikes could be aimed at missile launch pads, military equipment or facilities, but some of these facilities could be near neighbourhoods, farms or roads. So, innocent people could be killed, injured or left terrified,” Abood said.
Saudi Arabia, which supports the Yemeni government, has also come under repeated missile attacks by the Houthis, including two strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the latest on Saturday killing 12 people.
On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said Sanaa, Saada, and Amran were among the primary sources of Houthi missile threats. The coalition has noted that ongoing military operations are aimed at curbing the group’s ability to launch missiles on the kingdom.
Fear of displacement
More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting in Yemen escalated in recent weeks, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Most of those forced to leave their homes have come from Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, where the most intense ground fighting between government and Houthi forces has taken place.
Saleh Ayidh, a 50-year-old resident of Sanaa and father of five, fears the new air strikes will also force people from their homes in the north.
“Today, we see Sanaa as a safe place and distant from the front lines. For me, no place is safe in Yemen, particularly in the north, and war can spread anywhere,” he told Al Jazeera.
At the start of the Saudi-led coalition’s operation against the Houthis in March 2015, Ayidh’s family left the city for a home in the countryside. They lived there for six months, far from the assault on the Yemeni capital.
“Now we do not know what will happen to us. We will decide whether we need to leave the city if the air strikes keep intensifying,” Ayidh said. “Without safety, life is hard.”
Stocking up
The recent air strikes are widely viewed in Sanaa as a sign that war has returned to the capital, prompting residents to stock up on food and fuel.
When Operation Decisive Storm began in 2015, the cost of goods and fuel rose due to disruption to logistics and panic buying. The same trend is being seen again in Sanaa after the recent resumption of hostilities.
Grocery owner Nashwan, 24, has boosted his inventory of essentials such as rice, cheese, milk, biscuits, cooking oil and sugar, before they become too difficult to find.
He also stocked up on petrol, buying 100 litres to use for his minibus if a fuel crisis hits the capital.
“These commodities may become expensive in the coming days. If the war keeps escalating, buying them would cost me more,” Nashwan said. “I do not want to feel the impact of the war immediately.”
Any road closures or a decline in imports caused by the war and a Saudi naval siege on Houthi areas will present major challenges for civilians.
“Rising prices of food and fuel are a real worry for the entire population amid the war and will worsen the humanitarian situation in Yemen,” Wafiq Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera.
Last week, the UN World Food Programme warned that three-quarters of families in parts of Yemen were going hungry.
There are fears an escalation of the fighting will lead to a more intense food crisis across Yemen, which the WFP has already described as “absolutely devastating”.
Yemen fighting
Despite the optimism of the internationally recognised government when announcing Operation Dawn of Yemen, few in Sanaa believe it has the ability to recapture the capital from the Houthis any time soon.
Raiman al-Hamdani, a London-based Yemen analyst, said government forces are big on paper, but remain scattered across multiple fronts, while soldiers are using outdated gear.
“They can hold their lines but can’t push the Houthis out of their mountain strongholds,” Raiman told Al Jazeera last week.
Fuad Ali, 40, a university graduate in Sanaa, said the Saudi-backed government has lost the public’s trust, particularly its claim that it could capture the capital after it suffered a series of embarrassing military defeats in recent weeks on the coast.
“The government has failed to seize the coastal Hodeidah province or Al-Jawf desert province. The fight there could be easier given the topography. How can it recapture the mountainous Sanaa?” Ali told Al Jazeera.
Operation Dawn of Yemen will bring more “destruction to the country’s facilities and increase civilian casualties”, he added.
Ali doubts the operation will return the government to Sanaa. But he also believes the government and Saudi-led coalition have learned their lessons from 2015, when huge civilian casualties from air raids drew international condemnation.
“I am still optimistic that Operation Dawn of Yemen will not damage Sanaa as Operation Decisive Storm did,” Ali said.

====================================================================================================

Archaeologists reveal huge stretch of ancient Lower Aqueduct into Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:39:47 UTC
19:39:47 KST

A 300-meter stretch of the Lower Aqueduct into Jerusalem has been revealed exactly where archaeologists thought it would be – about 5 kilometers south of Temple Mount, near Kibbutz Ramat Rachel. It was unearthed during works to build a new neighborhood, the Israel Antiquities Authority announced on Sunday.
Knowledge of the aqueduct was actually never lost since the structure remained in use for over 2,000 years, apparently since the Hasmonean period in the late second century to first century B.C.E. In fact it only fell out of favor about a century ago, when newfangled inventions such as electricity enabled better alternatives. But it was covered over by the debris and detritus of time; and archaeologists assessed where it was based on surveys starting in the 1970s, explains Benyamin Storchan, co-director of the IAA excavation together with Gil Freid and Rotem Cohen.
In addition, there aren't many options to route a constantly declining water conduit from the Gush Etzion settlement bloc about 12 km southwest, where this structure begins, to the Old City of Jerusalem. Hence even though this section of the aqueduct hadn't been located before – the archaeologists had an idea where it had to be, and it was.
Note that pieces of this aqueduct can be seen here and there along its route, all but hidden in the modern development. This time the plans for the new neighborhood take this ancient element into consideration and will work around and showcase it, Storchan says.
The winding road deterrent
We cannot be sure the aqueduct was used without cease from the Hasmonean, Herodian and/or Roman periods until the British Mandate. It is possible that usage stopped here and there, but there is clear historic evidence of use in the Byzantine and later periods. One example is an inscription in Arabic from the Mamluk period associated with its reconstruction. Moreover, come their time, the Ottomans would line the aqueduct with ceramic pipes.
The British, says Storchan, even thought of reinvigorating the conduit in their time using long metal pipelines but gave up, because in order to maintain its decline from the point of origin, the aqueduct winds around hills, which short ceramic tiles can do but long straight pipelines can't.
In the day, actually, there were two ancient aqueducts into Jerusalem, the Upper and Lower, and neither has been securely dated. It appears however that this Lower one was built first, Storchan says, based on the assessment that the upper one seems more structurally sophisticated. It also seems to follow a straighter path, he adds.
That said, the "unsophisticated" Lower Aqueduct seems to have lasted longer than the fancier Upper one, he adds.
The starting point for Jerusalem's water system was natural springs in Gush Etzion. Each feeds into a small water channel that in turn feeds into the so-called Solomon's Pools in Bethlehem, which is just a large manmade reservoir. Thus the two aqueducts begin at Solomon's Pools.
The pools are traditionally linked to King Solomon some 3,000 years ago based on the verse: "I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees" – Ecclesiastes 2:6 – but it's a misnomer, Storchan says. This reservoir had nothing to do with the fabled king, but is instead apparently from the Hasmonean era, which lasted from 142 to 37 B.C.E.
So, from somebody's pools, the Lower Aqueduct runs through Bethlehem, looping around the Jerusalem hills and to the Armon Hanatziv neighborhood, passing beneath what is today the Abu Tor promenade where the ancients carved a tunnel through the mountain. A fine one, with shafts for ventilation and to remove quarrying debris. The path then proceeds looping around Hutzot Hayotzer, traverses the Guy Ben Hinnom valley, goes around Mount Zion and into the Old City, somewhere around the Dung Gate, to the Temple Mount.
One understands why the British decided to give up rebuilding this path using modern pipes.
This newly unveiled 300-meter stretch is the biggest found to date of this monumental structure, which runs 26 kilometers as it winds around the hills, the archaeologists say.
All in all, from its start, the aqueduct declines all of 40 to 30 meters in height, which was a tremendous feat of ancient planning, Storchan marvels. No later and more technically advanced civilizations changed a meter of the route, not the Byzantines nor the later Umayyads – it was good enough. "It wasn't as fancy as some of the aqueducts in Italy," he adds, but its engineering prowess was phenomenal.
Meanwhile, there is an academic debate about its dating. "The problem is that it was used for 2,000 years and each repair or subsequent phase of usage built on the old structure," he explains. To date it more precisely than pottery or coins can do – they can remain in circulation for decades or even longer – the archaeologists have to do a sort of reverse engineering, peeling off plaster layers. In short, this is in progress.
Sometime in the 20th century, archaeologists learned to date sites by changes in pottery styles; no reputable Israeli researcher would mistake a Roman cooking pot for a Byzantine vessel or an Umayyad creation. Plaster too changed over time, to a degree – it always needed lime, but in some eras it could be more pink, or more gray, Storchan explains. One Umayyad layer has small pebbles impressed into their plaster. That said, plaster isn't a date book. Another challenge with securely dating the aqueduct is that while its entire course had once been covered with stone slabs, those slabs are gone.
Things that never change
But two things were unchanging throughout its lifetime: the force of gravity, and theft.
Along the aqueduct in general, archaeologists have identified spots where the local farmers poked holes into the pipeline to steal the water, and we know this because they found the repaired holes, a lot of them.
"This was an official governmental structure, whether Hasmonean or Byzantine or whatever," Storchan points out.It wasn't a private project, it was a national one and that involved not only clever engineers but armed guards on patrol for villagers ruining the branch into which they were poking holes.
So we knew of the aqueduct and its route; now a large stretch has been found and what have we learned from it?
"Mainly that looking at it today, in many sections it looks like a terrace. The rear wall is covered with dirt while the front wall is exposed, like a step," Storchan says. "Excavating the back portion, we see that the sedimentology soil buildup was more gradual than thought – it hadn't been backfilled. The original Hasmonean construction of may have stood as a freestanding element. Through natural processes over 2,000 years it was covered by soil flow. It didn't seem to have bothered anyone that the backwall was becoming covered up," he added.
Augmenting the Gihon Spring and unreliable rain as a water source for Jerusalem, the Lower and Upper Aqueducts enabled the city to expand in the Hasmonean period, and would continue to provide water for the next 2,000 years.
"What's really cool about this is that we literally see a cross section of time in one element," Storchan sums up. Jerusalem archaeology can be a terrific mess, with layers upon layers and some of them mixed up, Roman ruins lying over Byzantine mosaics, for instance – horrible. It's partly due to destructions and partly due to repurposing. But in the aqueduct, you can see all the time periods in a single installation, one that brought water to the Temple Mount for ritual cleansing – plausibly at the very set of monumental mikvehs archaeologists revealed just last month.

Concerns are mounting over protests and clashes in Syria's Hasaka, where Arab demonstrators have confronted Kurdish residents. The US has expressed concern over the escalating unrest, Kurdish media outlet Rudaw reported.
The US is urging all sides to refrain from violence and resolve their differences through dialogue. The State Department made the comments in response to questions from Rudaw.
"The United States is closely monitoring and concerned by reports of unrest in Hasakah and urges all parties to exercise restraint, reject violence and incitement, and resolve differences through peaceful dialogue," a US State Department spokesperson told Rudaw’s Diyar Kurda.
Wladimir van Wilgenburg, an author, journalist, and expert on Kurdish affairs, also highlighted the tensions, noting that the Kurdish National Council in Syria (KNC) had issued a statement addressing the unrest.
The KNC “affirmed that the future of the Syrian Jazira region cannot be built through exclusion or the fueling of divisions, but rather through partnership and the safeguarding of the dignity and rights of all its people. It emphasized that this approach strengthens the prospects of building a democratic, pluralistic Syria founded on freedom and justice." The statement was distributed to Welat TV.
“The Council stressed that preserving relations among the region's inhabitants requires respect for ethnic and cultural distinctiveness, the rejection of accusations of treason, arrogance, and exclusion, and the prioritization of dialogue and national responsibility."
Arab-Kurdish tensions threaten Syria's integration efforts
The unrest in Hasaka has involved Arab demonstrators protesting against the Kurdish population. The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) previously controlled the city until an agreement was reached with the central government in January 2026.
That agreement followed clashes between the SDF and Damascus. The SDF had received US backing since 2015 and played a central role in the campaign against ISIS, defeating the terrorist organization and liberating areas such as Hasaka from its control.
Hasaka has a mixed Arab and Kurdish population, making it a potential flashpoint for ethnic tensions. Some Arab residents have long resented Kurdish rule.
According to reports, Arab protesters are demanding control of the city's governing institutions. A compromise arrangement currently allows Kurdish officials to retain influence and authority in Hasaka and other areas previously administered by the SDF.
“Tensions escalated after protesters targeted Kurdish symbols, including flags and an image of a woman's braid, which has recently emerged as a symbol of Kurdish resistance in northeast Syria (Rojava),” Rudaw noted.
“Kurdish residents subsequently staged counter-protests, leading to confrontations with state-affiliated security forces. Footage circulated by the UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) showed security forces firing into the air to disperse demonstrators.”
Several issues are contributing to the tensions, including Kurdish-language instruction in schools and the use of Kurdish on government signs. Relations between Arab tribes and former SDF members have also remained strained.
In September, a Kurdish soldier was murdered, while other Kurds died in a prison riot in Kobane.
Damascus and local authorities have generally sought to reduce tensions. However, efforts to preserve stability have often meant that perpetrators on either side have not faced charges.
The Syrian government has also sought to integrate the SDF into the new Syrian army, with some Kurdish commanders retaining senior positions. Sipan Hamo, a prominent SDF commander, became a deputy defense minister.
Hasaka Governor Nour al-Din Ahmed, who is Kurdish, said on Friday that individuals and groups opposed to the integration agreement between the Kurdish administration in northeastern Syria and the central government were responsible for fueling unrest.
“His remarks came amid rising tensions in Hasaka city, where pro-government protesters have attacked Kurdish symbols, prompting counter-protests by Kurdish residents,” Rudaw noted.
Meanwhile, the US said it “supports a unified, sovereign Syria in which Kurds and all other communities enjoy equal citizenship, security, and meaningful participation in governance.”
The US State Department went on to say, "We urge the Syrian government, which includes Kurdish leaders, and local authorities to uphold their commitments, address legitimate concerns, and take practical steps to rebuild trust,” Rudaw added.
Ahmed also addressed opposition to the integration process.
"Some figures and parties oppose the agreement [between the SDF and Damascus] and do not want it to be implemented. So they have sought to play with the emotions of the community by finding pretexts to mobilize the public.”
Ahmed was appointed governor by the SDF and approved by Damascus. He is a key figure in efforts to reconcile the former SDF-held areas with the central government and integrate their institutions.
Former SDF commander Mazloum Abdi also spoke in Hasaka province on Friday, reiterating his commitment to integration.
It remains unclear when the tensions will subside.
Saddam Hussein imagery highlights deeper ethnic divisions
Some protesters carried an image of former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein during a demonstration on Friday.
Several Arab tribes in the Middle Euphrates River Valley near Hasaka have longstanding ties to Iraqi tribes and historically tended to support Saddam Hussein.
Many Kurds are aware of the genocide Saddam committed against the Kurdish population in Iraq. Displaying his image therefore sends a message of hostility toward Kurds.
The use of Saddam's image also highlights the continuing sentiments of some Arab tribes, whose historical connections to Iraq may be stronger than their ties to Syria.
Syrian state media appears to be ignoring the clashes in Hasaka. North Press, a media outlet based in eastern Syria, has also largely avoided covering the unrest.
This may reflect a belief that avoiding publicity will help tensions dissipate.
Meanwhile, the Syrian government announced on Sunday that it was seeking to develop a national approach to combating hate speech.
The initiative brought “together relevant national institutions and experts from the Office of the United Nations Special Envoy for Syria to discuss priorities, coordination and preparations for a national policy.”
Syrian state news agency SANA reported that the meeting was “organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates at the Golden Mazzeh Hotel; the workshop examines public discourse in Syria, international principles and standards, approaches adopted in other countries, and the existing national framework and challenges in addressing hate speech.”
The tensions in Hasaka illustrate that combating hate speech requires more than holding meetings.

Modi is in trouble
The CJP protests sweeping through the country have exposed India’s hollowed-out democracy.

The fact that this process helped sway elections is no longer up for debate. That the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw SIR, is not resigning – out of shame – is astonishing. Even more so now that a corruption case from 2006 against him has resurfaced.
The chaotic, angry, defiant tableaux in the streets of New Delhi and beyond represent a reckoning that has been long in the making. The young, diverse protesters are a stark contrast to Modi and his cabinet – old, humourless men, who have bet on a strategy of demonisation and exclusion to succeed. His cabinet is filled with men full of self-importance, who had, mistakenly, wagered that crimes of elected officials should be tolerated and that a country can be governed indefinitely by creating fissures and manufacturing enemies.

In the process, he has presided over the shredding of the Constitution of India.
Now that all this has come back to haunt him – in the form of “cockroaches” he is unable to exterminate – Modi has turned New Delhi into a fortress and unleashed all the power he has at his disposal on unarmed protesters. As his rule draws to a close — for now, the writing is on the wall — it can be safely said that history books will cast Modi in his proper role as the man who caused an entire generation of Indians to lose all respect for the government, the army, the Delhi Police, as well as the whole structure of governance.

One year after Trump's Gaza ceasefire, questions remain about possible next steps - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
10:31:37 UTC
19:31:37 KST

The Gaza ceasefire took shape a year ago. In September 2025, US President Donald Trump was able to network with key Arab leaders in meetings that eventually led to a ceasefire in Gaza.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law who has played a key role in the 20-point peace plan, posted about the significance of the one-year anniversary of the ceasefire.
“One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible,” he wrote.
He noted how important it was to end the devastating war. He wanted an agreement that created “a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.”
Kushner praised the progress since October 9, 2025, when Hamas accepted Trump’s 20-point peace plan. He noted some of the milestones since that day. On October 13, “all 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.”
He also noted how the UN backed the US plan. He didn’t mention all the important pieces that came together in the following weeks. For instance, the US-backed Civil-Military Coordination Center (CMCC) in Kiryat Gat was set up. This was set up largely by US Central Command and brought together a number of countries.
The concept was to coordinate aid deliveries and monitor the ceasefire. By January 2026, Kushner notes that the UN said: “100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.”
In January 2026, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza was established. This is supposed to be the Palestinian technocratic government for Gaza. So far, Israel has not permitted it to operate in Gaza.
Two million civilians are still stuck under Hamas rule in around 40% of Gaza. The Board of Peace, established as part of the Trump plan, has tried to do some work on the sidelines to see what might happen after Israel’s elections. In general, the theory is that Israel won’t do anything on Gaza until after the elections.
For instance, the peace plan was supposed to see the creation of an international security force. This ISF only seems to have a few dozen personnel so far. Albania and Kosovo were some of the first to come forward.
In June, reports indicated that Morocco and Greece might help support it. Reports also indicated that Kazakhstan would be helpful. Israel, meanwhile, has ejected some countries from the CMCC due to diplomatic disputes.
On the border of Gaza, a new logistics facility called LSA Endurance has taken shape. However, a lot remains to be seen. Kushner noted that the remains of all the deceased hostages had been returned by late January 2026.
He also noted that on July 31, “Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nikolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.”
The last thing on the Kushner list is a meeting on September 23 where the “Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.”
Board of Peace efforts overshadowed by Iran war
Some of the work of the Board of Peace has been overshadowed by the war with Iran. The US administration has been sidetracked to some extent. It also has to deal with other fronts that Israel is involved with. For instance, the administration has had to help Israel in Lebanon with the Lebanese government, where the US also backs a ceasefire.
The US also tried to smooth relations between Israel and Damascus and to prevent Israel-Turkey relations from becoming a crisis. At the same time, recent reports indicate Iran is rebuilding its missile and drone program, and Hamas continues to recruit in Gaza.
Kushner noted that “There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.”
The challenge in Gaza is that it’s not clear what comes next. Arab News noted that “Reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory called for under the ceasefire plan has still not materialized.”
The report said Israel controls around 70% of Gaza. “Nothing has changed for the better; everything has gotten worse, they lie to us, it is all lies,” Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, told AFP. The AFP article is the basis for the Arab News report.
It said, “On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways that have been cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance blown-out windows gape from the facades of buildings that remain standing.” This report also said that around “82% of all standing structures in Gaza are either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026 per the UN.”
It noted that the concept of the plan was for there to be a political transition in Gaza away from Hamas rule. This has not happened. In the past, Israel has accepted Hamas rule in Gaza, and prior to October 7, 2023, there was cash entering Hamas-run Gaza from Doha.
The Hamas leadership continues to live in Qatar. As such, it’s not clear if the promised change under the Trump plan will happen.
The Arab News report and others paint a concerning picture of Gaza. People there said little has changed. While Kushner has praised the peace deal, the question is going to be what will happen next. This has always been the challenge in the past as well. Getting a ceasefire is one thing. Changing the status quo is another.
Israeli voices call to resettle Gaza Strip
Some voices in Israel’s politics have vowed to re-settle Gaza and have encouraged people to emigrate from the enclave. There do not appear to be many voices discussing how to remove Hamas or whether policymakers in Jerusalem want Hamas removed. The war largely resulted in moving people in Gaza from place to place, with Hamas hiding among them.
The most recent IDF data said that the Israeli military carried out 100,000 strikes in Gaza in three years of war. Many of these were carried out in the first months of the fighting.
The IDF also said that it eliminated four heads of Hamas military branches along with 17 brigade commanders, approximately 60 battalion commanders, and approximately 300 company commanders. Hamas only had 24 battalions and five regional brigades.
As such, it would appear that in many cases the brigade commanders and battalion commanders were eliminated twice.
The same goes for the company commanders. What this means is that Hamas replaced the ones who were killed, and then the replacements were killed. Israel also estimates it has eliminated 4,000 of the 6,000 people who attacked Israel on October 7, some of them Hamas and some of them members of other groups or civilian looters.

The struggle for basic subsistence has left society paralyzed, angry, and exhausted. While ordinary citizens are denied prosperity and opportunity, money continues flowing to notorious religious institutions, the shadowy Shi’ite clerical mafia, the machinery of repression, and the regime’s vast propaganda apparatus.
The regime is releasing criminals from prison, arming them with swords, knives, and sledgehammers, and unleashing them to threaten Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the only alternative and leader of Iran’s national uprising – including explicit threats against his life.
Alongside the regime stands a jealous, ambitious, and self-aggrandizing opposition: religious-nationalists, reformists, communists, Kurdish separatists (KDPI, Komala), anti-Israel and anti-American terrorists such as the Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK), discredited human-rights activists, and mercenaries. Much of this opposition acts in concert, little more than puppets performing before cameras.
In the event of an American and Israeli attack, the regime intends to drag Iran into civil war and reactivate Islamic terrorist networks through the mosques. Its organic relationship with al-Qaeda and ISIS is becoming increasingly unmistakable, while Iran’s borders remain open to them. Hashd al-Shaabi, the Fatemiyoun, the Zainabiyoun, and others are integral components of the Islamic Republic’s machinery of repression.
The regime’s propaganda apparatus promotes weapons training, as though a regime nearing collapse is preparing its supporters for urban warfare. Under the banner of confronting America and Israel, it provides military training with an unmistakable objective: to bring war into Iran’s cities, streets, and alleyways. Islamic terrorists know neither peace nor the value of life and security.
Across Iranian cities, the atmosphere is increasingly one of war. People whisper: Will Trump launch the final attack? The country hangs like a pendulum in uncertainty, with law and order unraveling. The mullahs intensify street propaganda to drown out protest, yet a national uprising looms. The regime calls participants in its street spectacles – its “Islam Party” – fedayeen, echoing the political theater of Saddam Hussein and Muammar Gaddafi.
The Revolutionary Guards and security officials squander their days in endless meetings, terrified by the deepening crisis and sheltering behind a bankrupt, discredited government. Agriculture, industry, and production have ground to a halt. There is no coherent plan to regain control. The regime’s security calculations are unraveling.
Iranians await another war in the hope that the bloodthirsty wolf of the Islamic Republic will finally be brought down. They hope Trump will finish the job – or allow Israel to eliminate the regime’s thugs and criminals, layer by layer.
Meanwhile, the regime intensifies killings and executions, hoping to prevent economic misery, relentless inflation, soaring prices, and mounting social anguish from erupting into the “final battle.” Iran is passing through fateful days as urban repression intensifies. The regime’s ultimate nightmare is a popular uprising. A regime that kills its own people for daring to protest will stop at no crime to preserve its rule.
And yet, behind every headline about war, sanctions, missiles, and nuclear negotiations lies another Iran – the Iran of ordinary people who simply want to live. They want to raise their children without fear, put food on the table, walk their streets without repression, speak without looking over their shoulders, and grow old in the country they love.
For nearly half a century, generations of Iranians have watched their lives disappear into prisons, graves, exile, poverty, and shattered dreams. They are not asking the world to give them a country. They already have one – an ancient and beloved homeland called Iran.
They are asking for the chance to take it back. Ninety million people have waited long enough. In memory of the 50,000 slaughtered in Tehran’s streets by the Shi’ite mullahs and IRGC thugs, who cried out, “This is the final battle – Pahlavi will return!” Iran deserves to live again. “Make Iran Great Again!”
Let us hope Washington has the resolve and unwavering will to make it happen.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard
