====================================================================================================

How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:35:09 UTC
14:35:09 KST

How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election
Israel’s election appears less a demand for change than a further entrenchment of the jingoism that surged after October 7, 2023.
As Israel entered the final month before its October 27 election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a chilling warning to share.
Israel’s enemies, he said on September 29, were plotting an attack on the country before the vote. Without providing any evidence, he then quickly referred to continuing attacks by Israeli troops in the Gaza Strip, where he said they had killed more than 100 “terrorists” in recent weeks.
That link drawn by Netanyahu – between the genocidal war on Gaza that began after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, the upcoming elections, and Israel’s national security – was not coincidental, say analysts.
Netanyahu’s insistence that he alone can secure Israelis from a range of threats they face from across the country’s borders, they say, lies at the heart of his re-election campaign, even as his alleged failures during the attack three years ago and in securing the quick release of captives have offered his opponents ammunition.
When a Flydubai flight packed with Israeli passengers on their way from Dubai to Tel Aviv a day after his recent warning nearly crashed after a co-pilot attacked his pilot with an axe in the cockpit, Netanyahu was quick to seize on the incident to argue that he is still man for the country’s top job.
Polls suggest that he faces a stiff test in what is the first general vote since the 2023 attacks, which led to the killing of 1,139 people in Israel and triggered the genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, where Israeli have attacks have since killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
Three years later, the war has become inseparable from the domestic debate over Israel’s direction while also accelerating a political shift to the right – with once-fringe positions on Palestinians now very much the mainstream view.
Few embody this transformation more than Israel’s far-right financial Minister Bezalel Smotrich, sanctioned by a number of Western countries and known for his incendiary and racist language and policies towards Palestinians.
In one of his characteristically inflammatory statements, Smotrich told Israeli outlet Ynet late last month that the Israeli army should “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do there what we did in Gaza”.
Less than two weeks later, Smotrich’s electoral ally Moshe Feiglin added fuel to the fire.
“The enemy is Gaza, not Hamas”, he told the Jerusalem Post, calling for the annexation of the besieged territory after the election. “The baby that will be born tomorrow in Gaza will do exactly the same,” he said, in reference to the 2023 attacks.
Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar said these are not “stray comments” from marginal figures but an electoral message from power-seeking politicians aimed at portraying Palestinians as “not a people with rights, but a demographic and security problem to be expelled, conquered or destroyed”.
He added: “The frightening reality is that the coming election risks becoming a competition not over whether Palestinian life should be protected, but over who can promise to erase it most aggressively.”
‘This is madness’
Following October 7, the younger generation in particular slid rightwards, said Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London.
He said the forces driving Israel to the right had been gathering for decades.
“The trend toward the right began after the Yom Kippur War in 1973, but it has intensified dramatically since October 7,” Bregman told Al Jazeera, referring to the bloody 19-day October War, or the 1973 Arab-Israeli War – a conflict between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria.
More recently, the far right has been emboldened through electoral politics as part of Netanyahu’s government since 2022 – the most right-wing government in Israeli history.
Another outspoken cabinet member alongside Smotrich is Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right provocateur who has previously been convicted of inciting racism and of supporting a terrorist organisation.
“Netanyahu’s greatest mistake – among many – was bringing figures like Ben-Gvir and Smotrich into his coalition,” said Bergman. “By doing so, he legitimised them as influential forces in Israeli politics.”
Ben-Gvir has been so cemented into Israel’s political system, he has hopes pinned on becoming the next Israeli defence minister, the analyst pointed out.
“This is madness. But that’s contemporary Israel,” said Bergman.
Analysts also pointed out that several parties running, including ones that are currently in power and a number that are challenging the current coalition, all advocate for the expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza, as one of the examples of the shift to the right.
Omar Baddar, director of Palthink for Strategic Studies, said the messaging from across the Israeli political and military spectrum in the lead-up to the election shows that there is “a consensus” to continue the attacks on Gaza, where nearly 1,500 have been killed since a “ceasefire” last year.
“They’re using the threats to get more votes,” he said, pointing out to what he described as the radicalisation of the society.
With the election approaching, added Baddar, Israeli leaders are seeking to undo one another: “Who[ever]’s more radical is more likely to get more votes.”
As Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher from inside Israel, writes, “what it means to be ‘right-wing’ in Israel today is above all to take a harder line on Palestinian national claims, security and territorial control.”
He adds: “On security and the Palestinians, a large part of Jewish Israeli politics already works from assumptions that would have been treated as right-wing a generation ago: Deep suspicion of a sovereign Palestinian state, a high tolerance for prolonged military control, and a stronger insistence on Jewish sovereignty as the starting point rather than one value among others.”
Observers and rights groups say the disparity is even evident in the electoral process. A prominent politician and Palestinian citizen of Israel, Sami Abu Shehadeh, has been forced to withdraw from the election over his remarks about the Gaza war, while Israeli far-right leaders have remained untouched despite their violent rhetoric against Palestinians.
Netanyahu’s security credentials endure
Recent polling indicates that the events of October 7 are top of mind for Israelis, who also have questions about who was responsible for the security failures of that day.
Just last month, reports surfaced indicating that Netanyahu had received two separate warnings about an imminent Hamas attack in 2023, from Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, and United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
Netanyahu’s two main rivals in the race for prime minister have cited the alleged warnings to call the prime minister “unfit” to remain at the helm of the country.
But Netanyahu has denied suggestions that he had been forewarned about the attack, and the reports do not appear to have had a significant effect on opinion polls.
While October 7 represents a profound rupture in Israelis’ sense of security, public trust in the Netanyahu government had already been badly shaken by its controversial judicial overhaul, introduced when the prime minister’s current coalition first came to power, said Mairav Zonszein, an Israel-Palestine analyst at the International Crisis Group based in Tel Aviv.
Despite these breaches of trust, the Israeli leader retains support.
“Israelis in general still see Netanyahu as kind of the guy on security. And more to the point, they don’t really see an alternative,” Zonszein told Al Jazeera.
A June survey by Mitvim – the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies found that the Israeli public supports its government’s military and security solutions, and rejects resolving the Palestinian issue and ending the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory. This is the case even while it has been concerned about international isolation and the decline of Israel’s international standing since the beginning of the genocidal war on Gaza, the survey reported.
Yet Israelis are also increasingly war-weary, even as they back the use of more force. Its troops – stretched between six fronts of war in the last few years – are bearing the brunt of this fatigue in Israeli society.
Israel’s Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday that nearly 30,000 soldiers and security personnel are facing psychological trauma since the war.
The ministry said its rehabilitation department’s budget has increased by 88 percent over the past three years to 10 billion shekels ($3.3m), with the majority supporting treatment for mental health conditions and post-traumatic stress disorder.
As Israel expands, the two-state solution fades
Still, Israel in recent months has been more and more vocal about its expansionist vision, with officials brazenly stating the goal of “Greater Israel”. The claim for the conquest is based on a biblical verse (Genesis 15:18-21).
For decades, Israel has ignored international law in its continuous occupation of Palestinian and Syrian land, and has shown little respect for its neighbours’ sovereignty, occupying more land in Syria, as well as in Lebanon in more recent years.
According to Najar, the political economist, the “complete dehumanisation” of Palestinians as evidenced during the campaign reveal that Gaza “is being presented to Israeli voters not as a catastrophe or a crime for which there must be accountability, but as a blueprint to be repeated elsewhere”.
In southern Lebanon, where Israel has been carrying out near daily attacks and and has occupied large swathes of land, residents have told Al Jazeera they expect little to change even if Netanyahu is defeated in the election.
Netanyahu’s main political challenger, Gadi Eisenkot – head of the Yashar party and former army chief of staff – is the father of the so-called Dahiyeh Doctrine, and is just as hawkish about expansion. That doctrine, since Israel’s war with the Lebanese group Hezbollah in 2006, calls for the use of huge force, even against civilian infrastructure, as a deterrent against enemies and was deployed in Israel’s recent wars, particularly in Beirut’s southern suburbs.
If it were up to Eisenkot, the Lebanon front of war would have never scaled down: He has accused Netanyahu of bowing to US pressure to halt operations in Beirut, and has insisted that the military should be able to attack Hezbollah anywhere in Lebanon.
For Israelis still reeling from the events of October 7, Eisenkot could fill the security void many are feeling, said Zonszein.
“They really … see the world as kind of very hostile towards them, the world not understanding what they went through on October 7, and [therefore why] the need to have these security buffer zones in Lebanon, in Syria, and Gaza,” she said.
A two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict is therefore out of the question, said the analysts – and has not even made a blip of an appearance in campaigning before the election.
The idea first emerged during the Oslo Accords more than 30 years ago, which set out a negotiating process aimed at resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, predicated on the belief that the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel was imperative to forge peace.
But since the Oslo process began in 1993, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank has ballooned from about 260,000 to more than 700,000, embedded deep inside West Bank areas that would be needed for a contiguous Palestinian state.
“The concept of a two-state solution is currently irrelevant and likely will remain so for another decade or two, if not longer,” said Bergman. “It is unlikely to become a reality in the foreseeable future, as no Israeli leader can propose it to the Israeli public after the events of October 7.”
The only way it could regain prominence is if there is substantial international pressure, including severe sanctions on Israel, and a non-violent intifada, or an uprising by Palestinians, he said.
The outright rejection of Palestinian statehood has simply become much more “acceptable”, said Zonszein.
“There’s several parties who advocate these views, whereas there isn’t a single Jewish Zionist Party that puts the need for a two-state solution or a Palestinian political process at the forefront,” she said.
Taken all together, Israel’s election appears less a demand for change than a further entrenchment of the jingoism that surged after October 7, 2023.
“[There’s] more and more movement towards more military force, more need for pushing the borders … out of a lot of fear that another October 7 could happen,” said Zonszein.

Riyadh airport attack kills 12, injures 309
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:33:00 UTC
14:33:00 KST

AP Photo
Yemen's Houthis threatened further attacks on Saudi airports and airspace on Oct. 11, urging passengers not to travel after a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people and injured 309.
The group stopped short of claiming responsibility for the Oct. 10 attack but said the kingdom's airports could be targeted, excluding those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," Military Spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X.
The attack was Saudi Arabia's deadliest in more than a decade and marked an escalation in Yemen's war. Riyadh supports the internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who captured stretches of the Red Sea coastline in a rapid offensive last month.
The group intensified attacks on King Khalid International Airport and other targets in Saudi Arabia over the past week. Three people were also killed in attacks on the airport on Oct. 8.
A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed the Iran-backed group for the Oct. 10 strike, calling it a "full-fledged war crime." A diplomatic source also attributed the attack to a Houthi missile.
The coalition said it would respond. Houthi media reported on Oct. 11 two Saudi strikes had targeted Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate.
A U.N. special envoy and several world leaders condemned the Riyadh attack. U.S. President Donald Trump called it "not acceptable" and said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," he said at the White House.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said the dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one citizen each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. Some of the 309 injured were in serious condition.
A Western diplomat based in Riyadh told AFP the official injury count appeared to give an incomplete picture of the aftermath and did not seem to include people with minor wounds.
Airport operations remained suspended into Oct. 11, a senior aviation source told AFP. Flight tracking service Flightradar24 said the closure had been extended until 2100 GMT.
A second aviation source involved in overseeing flights to Riyadh confirmed operations had stopped "until further notice." Radar and communications equipment had been damaged, according to information available to the source, who said the runways also needed assessment.
A passenger told AFP they witnessed a strike in the domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the passenger said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies advised their citizens to avoid the airport. Several embassies were barring staff from using it over the following week, a senior Western diplomat told AFP.
The Saudi-led coalition also reported a projectile had fallen near Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on the evening of Oct. 10.
The U.S. Embassy said on Oct. 11 its staff in the kingdom would need permission to use airports in Dammam and Jeddah. A similar requirement had been introduced for Riyadh days earlier.
The attack led health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said. Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month, according to emails sent to parents and seen by AFP.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the strike a "dangerous escalation." Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the "heinous attack," while Jordan described it as "brutal."
The attack was the kingdom's deadliest since May 2015, when an Islamic State suicide bombing killed 21 worshippers in the eastern Qatif governorate.
It also came ahead of Saudi Arabia's convention and entertainment season. Riyadh hosts a busy calendar of events, including an investment conference attended by foreign leaders and business executives.
The WPC Energy Congress opened in Riyadh on Oct. 11 after being delayed by the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war in February.
Saudi Arabia has led an international coalition supporting Yemen's government militarily since 2015. Military sources told AFP on Oct. 10 Saudi-backed government forces were advancing against the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key passage for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping, in areas the group captured last month.
The Houthis said they had repelled the advance. Yemen's government announced a counteroffensive last week to retake Houthi-held territory.
Claims by the opposing sides could not be independently verified because of rapidly changing conditions and limited access for journalists.

Middle East conflicts, energy supplies, to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:19:15 UTC
14:19:15 KST

Finance officials from around the world will gather in Thailand this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest energy supply shock ever, and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and the inflation and hardship it has caused will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held outside of Washington for the first time in three years.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be notably absent, dispatching two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said.
His decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine's battle against Russia's invasion, and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world's oil, pressures were building again. Soaring diesel prices, rising fertilizer costs, and a looming "super" El Niño weather effect that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are hitting at once.
Group of Seven countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who wants lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Trump announces diesel deal with Russia
Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices.
Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it's the combination... What's happening to fertilizer prices? What's happening to energy costs? What's happening to debt? It's that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months."
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva issued a similar warning in her traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings, telling the audience, "Winter is coming."
The IMF has signaled little change to its forecast of 3% global growth in 2026 and may slightly raise its forecast for next year. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia's invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.
Growing public debt leaves developing countries heavily vulnerable
One major headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden, which is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressure. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030.
Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.
Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue in developing countries on average.
Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt service payments for the poorest countries, but G20 diplomats said there is little appetite for such action now, as high debt levels and political pressures pose bigger hurdles this time.
Many lower-income countries worry about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper, reforms as a condition of approval, a change many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.
"Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse."
Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young.
The IMF risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many developing countries.
"As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said.
Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to the 10,000-plus travelers descending on Thailand's bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent attacks on Saudi airports.
Previous IMF-World Bank meeting took place after Oct. 7
The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after the October 7 massacre.
Three years later, the link between national security and international finance is clear, although finance officials at the time dismissed the Hamas attack as not an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council.
"Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we're currently experiencing with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago."
Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive, and they have to recognize that they don't live in the world they used to."

Pro-Israel demonstrators carried Iranian flags

Israeli expat recounts destruction, home collapse in magnitude 7.7 Panama earthquake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
05:18:50 UTC
14:18:50 KST

As a magnitude 7.7 earthquake shook Panama on Friday, Israeli Nurit Goren Elfant and her family felt lucky to be outside as their house, like many others in the area, collapsed.
Speaking to N12 News on Saturday, Elfant described the destruction and damage caused by the quake and subsequent aftershocks, some reaching up to magnitude 5.8.
“It happened a few minutes before one in the afternoon. It was something you can’t even imagine,” she recounted. “The ground shook at a level you don’t see in movies, and for 13 consecutive hours, there were tremors every few minutes. We were lucky to have been outside when our house was destroyed.”
Much of southern Panama was cut off from the internet in the aftermath of the quake, including in the coastal town of Playa Venao, an area where Elfant told N12 many Israeli families live. Only those who have access to satellite internet have been able to connect to the outside world.
“Some of these families lost everything,” Elfant continued, describing the experience of her fellow Israeli expats. “Everything completely collapsed.”
A tsunami warning sends families to higher ground
A Tsunami warning was issued during the tremors, leading to many of the families moving to higher ground in the mountains. Elfant’s family returned to lower ground earlier than others, but some of those who stayed got stuck in the mountains due to roads being blocked with debris and bridges collapsing.
Elfant told N12 that Israeli families were among those stuck up on the mountain on Friday afternoon as Shabbat approached.
A community that comes together
The Israeli community managed to organize a Shabbat meal despite the conditions.
"The rabbi of the Chabad house went up to the mountain; they took the food they had left at the Chabad house and what they could salvage from the supermarket, which was completely destroyed, and they set up an impromptu Shabbat meal there and a big kiddush for the entire Jewish community," Elfant said.
"I think there were over 200 people there. They stayed to sleep outside there. They are still without water and electricity, so we don't know what's happening to them."
Elfant’s family has been able to help some neighbors with two buses they previously converted into homes. "Because a bus can absorb shocks, we sleep in it and let other families live with us. Right now, five families live here on our farm. We have solar electricity, but there is no electricity in Vanu and the entire area," she explained to N12.
According to N12, the water supply in the area has been severely damaged, and people have little access to potable water. "Our well, which is 42 meters deep, has completely mixed up and is mainly producing basalt," says Nurit. "Because of the tremors, all the water tanks that people had for emergencies were flooded. We had a three-cubic-meter water tank that exploded."
To drink water, Elfant said she and her family will have to collect water from a stream or rainwater and boil it. They hope to get through the next month and rebuild their home.

Tehran showcases urban market management, food security expertise to foreign delegations
TEHRAN- Tehran Municipality’s first program in the series of specialized visits “Introducing Tehran’s Urban Management Capabilities,” focusing on urban markets, logistics, and food security, was held on Saturday, October 10, in cooperation with the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) and the Asian Mayors Forum (AMF).
In this program, representatives of foreign countries and international organizations visited the Jalal Al-e Ahmad Fruit and Vegetable Market and the Beihaghi Shahrvand Store and became acquainted with Tehran’s urban management capacities in supplying and distributing essential goods. After these visits, a specialized meeting was held aimed at examining areas for joint cooperation.
This program, held under the title “Specialized Visit to Tehran’s Urban Markets, Logistics and Food Security” by the International Deputy of the Communication Center of Tehran Municipality, was welcomed by those present.
The purpose of this measure was also to develop urban diplomacy and introduce Tehran’s management capacities to representatives of international organizations.
During the visit to the Shahrvand Store, a press conference was held in the administrative section of the store. Davood Qorbanian, CEO of Shahrvand Store; Mehdi Bakhtiari-Zadeh, CEO of the Organization of Markets; Hamid Reza Gholamzadeh, Head of the Communication and International Affairs Center of Tehran Municipality, as well as the Secretary-General of the Asian Mayors Forum; and Mohammad Ali Shafiei, International Deputy of the Communication and International Affairs Center of Tehran Municipality, were present, and specialized topics concerning urban market management, supply of goods, and food security were discussed.
Fruit and vegetable markets ready to transfer experience and develop export of Iranian products
The CEO of the Organization for Management of Fruit and Vegetable Markets of Tehran Municipality, referring to the capacity of the capital’s market network, announced the organization’s readiness to develop international cooperation in the fields of transferring technical knowledge, supplying and distributing food products, and expanding exports of Iranian products.
Emphasizing the municipality’s responsibility to ensure citizens’ food security, he said: Access to high-quality, healthy, and reasonably priced food products is one of the main axes of the municipality’s activity. In this regard, an extensive network of fruit and vegetable markets and Shahrvand stores has been formed across the city.
Bakhtiari-Zadeh added: Currently, about 320 fruit and vegetable markets are active in Tehran, and citizens can, on average, access one of the municipality’s food product distribution centers by traveling less than 900 meters.
Referring to quality control mechanisms, he said: To ensure the health of products, a direct supply chain and continuous testing are on the agenda, and goods that do not meet the required quality and health standards will not be allowed to enter the markets covered by the organization.
The CEO of the Organization for Management of Fruit and Vegetable Markets of Tehran Municipality, referring to the capacity for cooperation with the countries present at the meeting, stated: This complex can cooperate in transferring technical knowledge, exchanging experience, and presenting models of management and distribution of food products.
Referring to Iran’s agricultural capacity and the production of diverse products in different seasons of the year, he added: Cooperation with traders and economic actors can provide the basis for developing the export of fruit and vegetable products and protein products.
Bakhtiari-Zadeh noted: Currently, trade in agricultural products between Iran and some of the countries present at this meeting exists, and cooperation with Tehran Municipality’s extensive network can help strengthen these relations and develop export routes.
In the end, he expressed hope that this visit would pave the way for expanding commercial and technical cooperation with friendly countries and forming more sustainable relations in the field of supply, distribution, and export of food products.
Shahrvand ready to develop commercial cooperation and exchange experience with foreign companies
Davood Qorbanian, CEO of Shahrvand Company, also emphasizing the necessity of expanding international cooperation, said: Familiarizing representatives of countries and embassies with Tehran Municipality’s services can pave the way for strengthening relations among countries and developing commercial and trade communications.
Referring to the company’s capacities for cooperation with trade and retail actors in various countries, he stated: Shahrvand is ready to provide the ground for the exchange of knowledge, experience, and technology and the development of commercial exchanges. In this regard, we invite the representatives of the countries present to introduce capable companies from their countries to begin joint cooperation.
Qorbanian, who is also the vice chairman of the country’s Chain Stores Union, added: The possibility of developing communications and exchanging experience exists not only for Shahrvand Company but also for other chain stores in Iran.
Stating that Iran enjoys significant capacities in the production of agricultural products and foodstuffs, as well as a broad consumer market, he said: Foreign companies can identify new opportunities for developing their commercial activities by understanding the needs of the Iranian market.
The CEO of Shahrvand Company continued: The areas of cooperation are not limited only to the supply of food, agricultural products, and meat; they also include the field of retail technologies, including enterprise resource planning (ERP) software, store management, and marketing systems. Shahrvand Company is ready to benefit from the specialized knowledge and experience of foreign companies in these areas.
Qorbanian at this meeting, referring to the role of Shahrvand stores and fruit markets, added: Iranian producers and industries can use the capacity of Shahrvand stores to offer products, introduce brands, and access the consumer market. In return, this company can be a platform for introducing and offering products of various countries in the Iranian market; a cooperation that includes areas such as raw materials, agricultural and food products, packaged goods, and retail-related technologies.
He asked the representatives of the countries present to provide the ground for communication with capable companies and economic actors through their commercial counselors and the economic sections of their embassies.
In the end, Qorbanian expressed hope that these visits would lead to practical and sustainable cooperation among Shahrvand Company, Iranian traders, and foreign companies and provide the ground for market development, exchange of knowledge and technology, and mutual supply of the parties’ commercial needs.
Tehran municipality seeks to turn sister-city relations into practical economic cooperation
The Secretary-General of the Asian Mayors Forum at this meeting emphasized using the capacity of relations among cities to develop commercial cooperation, transfer experiences, and engage economic companies.
Referring to Tehran’s experience in large-scale distribution of goods and maintaining citizens’ access to essential products, he spoke of the capacity for cooperation with regional cities in the fields of export and import of products, transfer of technical knowledge, and provision of urban services.
Gholamzadeh also introduced the “Zero Inflation” initiative, aimed at stabilizing the prices of 12 essential goods for six months, as one of Tehran Municipality’s measures to support citizens.
Foreign diplomats emphasize Tehran’s capacity in supplying and distributing essential goods
At the end of the program, representatives of foreign countries and the Deputy Secretary-General of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO), in conversations with reporters, considered Tehran’s capacities in supplying and distributing food to be significant.
ECO emphasizes Tehran urban management’s role in strengthening regional food security
The Deputy Secretary-General of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) also considered the city’s experience in supplying and distributing food valuable and emphasized the role of municipalities in strengthening food security and citizens’ affordable access to essential goods even in crisis conditions.
Emre Hengut also called for the continuation of specialized visits and the exchange of experiences to develop cooperation among cities and regional institutions.
The list of guests present in the half-day tour organized by Tehran Municipality, included Kim Junpyo, Ambassador of South Korea, and his wife; Ahmad Soueidan, Ambassador of Lebanon; Khalid Ibrahim Elsheikh, Deputy Head of Mission in the Sudanese Embassy; Bahador Nazir, Counsellor of the Tajik Embassy; Mostafa Diabate, Counselor of the Burkina Faso Embassy; Vladislav Perpelkin, Counselor of the Russian Embassy; Hubert Przybyszewski, First Secretary of the Polish Embassy; Deputy Ambassador of Oman; Faizan Taimoor Saqib, Third Secretary in Embassy of Pakistan, Counselor of the Pakistani Embassy; Jadidzadeh, Economic Officer of the United Nations Coordinator’s Office; Chentaei Emre Angut, Deputy Secretary-General of ECO; and Lola Gheybollahzadeh, Head of ECO Coordination and Follow-up Department.
Overall, the specialized visit served as a practical step in strengthening Tehran’s urban diplomacy and presenting its integrated network of fruit and vegetable markets and Shahrvand stores as a working model for food supply, price regulation, and access to essential goods.
By bringing together foreign ambassadors, international organizations such as ECO and the Asian Mayors Forum, and Tehran Municipality officials, the program created a platform for exchanging technical knowledge, expanding trade in agricultural and food products, and encouraging joint investment and retail cooperation.
If followed by concrete agreements and sustained follow-up, such initiatives could help transform sister-city and international relations into tangible economic partnerships, enhance regional food security, and open new export and knowledge-exchange opportunities for both Iran and participating countries.

Voting under fire: how the IDF prepares for October 27 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:33:23 UTC
13:33:23 KST

Amid ongoing fighting and military operations on multiple fronts, the IDF is finalizing logistical preparations for Israel's October 27 election to the 26th Knesset, ensuring that every active-duty and reserve soldier can exercise the right to vote. While polling stations across the country will open on Tuesday, October 27, some soldiers will be able to cast their ballots as early as a week beforehand. Can soldiers join political parties? How can troops identify themselves at polling stations in Lebanon? And what happens if a soldier is called into combat on Election Day? Here is everything you need to know about voting in the IDF.
For a significant number of IDF personnel, this will be the first election in which they are eligible to vote. With the vote approaching amid a highly charged political climate, the military has instructed soldiers on active duty to refrain from expressing political opinions, engaging in political arguments or attempting to influence political views within their units.
The restrictions also extend to social media. Soldiers are prohibited from expressing political positions on any platform, including liking, commenting on, sharing or distributing posts by political parties or politicians. What is permitted? Soldiers may publicly follow the accounts of candidates or political parties solely to stay informed. Attendance at political gatherings or campaign events is also subject to strict conditions: soldiers may attend only as spectators, must wear civilian clothing and may not identify themselves as military personnel.
Reservists who are not on active duty are exempt from these restrictions on political expression and may voice political opinions online, provided they do not use military uniforms or IDF insignia.
How will I know when and where to vote?
Military polling stations will operate on Election Day from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Each unit will appoint an election officer responsible for informing soldiers of their polling station's exact location and operating hours.
Fixed polling stations will be established at military bases and facilities, while mobile stations will travel between troops stationed at military outposts, protecting communities, participating in training exercises or carrying out operational missions. Military polling stations will also operate in hospitals so that hospitalized soldiers registered with the IDF's medical liaison system, known as Ram 2, can vote.
Soldiers may vote at any military base where they are present on Election Day, even if it is not their permanent base. They may also choose to vote at a civilian polling station, provided they cast only one ballot. Voting more than once is a criminal offense.
How does identification work at military polling stations? 
Each military polling station will have an election committee consisting of two soldiers who will undergo training before Election Day and will be responsible for verifying voters' identities using military identification or valid civilian documents.
Active-duty soldiers may identify themselves using a military ID card, national identity card, valid driver's license bearing their photograph or valid Israeli passport accompanied by proof of military service. There is no need to bring the voter notification received by mail.
For combat troops operating beyond enemy lines without identification documents, including those deployed in Lebanon, identity verification may be carried out using military dog tags, identification by another soldier or a photographed copy of an identity document, such as a national ID card, driver's license or military ID.
At hospital polling stations, soldiers must present a military identification card bearing their photograph, whether as an enlisted soldier, officer or noncommissioned officer. Alternatively, they may present a civilian photo ID, such as a national identity card, driver's license or valid Israeli passport, together with a voting authorization form issued by hospital staff.
How does voting work?
Military voting uses a double-envelope system. Behind a privacy screen, soldiers place their chosen party's ballot slip inside a blue envelope. That envelope is then placed inside a white envelope bearing the soldier's personal details.
How are ballot secrecy and election integrity protected? 
At the end of voting, military ballot boxes will be transferred, locked, to the Central Elections Committee at the Knesset in Jerusalem for counting. The sealed ballot boxes will be collected by designated personnel trained as regional election officers and remain under their supervision until formally handed over at the Knesset.
How are the votes counted?
During the counting process, the blue envelope containing the ballot is separated for counting, while the white envelope bearing the soldier's personal information is destroyed. The entire process of opening ballot boxes and counting votes is conducted by the Central Elections Committee without IDF involvement.
When does early voting begin in the IDF? 
Combat soldiers deployed in operational areas and beyond enemy lines, including Gaza, Syria and Lebanon, will be eligible to vote beginning at 10 p.m. on October 20. Mobile polling stations will reach troops in the field to collect their ballots. Soldiers scheduled to participate in operational missions on Election Day will also be given the opportunity to vote in advance.
Can soldiers run for office or join political parties?
Soldiers are permitted to register as members of political parties, provided they do not identify themselves as military personnel. Senior civilian employees of the IDF and career military personnel may run as party candidates only if they terminate their military service at least 100 days before the election. Conscripts must arrange a deferment of military service at least 100 days before Election Day, while reservists on active duty must end their service at least 30 days before the election.
Can soldiers work at polling stations? 
Soldiers may work at civilian polling stations on Election Day in politically neutral roles, including election committee secretary, usher or election integrity inspector, provided they obtain their commander's approval. They may not serve as election committee members, party observers or employees of political parties.
Is photography allowed? 
As at civilian polling stations, photography is strictly prohibited inside military polling stations.
Do soldiers get Election Day off? 
Unlike civilians, IDF personnel are not entitled to a day off for the election. Military operations and routine activities will continue as usual.

US opens antitrust probe into TV networks halting Trump coverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:30:10 UTC
13:30:10 KST

US opens antitrust probe into TV networks for halting Trump coverage
Department of Justice says it’s investigating whether the White House press pool’s decision violated antitrust laws.
The United States Department of Justice has opened an investigation into television networks’ decision to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month.
A spokesperson said on Saturday that the department was investigating whether the networks violated federal antitrust laws by their boycott, which followed a White House decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organisations, including CNN.
The networks under investigation are ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News, said Emily Convington, the Justice Department spokesperson.
“Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” she said of the antitrust legislation.
“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations. Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media “fake news” and frequently clashes with reporters during encounters with the press.
The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.
The networks did not immediately comment on the announcement.
The Justice Department’s move came after the television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
The White House said on September 19 that covering the president was a “privilege – not a right”. The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.
CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool.
They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage, and share the footage with outlets around the country.
All of the five television networks that cover the White House, including Fox News, suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.
The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ordered the administration to “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” their access.
However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued.
Jose Zamora, the Committee to Protect Journalists’ Americas director, on Saturday criticised the administration’s decision to investigate.
“The government should not use antitrust investigations to intimidate news outlets defending press access,” Zamora said on X. “The public’s right to know depends on that access.”

One year after ceasefire, Gaza’s promised ‘day after’ has yet to arrive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
04:23:51 UTC
13:23:51 KST

One year after the ceasefire took effect in the Gaza Strip, all the Israeli captives have been returned, but much of what the agreement promised the Palestinians remains unrealized.
Israeli attacks have continued, the military withdrawal has stalled and partly reversed, governance arrangements remain incomplete, and large-scale reconstruction has yet to begin.
Most of Gaza’s roughly 2.1 million people remain displaced, many living in tents, damaged buildings, or amid rubble, as Palestinian authorities say the continuing attacks are an extension of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, launched on Oct. 8, 2023.
The ceasefire took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, after mediation by Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and the US providing for a phased Israeli withdrawal, expanded aid, new governance arrangements, and reconstruction.
Israeli captives returned
On Oct. 13, 2025, Hamas released the remaining 20 living Israeli captives as Israel freed 1,968 Palestinian detainees, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross.
The transfer of remains continued until Jan. 26, 2026, when the Israeli army announced the recovery of the last body.
Israeli attacks continue
But the ceasefire did not bring an end to Israeli attacks in Gaza.
Over the past year, Israeli violations of the agreement have killed more than 1,470 Palestinians and wounded over 5,180, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye said in August that continued Israeli attacks violated the agreement and were obstructing implementation of its second phase.
Israeli withdrawal reversed
Before the ceasefire was declared, the Israeli army controlled about 75% of Gaza.
The agreement initially brought a partial withdrawal to the so-called “yellow line,” leaving around 53% of the enclave under Israeli military deployment, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
But the pullback stalled and later reversed.
By late June, OCHA said Israeli forces had expanded westward beyond the yellow line, leaving 64.9% of Gaza under direct Israeli control or tighter restrictions.
By August, the UN said nearly two-thirds of the enclave was inaccessible to Palestinians or subject to severe restrictions.
Second phase remains stalled
A 15-point roadmap linked restrictions on the weapons of Hamas and other Palestinian factions to additional Israeli withdrawals, deployment of an international force, transfer of governance, and reconstruction.
Egypt, Qatar, and Türkiye said on Aug. 3 that Hamas and other Palestinian factions had accepted the roadmap, including its provision on weapons.
Later that month, eight countries, including Türkiye, Egypt, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, said Israel had rejected the roadmap, obstructing implementation of the broader plan.
Governance transition incomplete
A technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, headed by Ali Shaath, was formed in January to oversee civilian affairs during the transitional period.
But the transfer of governing responsibilities remains incomplete, while a planned international stabilization force has yet to be deployed.
Reconstruction still out of reach
Despite provisions to increase humanitarian aid, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said in September that Kerem Shalom remained the only operational crossing for goods after the Zikim crossing was closed in May.
Israeli restrictions also continued on materials needed for shelter and construction.
The UN, European Union, and World Bank estimate Gaza will need $71.4 billion over 10 years for recovery and reconstruction, including $26.3 billion in the first 18 months.
Their assessment found that 1.9 million Palestinians had been displaced and 371,888 housing units damaged or destroyed.
OCHA said in September that Israeli restrictions were still blocking urgently needed shelter supplies, including thousands of tents and construction materials.
One year after the ceasefire, the issue of the captives is closed. For Gaza’s displaced population, however, the promised transition from war to recovery has yet to arrive.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Israeli attacks on Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian figures.

Esra Tekin
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
The US Justice Department on Saturday launched an antitrust investigation into five major television networks after they temporarily refused to provide pool coverage of President Donald Trump, NBC News reported.
The probe targets NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN, and Fox News, which collectively make up the White House television press pool, and take turns covering the president’s public engagements and trips. They suspended pool participation last month after three major outlets – CNN, MS NOW, and website Politico – were all banned from the White House.
A Justice Department official confirmed that the five networks were issued “civil investigative demands” on Friday as part of the investigation.
“Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events. Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act,” said department spokeswoman Emily Covington.
“The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws.”
In the pool, the network assigned to pool duty shares its reporting materials, including video and audio recordings, with other news organizations.
When contacted for comment on the investigation, the White House did not provide a response.
ABC News said it had yet to receive a formal notice from the Justice Department but anticipated receiving one. NBC, CBS, and CNN declined to comment, while Fox News did not respond to a request for comment.
The investigation comes amid growing tensions between the Trump administration and the White House press corps.
In September, Trump accused journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico of spreading “FAKE NEWS” and barred their outlets from the White House grounds. The three later filed a legal challenge to the ban which is still playing out in court.

Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:41:58 UTC
12:41:58 KST

Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
Medical services in Taiz risk shutting down as fuel, medicines, and supplies run alarmingly low under Houthi blockade.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”.
Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”.
It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”.
Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said.
It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid.
It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities.
“Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said.
Taiz remains ‘major battleground’
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said southwestern Taiz is a ‘major battleground’ between the Houthis and troops of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Both sides claim to be gaining ground. Mawry confirmed that the strategic city of Mocha, the district of Dhubab, and Bab al-Mandeb remain under the control of the Houthi group.
Fellow at the Future Security Program of the New America think tank, Adam Baron, told Al Jazeera, Taiz could become “the real game changer” in the conflict.
But he warned, “its not just about military dynamics—the incipient siege on Yemen’s third largest city leaves roughly a million people trapped, creating real risks of a devastating humanitarian crisis.”
Renewed siege
The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast.
Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre.
The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed.
The renewed siege took shape in early October.
The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October.
Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”.
He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced.
Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58).
“We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said.
The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organisation have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril.
“Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organisation.

Shahar Nevo's double life as Bar-Ilan math professor accused of plotting massacre - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:17:20 UTC
12:17:20 KST

For more than two decades, Prof. Shahar Nevo built an extensive career in the world of mathematics: he graduated with honors, published dozens of studies, and taught generations of students at Bar-Ilan University.
Until this week, his name was known mainly in the hallways of the math department and among those who took his courses in calculus and analysis. His online presence consisted mainly of scientific articles, course pages, exams, and lecture summaries, with no interviews, public statements, or social media presence.
However, this academic career now exists under the shadow of a severe indictment: the 60-year-old professor is accused of preparing to execute an act of terrorism, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice. According to the indictment, he planned an attack for more than three years, with the aim of killing hundreds of Israeli Arabs.
Academic Background and Research Career
Nevo was born on October 12, 1966. He began his academic path at Tel Aviv University in 1984 and, three years later, completed a bachelor's degree in mathematics. In 1992, he moved to Bar-Ilan University, where he completed a master's degree in 1995 and a Ph.D. in 1999. He completed his master's studies summa cum laude, earning the Dean's Prize in 1996, and his doctoral dissertation was also praised. He wrote his research under the supervision of Prof. Lawrence Zalcman, an expert in complex analysis, and the two maintained a professional connection through the joint studies they published.
Upon completing his Ph.D. in 1999, Nevo joined the tenured academic faculty at Bar-Ilan. He started as a lecturer and, over the years, advanced through the ranks to Associate Professor in the Department of Mathematics.
According to his official profile, he specializes in complex analysis, operator theory, and matrices of rational functions.
Over the years, he accumulated 51 academic outputs, including 40 published papers. His research activity continued uninterrupted into recent years: in 2023, he co-authored a study with Zeev Shem-Tov published in the Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications, and in 2024, he published another study with Tomer Menaket.
Concurrently, he maintained long-standing international collaborations, including a series of publications with the German mathematician Jürgen Grahl from the University of Würzburg, alongside participation in conferences in Israel and abroad.
In 2012, he was among the organizers of an analysis session at the Israel Mathematical Union conference and even lectured there, and in 2017 he served as a visiting researcher at the School of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of Sydney in Australia.
Teaching Activity and Personal Profile
Alongside his research, Nevo remained an integral part of the teaching framework at Bar-Ilan. Traces of the courses he taught have been scattered online for over a decade - from exercise sheets and exams to lecture summaries prepared by students; in 2023, for example, a document titled "Summary of Infi 4 Course based on lectures by Prof. Shahar Nevo" was uploaded to the Math-Wiki website.
In the last academic year, he continued to lecture as usual. In the university's schedule, he is registered as a lecturer in the courses "Mathematics for Chemists C" and "Infinitesimal Calculus 4," and even appears as an academic advisor to students on the department website. The most recent retake exam (Moed B) for the calculus course took place on September 1 of this year, just weeks before his arrest.
Outside of academia, almost no public information exists regarding Nevo's personal life. According to the details of the case revealed in prosecution documents, he lives alone in Petah Tikva and holds a firearm license.
An examination of his past highlights the near-total absence of any non-professional dimension: despite decades at the university, dozens of studies, and generations of students, his digital footprint consists almost entirely of pure mathematics.
Online, an old personal website remains on the Bar-Ilan University server, including a curriculum vitae, a list of publications, and contact details, alongside various academic and professional profiles. Meanwhile, no public social media accounts can be definitively attributed to him, nor are there any past interviews or opinion pieces.
Even on the "Dargo" website, where students typically review teaching staff, a page exists under his name, but it has no reviews. His official page on the Department of Mathematics website, last updated on June 9 of this year, displayed him as Prof. Shahar Nevo and detailed his research areas before it was removed from the internet.
At Bar-Ilan University, officials quickly disavowed the veteran faculty member. Following the filing of the indictment, the institution stated that they "condemn and is shocked by the acts attributed to the lecturer," clarifying that he would be suspended immediately pending the conclusion of proceedings. Concurrently, his name was removed from the university's lecturers page.
The Terror Plot Details
According to the indictment filed by the State Attorney's Office to the Central District Court in Lod, the 60-year-old lecturer, a resident of Petah Tikva, planned to execute an extreme plan - which he conceived over several years out of an ideological motive. The defendant named his plan after an acronym for "Am Ya'ase Transfer" ("The Nation Will Execute a Transfer").
The Central District Attorney's Office attributes to the defendant in the indictment the commission of security offenses of preparation to commit an act of terrorism under the Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice, and is requesting that the court detain him until the conclusion of legal proceedings against him.
From the indictment filed by attorneys Roy Reis and Tomer Steinberg of the Central District Attorney's Office, it emerged that against the backdrop of the "Operation Guardian of the Walls" riots and later, with greater intensity against the backdrop of the Swords of Iron war, the defendant decided to plan and carry out numerous terror acts simultaneously, and to cause the deaths of many hundreds of Arab Israeli citizens, including Bedouins, throughout the entire country, including Arabs residing in east Jerusalem and the West Bank.
The plot was intended to cause their flight and permanent deportation to the territories of Jordan, Lebanon, and the Gaza Strip.

Gidi Dar’s Legend of Destruction, the movie that depicts the Jewish revolt against Rome and the destruction of the Second Temple through images, is now available for digital purchase in the US on platforms including Apple TV, Google Play, and Prime Video.
The English-language version features Oscar Isaac, Evangeline Lilly, Elliott Gould, Billy Zane, and Marilu Henner. It was directed by Dar, who has made such acclaimed films as Ushpizin and Eddie King, and it was written by Dar and Shuli Rand.
The two have collaborated frequently, and their upcoming film, The Wedding Entertainer (The Tale of Moishe Badhan), had its world premiere at the Tribeca Festival this year.
Legend of Destruction brings ancient Jerusalem to life through 1,500 original paintings by David Polonsky (who also worked on Waltz with Bashir) and Michael Faust.
The story follows Ben Batich, voiced by Isaac, an idealistic young man who joins the zealots rebelling against Rome, driven by anger at corruption and inequality. As the revolt that began in 66 CE descends into civil war, his pursuit of justice turns into fanaticism, helping the Romans to destroy the temple and retake control of Jerusalem.
Lilly voiced Queen Berenice, Gould played Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, Zane portrayed rebel leader Bar Giora, and Henner voiced Batich’s mother.
Film draws on The Jewish War, Talmudic legends, and historical research
Drawing on Josephus’s The Jewish War, Talmudic legends, and historical research, the film explored how a divided society can bring about its own downfall.
“By stripping away the illusion of 24 frames per second, we invite the viewer’s mind to fill in the gaps, creating not just motion, but emotional depth,” Dar said of its unusual visual approach.
Isaac said he quickly stopped noticing that the images were still paintings: “I felt like I was watching Gladiator.”
Lilly described the film as “a warning signal for the modern world.”
More information is available at legendofdestruction.com

Abbas delays elections until 2027, Palestinian democracy demands genuine reform - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-11
03:17:05 UTC
12:17:05 KST

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections on Saturday, replacing the November 28 vote with a promise of presidential and parliamentary elections on September 11, 2027.
His decree cited Israeli actions and deteriorating conditions across Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.
The difficulties facing election organizers are substantial. Gaza is devastated, Hamas remains armed, and movement restrictions complicate preparations. Those conditions require serious practical arrangements.
Abbas also owes Palestinians an explanation of how another postponement will produce a political system capable of holding its leaders accountable.
Palestinians last elected a president in 2005 and a legislature in 2006. Abbas’s presidential mandate expired in 2009. An entire generation has reached adulthood without choosing its national leadership.
Responsibility for that prolonged failure rests heavily with the Palestinian leaders who have retained power throughout it.
Palestinians need accountable leadership, Israel needs reliable security
Palestinians deserve the opportunity to replace their rulers peacefully. Israel also has an interest in credible Palestinian institutions that can maintain security, implement agreements, and exercise authority over armed factions.
Building such institutions requires sustained reform, enforceable rules, and leaders prepared to accept limits on their power.
Hamas’s victory in the 2006 legislative election and its subsequent violent takeover of Gaza must inform any discussion of another vote. The organization responsible for the October 7 massacre cannot acquire a legitimate claim to govern while retaining its terrorist infrastructure.
Its weapons threaten Israeli lives and the freedom of Palestinians to organize, campaign, and disagree.
Participation should therefore require renouncing terrorism, recognizing Israel, accepting existing agreements, and dismantling independent armed forces. These obligations must apply equally to every faction and be verified in practice.
Candidates running under alternative labels must face the same scrutiny when evidence establishes organizational ties to armed groups.
Eligibility rules should be published in advance and subject to independent review. Their enforcement must rest on documented conduct, with a fair appeal process protecting peaceful challengers from arbitrary exclusion by incumbents.
A credible election also requires an independent electoral commission, accessible voter registration, impartial courts, and protection for journalists and opposition candidates.
Voters must be able to criticize the Palestinian Authority without fear. Parties must commit to respecting the results and allowing future elections, including when their own hold on office is threatened.
Abbas must set clear reform deadlines ahead of September 2027 elections
Abbas should publish a timetable for those reforms, with deadlines that can be assessed before September 2027.
Preparations for polling and international monitoring should proceed alongside transparent public finances, scrutiny of security institutions, and action against incitement.
Public funds must be subject to safeguards preventing their use to reward or encourage terrorism.
These changes will face resistance from those whose influence depends on patronage, secrecy or coercion. International partners should make clear that another postponement carries political consequences.
Donors should condition support for governing institutions on measurable progress, with humanitarian assistance protected so ordinary Palestinians are spared the cost of their leaders’ failures.
Countries recognizing Palestine must demand accountable governance
Governments that have recognized a Palestinian state have a particular responsibility to insist on these standards. Their diplomatic commitments should be followed by scrutiny of how Palestinian institutions operate. Recognition creates no guarantee that a government respects its citizens, controls its territory, and intends to live peacefully alongside Israel.
Israel has responsibilities too. Its government should work toward practical arrangements for voting, election observers, and necessary movement, consistent with protecting Israeli citizens.
Specific restrictions should be justified by concrete security needs and reviewed when circumstances change. Facilitating credible Palestinian government can serve Israel’s long-term interests.
Jerusalem voting arrangements will require careful negotiation. Security concerns must be addressed through workable procedures, while Palestinian leaders must demonstrate that they are pursuing solutions in good faith. Progress on electoral independence, financial transparency, and political freedoms can begin immediately, even while difficult logistical questions remain unresolved.
The new election date should carry obligations that can be checked throughout the coming year. Abbas should face regular public scrutiny over what has changed, which commitments remain unmet, and who is responsible. Palestinian civil society deserves access to that information and space to challenge official explanations.
Palestinians need accountable leadership, and Israelis need reliable security.
Elections conducted within a reformed political system can advance both interests. The months ahead should be used to establish the freedoms, safeguards, and enforceable commitments that give a future vote meaning.

Tens of thousands of pro-Palestinian demonstrators turned out across Europe on Saturday, as activists marked three years of war in Gaza with rallies and marches in cities from London to Rome and Berlin.

The United States had the highest number of expected demonstrations across the two-week period, followed by Spain, Britain and Australia.
In the UK on Saturday, thousands of demonstrators marched through London, wearing keffiyehs and waving Palestinian flags. “Today we’re marching for Palestine in London to mark three years of Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people and demand our government go further to sanction Israel for its crimes. Britain must stop arming Israel now,” the group wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Footage posted by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign showed thousands of demonstrators marching through the British capital, waving Palestinian flags.
Police, counter-protestors present
Local police imposed restrictions on the march to “minimize the risk of serious disruption to communities.” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Carl Galvin was quoted in British media as saying that “Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”
He added that police would use their powers to require anyone deliberately concealing their identity with a face covering in the protest area to remove it.
British media also reported that a counter-protest organized by Stop the Hate was taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside the Metropolitan Police headquarters.

'From the river to the sea' chanted throughout Italy, Europe
Footage from Rome, Bologna and Turin showed thousands of protesters marching with signs and Palestinian flags. Some signs read, “From the river to the sea,” while another large banner read, “Against genocide, war, Zionism, and all complicity.”
Farther north, more than 1,000 demonstrators took part in a protest in Berlin, according to Die Welt. The demonstrators gathered outside the Chancellery in the afternoon, chanting “Free Palestine, free Palestine” and “F–k you, Israel.”
A smaller counterdemonstration took place across from the march, with participants waving Israeli flags and calling to “Free Berlin from Hamas,” the newspaper reported.
Berlin police had announced plans to deploy approximately 1,400 officers, including personnel from several other German states and the Federal Police.
In Switzerland, around 1,000 people gathered in Zurich to protest the war in Gaza. Swiss public broadcaster SWI reported that demonstrators observed a minute of silence during the march, which took place under a substantial police presence.
More demonstrations are expected around the world in the coming days to mark three years of war in Gaza. Several protests are scheduled to take place across the United States over the next 24 hours, while large demonstrations are expected in Australia on Sunday. A series of protests is also planned in Latin America in the coming days.
Earlier this week, the third anniversary of Oct. 7, 2023, was marked, commemorating the day Hamas led an invasion into southern Israel, killing approximately 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. Large pro-Palestinian demonstrations were held around the world that day and in the following days, including at numerous locations across the United States.
